Oki Electric Industry’s dual-biasing approach applies substrate bias to PMOS load transistors and source bias to NMOS drive transistors during standby, suppressing both leakage channels simultaneously without disrupting active-mode performance.

## Power Gating, Virtual Power Rails, and Dynamic Voltage Reduction

Power gating—inserting switch transistors (header PMOS or footer NMOS) between the supply rail and the SRAM cell array—is the most aggressive architectural approach to leakage reduction. By turning off the switch transistor during standby, the leakage path through inactive cells is interrupted. However, naive implementation creates floating ground nodes that degrade static noise margin, a trade-off that has driven significant innovation in virtual rail architectures.

IBM’s *Method and Apparatus for Reducing Leakage Current in an Integrated Circuit* (2008) and its counterpart (2009) introduce the virtual voltage rail concept: one or two virtual power control devices (header and/or footer transistors) are placed on the supply and ground paths of the SRAM array. Sensing elements monitor the virtual rail voltage and regulate it to a specific potential, thereby limiting—rather than completely eliminating—current through the cell. This avoids the floating ground node problem inherent to simple gated-ground designs while still achieving significant leakage reduction.

IBM’s *System and Method for Integrating Dynamic Leakage Reduction with Write-Assisted SRAM Architecture* (2009/2010) combines dynamic leakage reduction with write assistance in a single architecture. Power line selection circuitry per column converts the standard cell supply voltage to a lower voltage for unselected sub-arrays (suppressing leakage) and to an even lower voltage for cells being written (improving writability). This unified approach eliminates a common conflict between leakage reduction—which raises Vt or reduces voltage—and write assist, which also requires voltage reduction, enabling both benefits simultaneously. According to [the Semiconductor Industry Association](https://www.semiconductors.org), power consumption in memory arrays is among the top engineering constraints for advanced SoC design.

TSMC’s *Circuit for Memory Write Data Operations* (2017) implements a pulsed dynamic low cell voltage (LCV) circuit with configurable voltage levels and timing adjustments. By transiently reducing the cell supply during write operations and ensuring rapid recovery, the design minimises DC leakage while improving write margin. The patent explicitly identifies “significantly reduced DC leakage” and PVT-awareness among its advantages, directly addressing challenges at sub-14nm nodes.

ARM’s *Cache Power Management* (2021) introduces a system-level leakage management strategy: individual cache banks are powered down dynamically based on a real-time comparison of cache hit bandwidth against an equivalent memory bandwidth representing the leakage power cost. When hit bandwidth falls below the effective leakage power, the powered fraction of the cache is reduced. This per-bank power gating approach treats leakage as an economic variable, extending the concept from cell-level to architecture-level power management.

📌

**Key finding: PVT-adaptive minimum retention voltage**

Nanjing Low-Power Chip Technology Research Institute (2024) uses a MOS transistor voltage divider chain to generate a reference voltage that tracks temperature and global process variation. This reference dynamically adjusts the SRAM array supply in sleep mode, enabling the array to retain data at the minimum possible voltage under any PVT condition. An alternating power supply scheme ensures data retention remains stable even at extremely low retention voltages.

Etron Technology’s *Low Power SRAM Standby Repair Structure* (2009) addresses a distinct leakage source: defective SRAM cells in production silicon. By controlling a VSS enable (VSSEN) signal, NMOS transistors gate the VSS path to faulty cells; in normal mode, the path to defective cells is cut off to eliminate their standby current contribution. This post-repair leakage isolation reduces total chip standby power from manufacturing defects—a technique increasingly relevant as process variation grows at sub-3nm nodes.

## System and Architecture-Level Strategies: ECC, Sub-Threshold Cells, and CIM

Beyond device and circuit techniques, several patents address SRAM leakage reduction at the system or architecture level—exploiting error correction, non-uniform cache design, alternative cell topologies, and compute-in-memory integration to achieve leakage levels unreachable by device engineering alone.

### ECC-Assisted Voltage Reduction

Fudan University’s *Low Power Static Memory SRAM* (2016) exploits error-correcting code (ECC) to permit aggressive supply voltage reduction in standby mode. A voltage regulator steps down array VDD incrementally; after each reduction step, the ECC circuit reads the array and corrects any upset bits before the voltage is lowered further. This iterative process drives the array to the minimum viable retention voltage for each PVT condition, suppressing leakage to the lowest achievable level while maintaining data integrity through ECC correction on wakeup. The approach is validated by research published through [Nature](https://www.nature.com) Electronics on ultra-low-voltage SRAM operation.

### Non-Uniform Cache Associativity

Fujitsu’s *Reducing Power Consumption of Cache* (2007) introduces non-uniform cache associativity architecture: rather than assigning the same number of ways to every cache set, the design optimises the number of ways per set based on access frequency. Sets needing fewer ways have some ways powered down, reducing the active and leakage power of those bank portions. Code placement optimisation—reducing sequential cache-line streaming that forces all ways active—complements this hardware technique.

### 5T and 8T Cell Architectures

Qualcomm’s *Low Power 5T SRAM with Improved Stability and Reduced Bit Cell Size* (2016) addresses the root cause of leakage instability by using symmetric-sized cross-coupled inverters in a 5-transistor topology with a single access transistor. The symmetric design reduces sensitivity to Vt mismatch across process variations—a key concern at sub-3nm nodes where transistor variation is severe—while control logic dynamically shifts the supply voltage between read and write operations to optimise both SNM and write margin without increasing leakage.

The Institute of Microelectronics of the Chinese Academy of Sciences’ *Sub-Threshold SRAM Memory Cell* (2015) demonstrates that operating SRAM at sub-threshold or near-threshold supply voltages dramatically reduces both dynamic and static power. The 8T cell architecture with a dedicated pre-discharge read circuit avoids read-disturb issues that plague 6T sub-threshold designs, while the reduced voltage swing on internal nodes cuts leakage current proportionally. Xi’an Jiaotong University’s *Column-Interleaved SRAM Structure for Sub-Threshold Operation* (2013) implements a latch-type write driver that stabilises half-selected cells during write operations in sub-threshold arrays, enabling column-interleaving to reduce soft error rates and allow sense amplifier reuse—improving area efficiency without adding leakage overhead.

### Compute-in-Memory Leakage Recycling

Tianjin University’s *Low Power Low Leakage SRAM for Compute-in-Memory Chips* (2020) targets compute-in-memory (CIM) architectures where both write disturbance and leakage from half-selected cells are major concerns. A ground voltage elevation module raises the VSS of selected columns during write operations to boost write threshold voltage, while a bit-line charge recovery module recaptures the leakage charge from half-selected cells’ bit lines to drive the ground elevation—effectively recycling leakage energy. This approach is particularly relevant as AI inference workloads increasingly rely on CIM arrays, a trend tracked by [WIPO](https://www.wipo.int) in its annual technology trend reports on AI hardware.

## SRAM cache power leakage below 3nm — key questions answered

As transistor feature sizes shrink, sub-threshold leakage current grows exponentially with decreasing threshold voltage. At below-3nm nodes, even 100 picoamperes of leakage per cell aggregates to 100 milliamperes across a billion-cell array. Multiple leakage mechanisms—sub-threshold, gate, GIDL, and junction leakage—become co-dominant simultaneously, making single-mechanism solutions insufficient. For IoT and mobile SoCs that spend the majority of their time idle, SRAM cache arrays represent the largest share of standby leakage on-chip.

The most established approach is the use of higher threshold voltage (high-Vt) transistors in the memory cell array, achieved via thicker gate oxides or high-k dielectric gate oxides. Since off-state sub-threshold current decays exponentially with increasing Vt, deploying high-Vt devices in storage cells—while reserving low-Vt devices for performance-critical peripheral circuits—offers a favourable leakage-performance trade-off. IBM pioneered this multi-threshold device strategy for SRAM, establishing it as the foundational technique adopted by subsequent innovators including TSMC, Samsung, and Renesas.

Body biasing applies a reverse or forward bias to the transistor well (substrate), modulating threshold voltage through the body effect. By applying a reverse body bias (RBB) during standby, Vt is raised, exponentially reducing sub-threshold leakage. Oki Electric Industry demonstrated a dual-biasing approach addressing both PMOS and NMOS leakage channels simultaneously. However, for processes below 90nm, large parasitic capacitance and resistance of well nodes make rapid Vt switching impractical for high-speed SRAMs with 1 ns access times, as acknowledged by Renesas Technology (2008).

A virtual power rail inserts one or two power control devices (header PMOS or footer NMOS transistors) on the supply and ground paths of the SRAM array. Sensing elements monitor the virtual rail voltage and regulate it to a specific potential, limiting current through the cell during standby. IBM’s approach avoids the floating ground node problem inherent to simple gated-ground designs—which degrades static noise margin—while still achieving significant leakage reduction. The virtual rail method provides more controlled operation than complete power cutoff, preserving cell data throughout standby.

Fudan University’s approach (2016) exploits error-correcting code (ECC) to permit aggressive supply voltage reduction in standby mode. A voltage regulator steps down array VDD incrementally; after each reduction step, the ECC circuit reads the array and corrects any upset bits before the voltage is lowered further. This iterative process drives the array to the minimum viable retention voltage for each PVT condition, suppressing leakage to the lowest achievable level while maintaining data integrity through ECC correction on wakeup.

# Design of Stable 10T FinFET SRAM Cell for Operation in Sub-Threshold Regime

## Ajjay S. Gaadhe, Yuvraj V. Parkale

## **Citation :**

Ajjay S. Gaadhe, Yuvraj V. Parkale, "Design of Stable 10T FinFET SRAM Cell for Operation in Sub-Threshold Regime," *International Journal of Electrical and Electronics Engineering*, vol. 12, no. 6, pp. 206-213, 2025. *Crossref*, https://doi.org/10.14445/23488379/IJEEE-V12I6P118

## **Abstract**

The growing prevalence of portable electronic devices has led to an increased reliance on static random-access memory (SRAM) as a critical element in contemporary VLSI circuit design. To meet the rising demand for energy-efficient operation, sub-threshold SRAM design has gained attention for its ability to reduce power consumption. However, this approach presents challenges in maintaining adequate stability. This work investigates the development and evaluation of a 10-transistor (10T) FinFET SRAM bit cell to enhance stability. The paper provides complete design parameters along with an analysis of fin dimensions because they control the electrical performance in 10T SRAM cells. When properly set, fin width and height configurations allow drive strength and leakage balance, leading to increased noise margin performance. The proposed fin configuration and a separate read and write path establish an effective breakdown between read and write operations. The separation between read and write operations and control of drive strength of transistors enhances the stability of the entire system by preventing read disturbances when writing occurs, as well as write disturbances during reading. All simulations were executed through the Microwind 3.9 environment operated with 14 nm FinFET process technology. The results indicate that the 10T SRAM cell demonstrates significantly enhanced stability compared to the conventional CMOS and 6-transistor (6T) FinFET design. In particular, the 10T cell exhibits improvements of 65% in Read Static Noise Margin (RSNM) compared to conventional CMOS technology, maintaining the Write Static Noise Margin (WSNM) with incremental improvement. Besides, 10T FinFET cell demonstrates 4% improvement in RSNM and WSNM compared t 6T FinFET at the 14 nm technology node. These findings suggest that careful device sizing and architectural modifications can enhance SRAM reliability in advanced technology nodes.

VLSI, Microelectronics, FinFET, Write ability, Read stability, Static noise margin, Power.

args.key_excerpts: The paper provides complete design parameters along with an analysis of fin dimensions because they control the electrical performance in 10T SRAM cells., The results indicate that the 10T SRAM cell demonstrates significantly enhanced stability compared to the conventional CMOS and 6-transistor (6T) FinFET design., the 10T cell exhibits improvements of 65% in Read Static Noise Margin (RSNM) compared to conventional CMOS technology, 10T FinFET cell demonstrates 4% improvement in RSNM and WSNM compared to 6T FinFET at the 14 nm technology node., All simulations were executed through the Microwind 3.9 environment operated with 14 nm FinFET process technology.
args.summary: This webpage presents a research article titled "Design of Stable 10T FinFET SRAM Cell for Operation in Sub-Threshold Regime" by Ajjay S. Gaadhe and Yuvraj V. Parkale, published in the International Journal of Electrical and Electronics Engineering (vol. 12, no. 6, pp. 206-213, 2025). The study focuses on developing a 10-transistor (10T) FinFET SRAM bit cell to enhance stability in sub-threshold operation, which is critical for energy-efficient portable electronic devices. The authors analyze fin dimensions and propose a configuration with separate read and write paths to prevent read/write disturbances. Simulations were performed using Microwind 3.9 with 14 nm FinFET process technology. Key results show that the 10T cell achieves 65% improvement in Read Static Noise Margin (RSNM) compared to conventional CMOS technology, and 4% improvement in both RSNM and Write Static Noise Margin (WSNM) compared to 6T FinFET at the 14 nm node.

## Abstract

As the scaling of conventional SRAM faces fundamental physical and area limitations, novel device architectures are essential for next-generation computing. This paper proposes and comprehensively evaluates a novel 3-Tier 6T-SRAM cell based on a vertically stacked Complementary FET (CFET) architecture that incorporates 2D Transition Metal Dichalcogenides (TMDs) as channel materials. The proposed 3-Tier CFET architecture demonstrates a significant cell area reduction of approximately 29.5% compared with the Conventional 2-Tier structure. This miniaturization lowers the internal-node capacitance by 13–22%, yielding markedly better write performance (e.g. >39% lower write energy). By systematically adjusting the nanosheet stack ratios (PU: PD: PG), we precisely control the trade-offs between stability and speed. The optimized design (2P4N + 3N\_Access) improves read-access time by 11.9% while maintaining robust write characteristics. This synergistic optimization results in a 24.9% reduction in the Energy-Delay Product (EDP), indicating improved overall efficiency. These findings validate that the strategic integration of a 3-Tier CFET architecture with 2D TMDs channels provides a robust pathway to high-density, high-performance, energy-efficient SRAM for future high-performance computing and low-power mobile application.

## Introduction

Static Random-Access Memory (SRAM) is a critical component in modern computing systems, serving as cache memory, buffers, and registers that determine overall system performance and power efficiency. While the importance of high-density and high-performance on-chip SRAM is growing in state-of-the-art AI accelerators, the frequent data fetching between processing units and memory has become a major bottleneck that dominates the total system energy consumption[1](#ref-CR1 "Sadaf, M. Notably, the industry has observed an unprecedented slowdown in SRAM cell-area scaling since the 3 nm process node[8](/articles/s41598-026-37881-5#ref-CR8 "Liu, H. H. et al. CFET SRAM DTCO, interconnect Guideline, and benchmark for CMOS scaling. IEEE Trans. Electron. Devices. 70, 883–890 (2023)."),[9](/articles/s41598-026-37881-5#ref-CR9 "Liu, H. H. et al. CFET SRAM with Double-Sided interconnect design and DTCO benchmark. IEEE Trans. Electron. Devices. 70, 5099–5106 (2023).").

To overcome this density limit, the Complementary FET (CFET) architecture has emerged. The primary advantage of CFET technology is the vertical stacking of NMOS and PMOS transistors, which eliminates the physical spacing constraints between them. This allows for a silicon footprint reduction by up to 50% for a 6T-SRAM cell compared to FinFET or GAAFET-based SRAM cells, serving as a key driver for dramatically increasing SRAM density[10](#ref-CR10 "Shahin, S. et al. CFET beyond 3 nm: SRAM reliability under Design-Time and Run-Time variability. (2025). 
                  https://doi.org/10.36227/techrxiv.174140866.67003560/v1
                  
                "),[11](#ref-CR11 "Shon, M., Lee, J. & Yu, S. 3D Digital Compute-in-Memory Benchmark with A5 CFET Technology. In 2024 IEEE Asia Pacific Conference on Circuits and Systems (APCCAS) 16–19 (IEEE, Taipei, Taiwan, 2024). 
                  https://doi.org/10.1109/APCCAS62602.2024.10808252
                  
                "),[12](/articles/s41598-026-37881-5#ref-CR12 "Lee, J. et al. Monolithic 3D 6T-SRAM based on newly designed gate and Source/Drain bottom contact schemes. IEEE Access. 9, 138192–138199 (2021).").

However, Si-based CFET structures present several limitations. First, as NMOS and PMOS transistors are vertically stacked, the small n-p separation distance induces significant parasitic capacitance. Furthermore, the increased device height leads to taller vias connecting upper-level signal lines to lower-level devices, increasing parasitic resistance. This exacerbates the overall RC delay, which can degrade circuit speed and increase power consumption[7](/articles/s41598-026-37881-5#ref-CR7 "Lu, Y. C., Huang, J. K., Chao, K. Y., Li, L. J. & Hu, V. P. H. Projected performance of Si- and 2D-material-based SRAM circuits ranging from 16 Nm to 1 Nm technology nodes. Nat. Nanotechnol. 19, 1066–1072 (2024)."),[13](/articles/s41598-026-37881-5#ref-CR13 "Liu, C. et al. 2D Materials-Based static Random‐Access memory. Adv. Mater. 34, 2107894 (2022)."),[14](/articles/s41598-026-37881-5#ref-CR14 "Hu, V. P. H. et al. Energy-Efficient monolithic 3-D SRAM cell with BEOL MoS2 fets for SoC scaling. IEEE Trans. Electron. Devices. 67, 4216–4221 (2020)."). Second, the scalability of Si-based transistors is fundamentally limited by the physical constraints of reducing channel thickness. Quantum confinement and surface roughness scattering effects that occur when reducing the Si channel thickness below 3 nm cause severe mobility degradation and increased leakage current[15](#ref-CR15 "Liu, Y. et al. Promises and prospects of two-dimensional transistors. Nature 591, 43–53 (2021)."),[16](#ref-CR16 "Kumar, V. P. & Panda, D. K. Review—Next generation 2D material molybdenum disulfide (MoS2): Properties, applications and challenges. ECS J. Solid State Sci. Technol. 11, 033012 (2022)."),[17](#ref-CR17 "Fiori, G. et al. Electronics based on two-dimensional materials. Nat. Nanotech. 9, 768–779 (2014)."),[18](/articles/s41598-026-37881-5#ref-CR18 "Miró, P., Audiffred, M. & Heine, T. An atlas of two-dimensional materials. Chem. Soc. Rev. 43, 6537–6554 (2014)."). Finally, fabricating high-quality Si channels requires a high thermal budget, which can degrade the performance of underlying devices during 3D vertical integration[13](/articles/s41598-026-37881-5#ref-CR13 "Liu, C. et al. 2D Materials-Based static Random‐Access memory. Adv. Mater. 34, 2107894 (2022).").

Beyond these material-level challenges, the conventional 2-Tier CFET architecture introduces its own set of structural constraints that hinder performance optimization. A standard 6T-SRAM cell consists of Pull-Up (PU), Pull-Down (PD), and Pass-Gate (PG) transistors, each requiring different drive strengths for optimal performance in terms of stability, speed, and power[19](/articles/s41598-026-37881-5#ref-CR19 "Agal, A. & Krishan, B. 6T SRAM Cell: Design And Analysis. 4 (2014)."). However, the Conventional 2-Tier CFET 6T-SRAM architecture has a structural limitation wherein the PD and PG transistors are grouped in the same tier, making it difficult to independently optimize the three transistor types according to their functional requirements.

To simultaneously overcome the material and structural limitations faced by existing Si-based 2-Tier CFETs, this work proposes an integrated strategy with two key innovations: (1) replacing the channel material with 2D Transition Metal Dichalcogenides (TMDs) and (2) advancing the device architecture to a 3-Tier structure.

First, introducing 2D TMDs as the channel material resolves the 3D integration limits imposed by the physical thickness of Si channels. The atomically thin nature of 2D TMDs (~ 0.7 nm) allows for vertical stacking without significantly increasing the total device height, leading to a reduction in parasitic capacitance and resistance. Furthermore, the thin body maximizes the electrostatic gate control over the channel, effectively suppressing the Short Channel Effect (SCE). The excellent interface properties, which are free of dangling bonds, and high carrier mobility further support the implementation of high-performance channels[20](/articles/s41598-026-37881-5#ref-CR20 "Lee, J., Jung, H., Jin, D. & Jeon, J. Exploring optimal TMDC multi-channel GAA-FET architectures at sub-1nm nodes. J. Sci.: Adv. Mater. Devices 10, 100931 (2025)."). Finally, since 2D TMDs materials can be processed at relatively low temperatures[21](/articles/s41598-026-37881-5#ref-CR21 "Zhu, J. et al. Low-thermal-budget synthesis of monolayer molybdenum disulfide for silicon back-end-of-line integration on a 200 mm platform. Nat. Nanotechnol. 18, 456–463 (2023)."), multi-layer stacks of 3-Tiers or more can be stacked without causing thermal damage to the underlying devices, a decisive advantage for vertical integration. Recent advancements in 2D TMDs have opened new opportunities for promising candidates of future low-power and high-reliability SRAM memories. The TMDFETs have demonstrated superior characteristics such as improved static noise margins, reduced leakage power, and enhanced robustness against process variations compared to conventional CMOS technology[22](/articles/s41598-026-37881-5#ref-CR22 "Abbasian, E., Gholipour, M. & Izadinasab, F. Performance evaluation of GNRFET and TMDFET devices in static random access memory cells design. Circuit Theory Apps. 49, 3630–3652 (2021)."),[23](/articles/s41598-026-37881-5#ref-CR23 "Abbasian, E., Birla, S. & Gholipour, M. A 9T high-stable and Low-Energy Half-Select-Free SRAM cell design using TMDFETs. Analog Integr. Circ. Sig Process. 112, 141–149 (2022).").

Concurrently, the introduction of the 3-Tier architecture enables the independent performance optimization of the PU, PD, and PG transistors. Unlike the 2-Tier structure, this work adopts a 3-Tier CFET architecture that vertically separates the two PU/PD CFET inverters and the two PG NMOS transistors. This structural separation enables unparalleled design flexibility by allowing the number of nanosheet stacks to be freely adjusted to tune the effective channel width (Weff​) of each transistor. This presents a new design paradigm for precisely optimizing stability, access time, and power consumption without complex assist circuits.

The proposed 3-Tier architecture provides significant advantages in integration density, leading to an approximate 29.5% reduction in bitcell area compared to the Conv. 2-Tier CFET 6T-SRAM structure. This structural miniaturization further decreases internal node (Q) capacitance by 13–22%, leading to significantly improved write performance. Consequently, all 3-Tier models exhibit more than a 42% reduction in write energy, with the write-specialized (2P3N) model achieving over 50.3% energy savings. Moreover, by precisely adjusting nanosheet stack ratios, we effectively balance the stability-speed trade-off, and our final proposed design (3-Tier 2P4N+3N\_Access) delivers the fastest Read Access Time (RAT) with an 11.9% improvement while simultaneously reducing the Energy-Delay Product (EDP) by 24.9%, ensuring an optimized and well-balanced overall performance.

The objective of this study is to quantitatively evaluate the advantages of the 3-Tier CFET SRAM over the Conv. 2-Tier structure in terms of performance, cell stability, and energy efficiency, and to provide a design guide for an optimized 3-Tier cell based on parasitic RC analysis. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: The section "[Simulation environment](/articles/s41598-026-37881-5#Sec2)", describes the device-to-circuit simulation framework, TCAD/SPICE modeling methodology, and the proposed 3-Tier structure. The section "[The results and discussion](/articles/s41598-026-37881-5#Sec5)", provides a comprehensive comparative analysis of parasitic RC, Static Noise Margin (SNM), Dynamic Access Times (RAT/WAT), and Energy Efficiency (EDP). Finally, the section "[Conclusion](/articles/s41598-026-37881-5#Sec12)", summarizes the key findings of this work and discusses the potentials and technical challenges of the proposed 3-Tier architecture as a next-generation SRAM.

## Simulation environment

### Device architecture, layout and conceptual fabrication flow

To verify the feasibility and analyze the electrical characteristics of the proposed 3D device structures, we used the Synopsys Sentaurus TCAD tool as the core simulation framework.

The standard 6T-SRAM cell, which serves as the foundation of this research, is depicted in the circuit diagram in Fig. [1](/articles/s41598-026-37881-5#Fig1)(b). The cell consists of two primary components. The core data storage unit is a latch formed by two cross-coupled CMOS inverters, composed of PU1/PD1 and PU2/PD2 transistors, respectively. This latch structure stably stores one bit of data on two complementary internal nodes (Q and QB). Data access is controlled by two Pass-Gate transistors (PG1 and PG2), which are gated by the Word Line (WL). When the WL signal is asserted, these transistors turn on, connecting the Q, QB to the external Bit Lines (BL, BLB) to enable read and write operations.

The two SRAM structures proposed in this work maintain this fundamental 6T-SRAM operation principle but are based on a next-generation CFET architecture with vertically stacked transistors. The 3D structures, shown in Fig. [1](/articles/s41598-026-37881-5#Fig1)(a), were designed based on the 1 nm technology node specifications from the International Roadmap for Devices and Systems (IRDS) 2023[24](/articles/s41598-026-37881-5#ref-CR24 "2023 IRDS Chairman’s Editorial (2023)."). A key design rule, the Contacted Poly Pitch (CPP), was set to 38 nm to ensure alignment with future technology nodes. Furthermore, to mitigate the parasitic overheads, a double-sided interconnect design was adopted. This architecture employs a Backside Power Delivery Network (BSPDN), which places the WL and BL signal lines on the Frontside while connecting the VDD and VSS power lines directly to the transistors from the Backside. This approach reduces crosstalk and optimizes the power delivery path[25](/articles/s41598-026-37881-5#ref-CR25 "Lee, S. et al. Breakthrough Design Technology Co-optimization using BSPDN and Standard Cell Variants for Maximizing Block-level PPA. In 2023 IEEE Symposium on VLSI Technology and Circuits (VLSI Technology and Circuits) 1–2 (IEEE, Kyoto, Japan, 2023). 
                  https://doi.org/10.23919/VLSITechnologyandCir57934.2023.10185417
                  
                "),[26](/articles/s41598-026-37881-5#ref-CR26 "Fukutome, H. et al. Demonstration of Logic-Block Performance-Power-Area Gain by 1st Generation Back Side Power Delivery Network for SoC and HPC Applications Beyond 2 nm Node. In 2025 IEEE Custom Integrated Circuits Conference (CICC) 1–6 (IEEE, Boston, MA, USA, 2025). 
                  https://doi.org/10.1109/CICC63670.2025.10983110
                  
                "). These design criteria were applied equally to the FEOL (Front-End-Of-Line) stage of both the 2D TMDs Conv. (2-Tier) CFET 6T-SRAM and the proposed 2D TMDs 3-Tier CFET 6T-SRAM to allow for a clear comparison of performance based on structural differences. In respect to our Conv. 2-Tier (8T) and proposed 3-Tier (9T) CFET architectures, an important consideration is the presence of surplus, unconnected transistors when implementing a standard 6T-SRAM cell. Specifically, the 2-Tier configuration leaves two PMOS transistors unused, whereas the 3-Tier configuration results in one PMOS and two NMOS transistors remaining floating. The key geometric parameters and metal design rules used in the simulations are detailed in Tables [1](/articles/s41598-026-37881-5#Tab1) and [2](/articles/s41598-026-37881-5#Tab2), respectively.

The layouts of the resulting 3D devices are presented in Fig. [1](/articles/s41598-026-37881-5#Fig1)(c) and (d). In the Conv. 2-Tier structure, PU and PD transistors are arranged horizontally, resulting in a cell width of 2 x CPP = 76 nm. In the proposed 3-Tier structure, the PU, PD, and PG transistors are all stacked vertically, leading to a cell width of 3 x CPP = 114 nm. The bitcell area is calculated using the formula: Area= Cell Height(HCell) × Cell Width(WCell). The 3-Tier CFET 6T-SRAM designed in this study has an area of 8,892 nm² (78 nm x 114 nm), which is a 29.5% reduction compared to the Conv. (2-Tier) CFET 6T-SRAM area of 12,616 nm² (166 nm x 76 nm). This clearly demonstrates that the proposed 3-Tier structure is highly effective at improving integration density and overcoming the area scaling challenges inherent to SRAM. Notably, the achieved cell area is competitive against that of the state-of-the-art Si-based CFET via-optimized 6T-SRAM[27](/articles/s41598-026-37881-5#ref-CR27 "Lee, J., Ahn, S., Lee, J., Jeon, J. & Via-Optimized,. CFET 6T SRAM: Performance, stability, manufacturability, and scalability. IEEE Trans. Electron. Devices 
                  https://doi.org/10.1109/TED.2025.3637774
                  
                 (2025)."), and a detailed comparison is provided in Supplementary Table [S1](/articles/s41598-026-37881-5#MOESM1) online.

P. H. et al. Energy-Efficient monolithic 3-D SRAM cell with BEOL MoS2 fets for SoC scaling. IEEE Trans. Electron. Devices. 67, 4216–4221 (2020)."),[30](#ref-CR30 "Mortelmans, W. et al. In 2024 IEEE Symposium on VLSI Technology and Circuits (VLSI Technology and Circuits) 1–2 (IEEE, Honolulu, HI, USA, 2024). 
                  https://doi.org/10.1109/VLSITechnologyandCir46783.2024.10631395
                  
                "),[31](#ref-CR31 "Chung, Y. Y. et al. Monolayer-MoS2 Stacked Nanosheet Channel with C-type Metal Contact. In 2023 International Electron Devices Meeting (IEDM) 1–4 (IEEE, San Francisco, CA, USA, 2023). 
                  https://doi.org/10.1109/IEDM45741.2023.10413837
                  
                "),[32](/articles/s41598-026-37881-5#ref-CR32 "Chung, Y. Y. et al. Stacked Channel Transistors with 2D Materials: An Integration Perspective. In IEEE International Electron Devices Meeting (IEDM) 1–4 (IEEE, San Francisco, CA, USA, 2024). 
                  https://doi.org/10.1109/IEDM50854.2024.10873421
                  
                "). A critical aspect of the stacked structure is the protection and mechanical support of the 2D TMDs channels, which are vulnerable to contamination and physical damage during fabrication. To ensure structural integrity, each channel is encapsulated by an Al₂O₃ Protection Layer, which offers excellent interface properties and a high dielectric constant. Furthermore, the channels are separated from each other by a Sacrificial (SAC) dielectric layer. This SAC layer serves the dual purpose of reserving space for subsequent gate formation and protecting the TMDs material during the channel release process. Finally, the gate electrode is designed with TiN metal within a High-k Metal Gate (HKMG) stack to minimize gate leakage current and enable stable control of the threshold voltage.

The step-by-step process flow is as follows:

First Tier (Fig. [2](/articles/s41598-026-37881-5#Fig2)(a)): The process begins with the formation of the bottom-most transistor (the PU device), including its channel, source/drain regions, Middle-of-Line (MOL) metal interconnects and Middle Dielectric Isolation (MDI). Second Tier (Fig. [2](/articles/s41598-026-37881-5#Fig2)(b)): The sacrificial and channel material layers are sequentially deposited on top of the first tier. Subsequently, a Replacement Metal Gate (RMG) process is performed. The sacrificial layers are selectively etched to release the protected channel stack. The resulting cavity is then filled with the gate dielectric and gate metal. The gate structure is formed along the sidewalls of the active region (the nanosheet stack), and a sidewall spacer is deposited to define the physical shape of the gate electrode, provide insulation, and suppress gate leakage and SCEs. This Channel-First and Gate-Last approach protects the critical gate dielectric from potential damage during subsequent fabrications, enhancing device reliability. At this stage, Dual Work-function metal engineering is applied to set the appropriate threshold voltages for the PMOS and NMOS devices, respectively. Third Tier and BEOL (Fig. [2](/articles/s41598-026-37881-5#Fig2)(c)): After completing the lower-level interconnects such as the Buried Power Rail (BPR) and vias at the M0 level, the third tier (containing the PD device) is fabricated using the same process as the second tier. Finally, the full device is completed by processing the Frontside and Backside Back-End-of-Line (BEOL) layers to connect the signal and power lines.

### Device-to-circuit simulation framework

To comprehensively evaluate the performance of the proposed 2D TMDs-based 3-Tier CFET 6T-SRAM and compare it with the Conv. 2-Tier structure, a hierarchical simulation workflow was established. This workflow encompasses the entire process from device-level physical modeling to circuit-level performance analysis. As summarized in the flowchart in Fig. [3](/articles/s41598-026-37881-5#Fig3)(a), the framework consists of four key stages: (1) 3D Structure Design, (2) TCAD Device Simulation, (3) Parasitic RC Extraction, and (4) SPICE Circuit Simulation.

The initial stage of the simulation involves designing the virtual 3D device structures. As shown in Fig. [1](/articles/s41598-026-37881-5#Fig1)(a), two primary architectures were designed for comparative analysis: the Conv. 2-Tier CFET 6T-SRAM, where the PD and PG transistors are arranged horizontally, and the proposed 3-Tier CFET 6T-SRAM, which features a vertical stack of PU, PD, and PG transistors.

To obtain accurate and reliable simulation results, the physical behavior and electrical characteristics of each transistor were simulated using the Sentaurus Device tool, following a systematic process of material property definition, physics-based model setup, and experimental data calibration.

First, to ensure the reliability of the physics-based models, a calibration process was performed against measured data from actual 2D GAA-FET devices fabricated by IMEC[33](/articles/s41598-026-37881-5#ref-CR33 "Xi, F. et al. High-Performance Monolayer-2D Stacked Nanosheet FETs with High ION ~ 451 µA/µm and ION /IOFF > 109.                 "). As shown in Fig. [3](/articles/s41598-026-37881-5#Fig3)(b), the simulation parameters were systematically tuned to achieve a high degree of correlation between the measured current-voltage (I-V) characteristics and the TCAD simulation results, thereby ensuring the predictive accuracy of the models.

To achieve this high level of accuracy, material properties were carefully defined. Key parameters for the MoS₂ and WSe₂ channels, such as bandgap, electron affinity, effective mass, and permittivity, were defined based on Density Functional Theory (DFT) calculation results. Notably, to accurately model the anisotropic nature of 2D materials, where electrical properties differ depending on the crystal direction, distinct permittivity values were applied for the in-plane and out-of-plane directions. The key material parameters used in the simulation are detailed in Table [3](/articles/s41598-026-37881-5#Tab3).

The carrier transport phenomena within the 2D nanosheet channels were modeled using a combination of physics-based models. The fundamental charge carrier behavior was described using the Drift-Diffusion transport model. To account for the various scattering phenomena that occur in a realistic device environment, a comprehensive mobility model was implemented. The Thin Layer Inversion and Accumulation Mobility model was used to reflect surface roughness scattering, 2D Coulomb scattering, and phonon scattering within the thin-film channel. Additionally, the High-Field Saturation model was applied to simulate the velocity saturation effects that occur under high electric fields.

With the calibrated model, performance optimization was conducted by varying the number of nanosheet stacks for each transistor in the 3-Tier SRAM structure from two to four. Modifying the number of stacks not only alters the device characteristics by changing the external and channel resistance[38](/articles/s41598-026-37881-5#ref-CR38 "Lee, J., Kim, J., Jung, H., Hong, S. & Jeon, J. Optimization of performance and self-heating effects through selective nanosheet thickness modulation in 4-stack nanosheet fets. J. Phys. D: Appl. Phys. 58, 245108 (2025)."), but also adjusts the relative strengths of the PU, PD, and PG transistors, thereby changing the SRAM’s operational characteristics. A total of four SRAM cell configurations were designed and simulated for this analysis. Conv. (3P3N): The baseline model based on the Conv. 2-Tier structure[39](/articles/s41598-026-37881-5#ref-CR39 "Ahn, S., Kim, S. K., Lee, J. & Jeon, J. SRAM bitcell Design and Characteristics in the three-stacked CFET structure for CMOS scaling. In 2025 International Technical Conference on Circuits/Systems, Computers, and Communications (ITC-CSCC) 1–4 (IEEE, Seoul, Korea, Republic of, 2025). 
                  https://doi.org/10.1109/ITC-CSCC66376.2025.11137737
                  
                "), with each of the PU, PD, and PG transistors having 3 nanosheet stacks (PU: PD: PG = 3:3:3). 3-Tier (3P3N): The proposed 3-Tier structure with the same 3:3:3 stack ratio as the conventional cell, designed to isolate the performance impact of the structural change. 3-Tier (2P3N): A model with a weakened PU transistor (PU: PD: PG = 2:3:3), aimed at improving the Write Margin and reducing write power. 3-Tier (2P4N+3N\_Access): The final proposed optimized model, based on the 2P3N structure but with a strengthened PD transistor (PU: PD: PG = 2:4:3), designed to maximize Read Speed.

The parasitic resistance and capacitance that arise from the device structure and interconnects were precisely modeled. The parasitic RC components for each 3D SRAM structure were extracted using the Synopsys Raphael tool. The extraction scope included the entire path[40](/articles/s41598-026-37881-5#ref-CR40 "Luo, Y. et al. Layout optimization of complementary FET 6T-SRAM cell based on a universal methodology using sensitivity with respect to parasitic - and -values. IEEE Trans. Electron. Devices 69, 6095–6101 (2022).") from the source/drain (S/D), gate, and via contacts at the M0 level to the WL and BL/BLB metal lines and interconnects at the M1 and M2 levels. The extracted RC values were used to create a segmented model for each node in the SRAM cell. Critically, for metal films thinner than 10 nm, the size effect, where surface and grain boundary scattering increases resistivity as the film thickness approaches the electron mean free path, becomes significant. As reported in studies by institutions[41](/articles/s41598-026-37881-5#ref-CR41 "Shin, K. W. et al. Graphene as New Conductors in Back-End-Of-Line: Non-Catalytic Growth, Doping, Integration and Reliability. In 2024 IEEE International Electron Devices Meeting (IEDM) 1–4 (IEEE, San Francisco, CA, USA, 2024). 
                  https://doi.org/10.1109/IEDM50854.2024.10872993
                  
                "), this physical phenomenon was incorporated into our simulation by applying thickness-dependent resistivity values for the metal layers, as specified in Table [3](/articles/s41598-026-37881-5#Tab3).

The final stage involved integrating the device-level physical characteristics into a circuit-level simulation using HSPICE to evaluate key performance metrics such as SNM, access time, and Energy-Delay Product (EDP). First, the I-V and C-V data obtained from the TCAD simulations for each transistor were used to extract BSIM-CMG parameters and create a compact model. Figure [3](/articles/s41598-026-37881-5#Fig3)(c) shows excellent agreement between TCAD and the extracted SPICE model. Next, a complete SPICE netlist was constructed by integrating compact models with the parasitic RC components extracted in the third stage. To ensure the relevance of our simulations to future technology nodes, all electrical characteristics were evaluated at a supply voltage of 0.6 V, as specified by the IRDS 2023 roadmap for the 1 nm node.

### Parasitic RC decomposition in various CFET architectures

In this chapter, we investigate the performance optimization of the proposed 3-Tier CFET 6T-SRAM structure and conduct a quantitative comparative analysis against the Conv. 2-Tier architecture. The subsequent analysis provides a detailed comparative evaluation of key performance metrics based on the simulation results for each structure.

**Fig. 4**

![Fig. 4](//media.springernature.com/lw685/springer-static/image/art%3A10.1038%2Fs41598-026-37881-5/MediaObjects/41598_2026_37881_Fig4_HTML.png)

[Full size image](/articles/s41598-026-37881-5/figures/4)

**a** Schematic cross-sectional views illustrating the key parasitic resistance and capacitance components in the Conv. (2-Tier) and the proposed 3-Tier CFET 6T-SRAM architectures (a) Y-Y’ Cut View. **b**, **c** X-X’ Cut View of Conv. and 3-Tier SRAM each. Comparative analysis of parasitic components for the designs with varying nanosheet stack configurations (PU: PD: PG ratios) **d** Extracted MOL+BEOL resistance for critical nodes such as the BL, WL, Q/QB-node, and power rails (VDD, VSS) **e** Segmentation of the total BL capacitance, showing the proportional contribution from adjacent nodes. **f** Of its internal storage Q node Capacitance. **g** Of its total WL Capacitance.

This section analyzes the variations in parasitic components stemming from the structural differences between the proposed 3-Tier CFET SRAM and the Conv. SRAM. Figure [4](/articles/s41598-026-37881-5#Fig4)(a), (b), and (c) schematically illustrate the parasitic RC components between major nodes—such as the wordline (WL), bitline (BL), and internal storage node (Q) and adjacent elements, alongside cross-sectional views of each SRAM structure.

As depicted in Fig. [4](/articles/s41598-026-37881-5#Fig4)(d), which presents the nodal resistances at the BEOL and MOL levels, the most notable characteristic is the substantial increase in the Q and QB node resistance for the 3-Tier structure. It measures approximately 156.4Ω, an 87% increase compared to the 83.6Ω of the Conv. structure. This is attributed to the inherent vertical stacking of the 3-Tier architecture, which results in a more intricate current path connecting the internal nodes to the BL and power lines, thereby incurring additional via resistance.

For the 3-Tier (2P3N) and 3-Tier (2P4N+3N\_Access) models, reducing the number of PU transistor stacks from three to two resulted in a VDD path resistance of 41.1Ω, a decrease of approximately 20% from 51.4Ω. This reduction is because the decrease in PU transistor stacks lowers the overall vertical height of the device. Consequently, the vertical length of the via connecting the upper VDD metal line to the source of the PU transistor is shortened. Since via resistance is directly proportional to its length, this shortened via is a key factor in reducing the total parasitic resistance of the VDD power supply path.

The BL resistance exhibited a slight increasing trend in the 3-Tier structures, which is attributed to the increased length of the BL interconnects. The resistance values varied noticeably with the adjustment of nanosheet stacks within the 3-Tier architecture. This elevated resistance represents a potential drawback of the 3-Tier design, implying that it could adversely affect the DC margin.

The analysis of BL capacitance in Fig. [4](/articles/s41598-026-37881-5#Fig4) (e) reveals that the total BL capacitance is nearly identical across the structures, measuring approximately 63.9aF for the Conv. (3P3N) structure and 63.6aF for all 3-Tier structures. In the Conv. (3P3N) design, the coupling capacitance with the WL is the dominant component at 52.0aF, accounting for about 81.3% of the total. This is due to the larger interacting area between the source/drain metal connected to the BL and the WL gate metal in the more spread-out 2-Tier layout. Furthermore, coupling with the internal storage node (Q) is also significant at 8.4aF (approx. 13.1%), as the planar layout places the diffusion regions and local interconnects of the Q node in close physical proximity to the BL vias and metal lines. Conversely, the 3-Tier structure, with its scaled footprint achieved through vertical stacking, reduces interaction with the WL and Q nodes, lowering the WL-BL coupling to 47.3aF. Moreover, the vertical separation between the Q node (connected to the lower inverter) and the BL (connected to the upper PG) ensures that Q-BL coupling drops significantly to less than 0.9aF. However, this reduction is almost entirely offset by a sharp increase in lateral coupling capacitance with the adjacent bitline bar (BLB), which rises to 12.5aF (approx. 19.6%) due to the narrowed cell pitch. In conclusion, the 3-Tier architecture exhibits a structural trade-off: it reduces vertical parasitic capacitance (vs. WL, Q) at the expense of increased horizontal capacitance (vs. BLB), resulting in a total BL capacitance comparable to that of the Conv. (3P3N) structure.

As shown in the Q-node capacitance analysis in Fig. [4](/articles/s41598-026-37881-5#Fig4) (f), the total Q-node capacitance of the Conv. (3P3N) structure is approximately 377.9aF. In contrast, the 3-Tier (3P3N) structure with the same stack ratio exhibits a capacitance of 328.8aF, a reduction of about 13%. This demonstrates that the miniaturization achieved through the vertical stacking of the 3-Tier architecture is effective in reducing interactions between the internal node and surrounding conductors, thereby lowering parasitic capacitance. The 3-Tier (2P3N) model shows a further 10% reduction in total capacitance to 294.9aF compared to the 3-Tier (3P3N) model (328.8aF). The primary reasons for this decrease are the reduction in coupling with the QB node (from 170.1aF to 149.2aF) and with VDD (from 47.8aF to 36.7aF). This is a result of the smaller physical size of the weakened PU transistor (2P), which reduces the interaction between the Q node and the gate (connected to QB) and drain (connected to VDD) of that transistor. In the case of the 3-Tier (2P4N+3N\_Access) model, the increased number of PD stacks to four leads to an increase in coupling with VSS to 76.2aF, causing the total capacitance to rise back to 327.7aF, a level similar to the 3-Tier (3P3N) model. In summary, the 3-Tier architecture effectively reduces Q-node capacitance compared to the Conv. structure.

Finally, the WL capacitance, as shown in Fig. [4](/articles/s41598-026-37881-5#Fig4) (g), also demonstrates a significant reduction of approximately 40% in the 3-Tier structures compared to the Conv. structure. However, in modern industrial technology, the RC characteristics of the wordline are predominantly determined by array-level design variables, such as the wordline driver design, array size, and interconnect materials[42](#ref-CR42 "Wu, B., Stine, J. E., Guthaus, M. R., Fast & Area-Efficient, S. R. A. M. and Word-Line Optimization. In 2019 IEEE International Symposium on Circuits and Systems (ISCAS) 1–5 (IEEE, Sapporo, Japan, 2019). 
                  https://doi.org/10.1109/ISCAS.2019.8702518
                  
                "),[43](#ref-CR43 "Takeda, K. et al. Multi-step word-line control technology in hierarchical cell architecture for scaled-down high-density SRAMs. IEEE J. Solid-State Circuits 46, 806–814 (2011)."),[44](#ref-CR44 "Iyer, A. S., Kim, D., Mukhopadhyay, S. & Lim, S. K. Multi-Tier 3D SRAM Module Design: Targeting Bit-Line and Word-Line Folding. In Proceedings of the 43rd IEEE/ACM International Conference on Computer-Aided Design, 1–9 (ACM, Newark Liberty International Airport Marriott New York NY USA, 2024). 
                  https://doi.org/10.1145/3676536.3676810
                  
                "),[45](/articles/s41598-026-37881-5#ref-CR45 "Kang, S. M. & Leblebici, Y. CMOS Digital Integrated Circuits: Analysis and Design (McGraw-Hill, 2003)."). Therefore, this paper focuses exclusively on the optimization of the bitcell itself, which is directly related to read/write performance, and does not delve into a detailed performance analysis of the wordline, as that would require array-level optimization.

### Static stability evaluation

The static stability of an SRAM cell is a key performance metric that represents its ability to reliably retain data without corruption from external noise. Figure [5](/articles/s41598-026-37881-5#Fig5)(a) presents a comparison of the extracted Hold Static Noise Margin (HSNM) and Read Static Noise Margin (RSNM) values for each SRAM structure. Furthermore, Fig. [5](/articles/s41598-026-37881-5#Fig5)(b) visually illustrates the changes in stability for the 3-Tier structures through their Voltage Transfer Characteristic (VTC) butterfly curves during a read operation. HSNM and RSNM were measured using the butterfly curve method, where the maximum square inscribed in the smallest lobe of the curve determines the margin[5](/articles/s41598-026-37881-5#ref-CR5 "Abbasian, E. & Sofimowloodi, S. Energy-efficient single-ended read/write 10T near-threshold SRAM. IEEE Trans. Circuits Syst. I 70, 2037–2047 (2023)."),[46](/articles/s41598-026-37881-5#ref-CR46 "Ul Haq, S. et al. A CNTFET-based 10T static memory design immune to read and half-select disturbs for low-power wearable biomedical systems. IEEE Access. 13, 166222–166240 (2025).").

First, a comparison of stability was made between the Conv. (3P3N) and 3-Tier (3P3N) models, which share the same 3P3N transistor configuration. As shown in Fig. [5](/articles/s41598-026-37881-5#Fig5)(a), both models exhibit identical values for HSNM (214mV) and RSNM (201.4mV). This outcome is directly correlated with the parasitic resistance characteristics analyzed previously (Fig. [4](/articles/s41598-026-37881-5#Fig4)(d)). In the Hold state, the access transistors are turned off, isolating the cell from the external bitlines; thus, cell stability is determined solely by the internal inverter latch. The VTC of this latch is defined by the relative strengths of the PU path (VDD resistance) and the PD path (VSS resistance). Since the VDD and VSS path resistances are identical for both models, their HSNM values are also identical. Similarly, during the Read state, the VSS resistance of the PD transistor is the dominant factor for stability. As this path resistance is also the same in both models, no difference in RSNM is observed. Consequently, these results indicate that the structural transition from a 2-Tier to a 3-Tier architecture, in itself, has a negligible effect on the cell’s static stability, provided that the relative transistor strengths are maintained.

**Fig. 5**

![Fig. 5](//media.springernature.com/lw685/springer-static/image/art%3A10.1038%2Fs41598-026-37881-5/MediaObjects/41598_2026_37881_Fig5_HTML.png)

[Full size image](/articles/s41598-026-37881-5/figures/5)

Static Noise Margin (SNM) comparison and VTC (Voltage Transfer Characteristic) butterfly curves for the different SRAM architectures. **a** The bar chart compares the extracted Hold Static Noise Margin (HSNM) and Read Static Noise Margin (RSNM) for all four SRAM configurations. **b** The plot presents the VTC butterfly curves for the three 3-Tier models under the read condition.

Figure [5](/articles/s41598-026-37881-5#Fig5)(a) reveals a trend of gradually decreasing static stability as the transistor stacks are adjusted within the 3-Tier architecture. Compared to the baseline 3-Tier (3P3N) model, the final proposed 3-Tier (2P4N+3N\_Access) model exhibits a 4.8% reduction in HSNM and a 6.5% reduction in RSNM. While this stability degradation is partly due to subtle variations in the VSS and VDD path resistances, a more fundamental cause is the VTC asymmetric imbalance resulting from the altered PU: PD transistor strength ratio. The 3P3N model, which has the highest stability, is a symmetric structure with a balanced PU and PD strength. In contrast, the 2P3N and 2P4N models are intentionally designed with an asymmetric structure, weakening the PU while strengthening the PD, to enhance write performance and read speed. This asymmetry lowers the inverter’s switching threshold voltage (Vth), inducing a leftward shift in the inverter’s VTC. This shift, as seen in the butterfly curves of Fig. [5](/articles/s41598-026-37881-5#Fig5)(b), reduces the area of the inner square, thereby degrading the RSNM.

**Fig. 6**

![Fig. 6](//media.springernature.com/lw685/springer-static/image/art%3A10.1038%2Fs41598-026-37881-5/MediaObjects/41598_2026_37881_Fig6_HTML.png)

[Full size image](/articles/s41598-026-37881-5/figures/6)

The write stability of an SRAM cell is evaluated by the Write Static Noise Margin (WSNM). WSNM was estimated from a combination of read and write VTCs, which reflects the ease of flipping the storage node during write operations[47](/articles/s41598-026-37881-5#ref-CR47 "Abbasian, E., Gholipour, M. & Birla, S. This scientific article, published in Scientific Reports (volume 16, article 16857, 2026), proposes and evaluates a novel 3-Tier CFET (Complementary FET) 6T-SRAM cell architecture that incorporates 2D Transition Metal Dichalcogenides (TMDs) as channel materials for the Angstrom technology node. The key innovations are: (1) replacing silicon channel materials with 2D TMDs (MoS₂ for n-type, WSe₂ for p-type) and (2) advancing from a conventional 2-Tier to a 3-Tier stacked structure.

**Key Findings:**
- The 3-Tier architecture achieves a ~29.5% reduction in bitcell area (8,892 nm² vs. 12,616 nm²) compared to the conventional 2-Tier structure.
- Internal node (Q) capacitance is reduced by 13–22%, leading to >39% lower write energy.
- The write-specialized (2P3N) model achieves over 50.3% energy savings.
- The final optimized design (3-Tier 2P4N+3N_Access) delivers 11.9% improvement in Read Access Time and a 24.9% reduction in Energy-Delay Product (EDP).

**Methodology:**
The research used a hierarchical simulation workflow: 3D structure design in Synopsys Sentaurus TCAD, calibration against experimental data from IMEC's 2D GAA-FET devices, parasitic RC extraction using Synopsys Raphael, and SPICE circuit simulation with HSPICE. The supply voltage was 0.6V (per IRDS 2023 for 1nm node). Four configurations were compared: Conv. (3P3N), 3-Tier (3P3N), 3-Tier (2P3N), and 3-Tier (2P4N+3N_Access).

**Advantages of 2D TMDs:**
- Atomically thin (~0.7 nm) channels enable vertical stacking without significant height increase.
- Low-temperature processing allows multi-layer stacking without thermal damage.
- Excellent electrostatic control and interface properties.

**Advantages of 3-Tier Architecture:**
- Enables independent optimization of PU, PD, and PG transistors.
- Allows tuning of nanosheet stack ratios to control stability-speed trade-offs.
- Reduces parasitic capacitance through structural miniaturization.

**Limitations/Considerations:**
- The 3-Tier structure shows ~87% increase in Q/QB node resistance (156.4Ω vs. 83.6Ω).
- The optimized 3-Tier (2P4N+3N_Access) model exhibits 4.8% HSNM reduction and 6.5% RSNM reduction compared to the symmetric baseline.
- Static stability (HSNM/RSNM) is identical between Conv. 2-Tier and 3-Tier with the same transistor ratios, indicating the structural change alone does not affect stability.

# [Intel 18A Node SRAM Density On-Par with TSMC, Backside Power Delivery a Big Bonus](/332850/intel-18a-node-sram-density-on-par-with-tsmc-backside-power-delivery-a-big-bonus)

by [AleksandarK](/forums/members/aleksandark.187454/)     [Discuss (14 Comments)](/332850/intel-18a-node-sram-density-on-par-with-tsmc-backside-power-delivery-a-big-bonus#comments)

Intel has unveiled some interesting advances in semiconductor manufacturing at the International Solid-State Circuits Conference (ISSCC), showcasing the capabilities of its highly anticipated Intel 18A process technology. The presentation highlighted significant improvements in SRAM bit cell density. The PowerVia system, coupled with RibbonFET (GAA) transistors, is at the heart of Intel's node. The company demonstrated solid progress with their high-performance SRAM cells, achieving a reduction from 0.03 µm² in Intel 3 to 0.023 µm² in Intel 18A. High-density cells showed similar improvement, shrinking to 0.021 µm². These advancements represent scaling factors of 0.77 and 0.88 respectively, which are significant achievements in SRAM technology, once thought to be done with scaling benefits.   
   
 Implementing PowerVia technology is an Intel-first approach to addressing voltage drops and interference in processor logic areas. Using an "around the array" scheme, Intel strategically applies PowerVias to I/O, control, and decoder elements while optimizing bit cell design without a frontal power supply. The macro bit density of 38.1 MBit/mm² achieved by Intel 18A puts the company in a strong competitive position. While TSMC reported matching figures with their N2 process, Intel's comprehensive approach with 18A, combining PowerVia and GAA transistors, could challenge Smausng and TSMC, with long-term aspirations to compete for premium clients currently served by TSMC, including giants like NVIDIA, Apple, and AMD.

args.summary:
This LinkedIn post by Richard Platt reports that Intel Foundry's 18A process has achieved an SRAM density of 38.1 Mb/mm², matching TSMC's N2 process — a significant breakthrough for Intel's foundry ambitions. The 18A "high-density" version shows this density in a large array configuration. However, the article cautions that the true test lies in High Volume Manufacturing (HVM) yields and how the processes perform once in the supply chain. For comparison, TSMC's N2 process has shown a 12% improvement in SRAM density (with high-performance SRAM seeing 18% improvement) due to its transition from FinFET to nanosheet (GAA) technology.

Additional related posts within the feed provide further context:
- Intel has officially begun production of its 18A process node ahead of TSMC's N2, featuring second-generation RibbonFET transistors and PowerVia backside power delivery, promising up to 25% better performance or 36% lower power consumption vs. Intel 3, with 30% increased transistor density.
- Intel's Arizona Fab 52 is now producing 18A chips (the first 2nm-class U.S.-built process), with defect density reported at T 0.4/sqcm (translating to ~64% Murphy yield pre-production, expected to reach 75%+ by December).
- The first 18A-based processor, Panther Lake (Intel Core Ultra Series 3), debuted on October 9, 2025, offering up to 50% faster CPU/GPU performance and up to 180 TOPS of AI acceleration.
- Intel is also reportedly in early talks to secure AMD as a foundry customer.
- A commenter noted that if Intel's process technologies approach TSMC's levels, its chip designs become very competitive, potentially driving revenue growth and attracting pension fund investments.

# Outer wall forksheet to bridge nanosheet and CFET device architectures in the logic technology roadmap

Improved manufacturability and performance compared to the earlier inner wall forksheet

Summary

In 2017, imec introduced the forksheet as a scalable device architecture to extend the gate-all-around (GAA) nanosheet-based logic roadmap in the least disruptive way possible.

Concerns about manufacturability gave way to an improved forksheet architecture: the outer wall forksheet.

At VLSI 2025, imec showed simulations highlighting the benefits of the outer wall forksheet compared to the earlier inner wall design: easier fabrication, superior gate control, connected n-p gates, and the ability to achieve full channel stress.

The outer wall forksheet architecture is an attractive option for the industry to extend the nanosheet era to the A10 node, in anticipation of the CFET going into mass production.

## The near-term logic technology roadmap: three generations of GAA nanosheet technology

Leading foundries and IDMs are advancing toward mass production of the **2nm** (or equivalent) technology node, in which **gate-all-around (GAA) nanosheet transistors** play a central role. The GAA [nanosheet](/en/articles/entering-nanosheet-transistor-era-0) device architecture has been introduced as a successor to FinFET technology to allow further downsizing of SRAM and logic standard cells.

The main feature of the GAA nanosheet device is the vertical stacking of two or more nanosheet-shaped conduction channels, with one stack for p and one stack for n devices contained in a logic standard cell. This configuration allows designers to shrink logic standard cell height further, which is defined as the number of metal lines (or tracks) per cell times the metal pitch. Designers can also choose to make the channels wider, trading cell height for larger drive current. In addition to area scaling, GAA nanosheet transistors offer another advantage over FinFETs: the gate surrounds the conduction channels on all sides, improving gate control over the channel, even for short channel lengths [1].

![Article Outer-wall forksheet](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fdrupal.imec-int.com%2Fsites%2Fdefault%2Ffiles%2F2025-06%2FFigure%25201%2520-%2520TEM%2520GAA%2520nanosheet%2520transistors.jpg&w=3840&q=75)

*Figure 1 – TEM image of GAA nanosheet devices.*

Do you want regular updates on imec’s semiconductor research?

[Click here](/en/expertise/cmos-and-beyond-cmos/stay-informed-about-imecs-semiconductor-research)

**GAA nanosheet technology** is expected to last for at least **three technology generations** before chip makers transition to the [complementary FET (or CFET) technology](/en/articles/imec-puts-complementary-fet-cfet-logic-technology-roadmap).

Because of its nMOS-pMOS vertically stacked structure, the **integration complexity** of the CFET is significantly higher than that of regular nanosheet devices. This makes **CFET** mass production feasible only from the **A7 node** onwards, according to imec’s roadmap. This means the **GAA** nanosheet era must be **stretched to at least the A10 technology node**, where **cell heights** are expected to be as small as **90nm**. Shrinking GAA nanosheet-based standard cells without compromising performance is, however, **challenging**.

This is where the **forksheet device architecture** may bring relief, a non-disruptive technology with larger scaling potential than regular GAA nanosheet technology.

## The forksheet: scaling booster to extend the GAA nanosheet ‘family’ to A10

In 2017, imec introduced the forksheet device architecture, first as a scaling booster for SRAM cells [2], and later as a logic standard cell scaling enabler [3]. Distinctive of its first implementation is a **dielectric wall** that is put in **between nMOS and pMOS** devices before gate patterning. As this wall is placed in the middle of a logic standard cell, the architecture is referred to as the **‘inner wall’ forksheet**. The wall physically isolates the p-gate trench from the n-gate trench, allowing a much **tighter n-to-p spacing** than possible with either FinFET or nanosheet devices. This allows further **cell area scaling** (up to 90nm cell height) while still offering a **performance gain**. In this ‘inner wall’ configuration, the sheets are controlled by a **tri-gate forked structure**, to which the device owes its name.

![Article Outer-wall forksheet](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fdrupal.imec-int.com%2Fsites%2Fdefault%2Ffiles%2F2025-06%2FFigure%25202%2520-%2520TEM%2520inner-wall%2520forksheets.JPG&w=3840&q=75)

*Figure 2 – TEM image of inner wall forksheet devices.*

At VLSI 2021, imec demonstrated the **manufacturability** of the 300mm inner wall forksheet process flow [4]. Electrical characterization of the **fully functional** device confirmed that the forksheet is the most promising device architecture to extend the logic and SRAM nanosheet scaling roadmaps into the **A10 node**. Since the integration flow reuses much of the nanosheet production steps, the technology evolution from nanosheet to forksheet can be regarded as **non-disruptive.**

## Manufacturability of the ‘inner wall’ forksheet is being challenged

Despite successful hardware demonstrations, a few concerns about manufacturability remained, making imec rethink and improve its initial forksheet device architecture. The main **challenge** relates to the **manufacturability of the inner wall** itself. To achieve 90nm logic standard cell height, the dielectric wall needs to be **extremely thin**, in the 8-10nm range. But, being fabricated early in the device process flow, the wall is exposed to all subsequent front-end-of-line (FEOL) etching steps that may further thin the wall, putting considerable demands on the **choice of the material** from which the wall is made. Also, to enable process steps specific to either n or p (such as p/n source/drain epi), a dedicated mask must precisely land on the thin dielectric wall, challenging **p/n mask alignment**.

In addition, 90% of the devices in real-life implementations have a common gate for the n and p channels. In standard cells with inner wall forksheet devices, the dielectric wall obstructs such a **p-n connected gate**. This is, unless the gate is made higher to cross the wall, which in turn increases parasitic capacity.

Finally, chip makers are concerned about the **tri-gate architecture**, where the gate only surrounds the channels on three sides. Compared to GAA structures, the gate risks losing control over the channel, especially at short channel lengths.

## The ‘outer wall’ forksheet: a dielectric wall at the cell boundary

At the 2025 Symposium on VLSI Technology and Circuits (**VLSI 2025**), imec researchers presented a novel forksheet device architecture, which they named the ‘**outer wall’ forksheet** [5]. They have shown through TCAD simulations how this outer wall forksheet improves on its previous design by providing **reduced process complexity** and **superior performance** while preserving **area scalability**.

![Article Outer-wall forksheet](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fdrupal.imec-int.com%2Fsites%2Fdefault%2Ffiles%2F2025-06%2FFigure%25203%2520-%2520Imec%2527s%2520logic%2520technology%2520roadmap_0.jpg&w=3840&q=75)

*Figure 3 – Imec’s logic technology roadmap, showing the extension of the nanosheet era from 2nm to A10 node with the outer wall forksheet, before transitioning to CFET for A7 and beyond (as presented at VLSI 2025).*

The outer wall forksheet places the **dielectric wall at the standard cell boundary**, turning it into a **p-p or n-n wall**. This allows each wall to be shared with its neighboring standard cell and to be made **thicker** (to around 15nm) without compromising the **90nm cell height**.

Another distinctive feature is the **wall-last integration approach**. The overall process flow starts with forming a wide Si/SiGe stack – a step that recurs in any GAA technology. The Si layers of this stack will form the nanosheet-shaped conduction channels, after SiGe has been etched away during the nanosheet channel release step. The dielectric wall will eventually divide this stack into two, with two FETs of similar polarity ending up at opposite sides of the wall. The wall itself is processed near the end of the integration flow, i.e., after nanosheet channel release, source/drain etch back, and source/drain epi growth. A replacement-metal-gate (RMG) step completes the integration flow.

![Article Outer-wall forksheet](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fdrupal.imec-int.com%2Fsites%2Fdefault%2Ffiles%2F2025-06%2FFigure%25204%2520-%2520Inner-wall%2520vs%2520outer-wall%2520forksheet_0.jpg&w=3840&q=75)

*Figure 4 – Schematic representation of (top) inner wall and (bottom) outer wall forksheet architectures (as presented at VLSI 2025).*

## 5 key improvements of the outer wall forksheet over inner wall designs

**Inner and outer wall forksheets** have two **advantages in common** over GAA nanosheet devices. In terms of area scaling, they are both capable of achieving **90nm logic standard cell height at the A10 node**, which compares favorably with the 115nm cell height in A14 nanosheet technology. A second common advantage is a **reduced parasitic capacitance**: the two FETs on opposite sides of the wall (either n and p in case of the inner wall, or n and n/or p and p in case of the outer wall) can be put much closer together than in a scaled nanosheet-based cell without causing a capacitance problem.

In addition, the **outer wall forksheet** promises to outperform the inner wall design in **five key aspects**.

First, the **dielectric wall** is spared several aggressive FEOL steps because of the wall-last integration approach. Therefore, it can be made from **mainstream silicon dioxide.** During the wall-last process step, the wall is formed by trench formation in the wide Si/SiGe stack and SiO2 dielectric fill.

Second, since the wall is placed at the cell boundary, its **width can be relaxed** to about 15nm, leading to process simplification.

Third, the **gates of the n and p devices** within one standard cell can now be **easily connected** without having to cross the dielectric wall.

Fourth, the outer wall forksheet is expected to offer **superior gate control** over an inner wall device, linked to the ability to form a **Ω-gate** instead of a tri-gate forked structure. The wider dielectric wall makes it possible to do a few-nm etch-back of the wall during the final RMG step. This allows the gate to partially wrap around the fourth edge of the channel, resulting in a W-shaped gate with increased control over the channel. From TCAD simulations, imec researchers found that etching away 5nm of the dielectric wall was most optimal, boosting the drive current by ~25%.

![Article Outer-wall forksheet](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fdrupal.imec-int.com%2Fsites%2Fdefault%2Ffiles%2F2025-06%2FFigure%25205%2520-%2520Omega%2520gate_0.jpg&w=3840&q=75)

*Figure 5 – The effect of wall etch-back on gate formation: from tri-gate to Ω-gate, and to GAA (as presented at VLSI 2025).*

The fifth aspect is linked to the potential of the forksheet integration flow to **provide full channel strain**, an additional performance booster benefiting drive current. In general, full channel strain can be obtained by implementing **source/drain stressors**. This method has proven very effective in (p-type) FinFETs but challenging to obtain in GAA nanosheet and inner wall forksheet device architectures. Conceptually, the idea is to incorporate Ge atoms into the source/drain region. Being larger than the Si atoms, they induce a compressive strain into the Si channel, boosting the mobility of the charge carriers.

The reason why fully effective source/drain stressors can be achieved in outer wall forksheet devices is **because of the wall-last approach**. Before the wall is made, a hard mask continues to cover the middle part of the wide Si/SiGe stack, the part that later serves to form the wall (Figure 6). The ‘Si spine’ underneath this hard mask can now serve as a seed crystal during the source/drain epi growth, acting as a Si ‘template’ that continues from one gate’s channel to the next. This is similar to the Si subfin in FinFET technology: imagine turning the source/drain epi module 90° (Figure 7). Without such a Si crystal template, vertical defects would form at the source/drain epi interfaces, which would lift the compressive strain formed within the Si channels.

![Article Outer-wall forksheet](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fdrupal.imec-int.com%2Fsites%2Fdefault%2Ffiles%2F2025-06%2FFigure%25206%2520-%2520Start%2520of%2520the%2520outer-wall%2520forksheet%2520process%2520flow_0.jpg&w=3840&q=75)

*Figure 6 – At the start of the outer wall forksheet process flow, a ‘pre-wall’ hard mask (brown) is deposited on top of the wide Si (gray)/SiGe (purple) layer stack. This way, a Si ‘seed crystal’ underneath the hard mask supports source/drain epi growth (as presented at VLSI 2025).*

![Article Outer-wall forksheet](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fdrupal.imec-int.com%2Fsites%2Fdefault%2Ffiles%2F2025-06%2FFigure%25207%2520-%2520Comparison%2520Si%2520sub-fin%2520in%2520FinFET%2520and%2520Si%2520spine%2520in%2520FSH_0.jpg&w=3840&q=75)

*Figure 7 – The Si spine in the outer wall forksheet (right) provides a continuous Si crystal template from one gate’s channel to the next. This is conceptually similar to the Si subfin in FinFET technology (left) (as presented at VLSI 2025).*

## Outer wall forksheet in SRAM and ring oscillator designs: a PPA benchmark

Finally, imec conducted a benchmark study to quantify the **power-performance-area (PPA) benefits** of the outer wall forksheet.

The **area benefit** over nanosheet architectures becomes apparent when comparing the areas of the A10 outer wall forksheet and the A14 nanosheet-based SRAM bit cells. Layouts reveal a 22 percent area reduction for **outer wall forksheet-based SRAM cells**, arising from the p-p and n-n spacing reduction that comes on top of a scaled gate pitch.

Another key metric for performance evaluation is the **simulated frequency of a ring oscillator**, expressed as the ratio of the effective drive current and the effective capacitance (Ieff/Ceff). Simulations show that for the A10 node, an outer wall forksheet is needed to remain on par with the frequency metrics of the previous A14 and 2nm nodes, provided that full channel stress can be enabled in all these device structures. Implementing full channel stress in nanosheet (2nm and A14) and inner wall forksheet devices has proven challenging, its absence leading to an estimated 33 percent loss of drive current. The ability to implement effective **source/drain stressors** in outer wall forksheet devices is, therefore, expected to yield a further **performance advantage** in ring oscillator designs.

![Article Outer-wall forksheet](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fdrupal.imec-int.com%2Fsites%2Fdefault%2Ffiles%2F2025-06%2FFigure%25208%2520-%2520Ring%2520oscillator%2520simulations_0.jpg&w=3840&q=75)

*Figure 8 – Ring oscillator simulation results (with and without back-end-of-line (BEOL) load) (as presented at VLSI 2025).*

## Outlook and conclusion

The **forksheet** device architecture was introduced by imec to extend the nanosheet-based logic technology roadmap into the **A10 technology node**, in anticipation of CFET being ready for mass production. Manufacturability issues caused imec to abandon its original inner wall forksheet design and develop an **‘upgraded’ version**: the **outer wall forksheet**. Compared to the inner wall forksheet, the new design ensures **improved manufacturability** while **boosting performance** and **preserving area scaling**.

Looking forward, imec is currently **investigating the compatibility** of the outer wall forksheet design **with the CFET architecture** and to what extent CFET can gain PPA benefits from this innovative scaling booster.

args.summary:
Imec introduced the "outer wall forksheet" device architecture at VLSI 2025 as an improved evolution of their earlier "inner wall" forksheet design. The forksheet architecture was originally introduced in 2017 to extend the gate-all-around (GAA) nanosheet-based logic roadmap to the A10 technology node, bridging the gap before complementary FET (CFET) technology becomes viable for mass production starting at the A7 node.

The original inner wall forksheet placed a dielectric wall between nMOS and pMOS devices, enabling tighter n-to-p spacing and cell area scaling down to 90nm cell height. However, it faced manufacturability challenges: the wall needed to be extremely thin (8-10nm), was exposed to aggressive front-end-of-line (FEOL) etching steps, required precise p/n mask alignment, obstructed p-n connected gates, and used a tri-gate structure with limited channel control.

The new outer wall forksheet places the dielectric wall at the standard cell boundary (as a p-p or n-n wall), allowing it to be thicker (~15nm) and shared with neighboring cells. Key improvements include: (1) a wall-last integration approach using mainstream silicon dioxide, (2) relaxed wall width for process simplification, (3) easily connected n-p gates, (4) superior gate control via a Ω-gate structure (achieved by 5nm wall etch-back, boosting drive current by ~25%), and (5) the ability to achieve full channel strain through effective source/drain stressors, enabled by a Si spine that acts as a seed crystal template.

Benchmarking showed a 22% area reduction for outer wall forksheet-based SRAM cells compared to A14 nanosheet designs. Ring oscillator simulations indicated the outer wall forksheet maintains frequency performance at the A10 node, provided full channel stress can be enabled. Imec is now investigating compatibility of the outer wall design with CFET architecture.
