**Nvidia DWDM (Paper 23.1):** Proposes 32 Gb/s per lambda with 8 wavelengths multiplexed using DWDM, plus 9th wavelength for clock forwarding. OCI MSA (Optical Compute Interconnect) standard focuses on 200 Gb/s bi-directional links using 4 lambdas of 50G NRZ. Three CPO integration levels: On-Board Optics, Substrate CPO (near-term), and Interposer CPO (long-term).

**Marvell Coherent-Lite Transceiver (Paper 23.2):** 800G transceiver for datacenter campuses (tens of km). Uses O-band wavelengths (near-zero dispersion) vs. C-band for traditional coherent. Only 3.72 pJ/b excluding silicon photonics, half of full coherent transceivers. Measured over 40km with <300ns latency.

**Broadcom 6.4T Optical Engine (Paper 23.4):** 64 lanes of ~100G PAM4 modulation. Tested in Tomahawk 5 51.2T CPO system. Uses Fan-Out Wafer-Level Packaging (will switch to COUPE in future).

## High-Speed Electrical Interconnects

**Intel UCIe-S (Paper 8.1):** Compatible D2D interface on Intel 22nm process, up to 48 Gb/s/lane (UCIe-S) or 56 Gb/s/lane (custom) over 16 lanes, up to 30mm on standard organic package. Likely prototype for Diamond Rapids Xeon CPUs.

**TSMC Active LSI (Paper 8.2):** Active Local Silicon Interconnect (aLSI) improves signal integrity, reduces PHY area. Bump pitch reduced from 45µm to 38.8µm, PHY depth from 1043µm to 850µm. Edge-Triggered Transceiver adds only 0.07 pJ/b. Total power 0.36 pJ/b at 0.75V. Can integrate embedded deep trench capacitors for power delivery.

This article discusses the end of SRAM memory scaling, a critical challenge for major chipmakers (NVIDIA, Intel, Apple, AMD, etc.). It achieves nanosecond access times, low voltage operation, and a density of 0.016 µm²—about 23% more area-efficient than TSMC's N3 SRAM.

The author predicts SRAM will remain in use for L1/L2 cache for the next couple of decades, while new memory technologies may first appear in DRAM and L3 cache as they mature. --- SOURCE 1: TSMC's N2 process has a major advantage over Intel's 18A: SRAM density | Tom's Hardware ---
URL: https://www.tomshardware.com/tech-industry/tsmcs-n2-process-has-a-major-advantage-over-intels-18a-sram-density

SUMMARY:
<summary>
Tom's Hardware reports that TSMC's N2 (2nm-class) process has a significant SRAM density advantage over Intel's 18A (1.8nm-class) process, according to the ISSCC 2025 Advance Program.

Intel's 18A features a high-density SRAM bit cell size of 0.021 µm² (approximately 31.8 Mb/mm²), a major improvement over Intel 4's 0.024 µm² but comparable to TSMC's N3E and N5. By contrast, TSMC's N2 shrinks HD SRAM bit cell size to about 0.0175 µm², enabling an SRAM density of 38 Mb/mm² — roughly 19% higher than Intel 18A.

Both 18A and N2 rely on gate-all-around (GAA) transistors, but TSMC has managed to shrink its SRAM bit cell more aggressively than Intel. However, Intel's 18A has two major advantages: GAA transistors and a backside power delivery network (BSPDN), which improves power delivery and can increase logic density. The article notes that for modern chip designs, logic density is more important than HD SRAM density, but this metric cannot yet be directly compared between the two processes.

The table comparing SRAM densities:
- Intel 4: 27.825 Mb/mm² (0.0240 µm²)
- Intel 18A: 31.8 Mb/mm² (0.0210 µm²)
- N3: 33.55 Mb/mm² (0.0199 µm²)
- N3E: 31.8 Mb/mm² (0.021 µm²)
- N2: 38 Mb/mm² (0.0175 µm²)

SRAM is noted as one of the hardest things to scale with modern process technologies due to design intricacies, stability/reliability requirements, and increased variability at smaller nodes. The article also notes that power consumption for SRAM on these nodes is not yet known. HVM for N2 is expected in H2 2025.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 6: Imec Reveals Sub-1nm Transistor Roadmap, 3D-Stacked CMOS 2.0 Plans | Tom's Hardware ---
URL: https://www.tomshardware.com/news/imec-reveals-sub-1nm-transistor-roadmap-3d-stacked-cmos-20-plans

SUMMARY:
<summary>
Imec, the world's most advanced semiconductor research firm, revealed its sub-1nm silicon and transistor roadmap at its ITF World event in Antwerp, Belgium, outlining timelines through 2036 for major process nodes and transistor architectures. The roadmap details a transition from standard FinFET transistors (lasting until 3nm) to Gate All Around (GAA) nanosheet designs entering high-volume production in 2024, followed by forksheet designs at 2nm and A7 (0.7nm), and breakthrough designs like CFETs and atomic channels at A5 and A2.

Key milestones include:
- **2024**: GAA/nanosheet transistors debut with 2nm node (Intel's RibbonFET with 20A node, Samsung's high-volume GAA)
- **2025**: TSMC's N2 node with GAA
- **2028**: Complementary FET (CFET) transistors arrive with 1nm node (A10), stacking N- and PMOS devices atop each other
- **2030s**: Sub-1nm era (A7 = 0.7nm)

Imec also outlined its **CMOS 2.0** paradigm, which involves breaking chips into smaller functional units (caches, memories) and stacking them in 3D arrangements. This approach relies heavily on **backside power delivery networks (BPDN)** that route power through the backside of transistors, separating power delivery from data transmission interconnects. Intel's PowerVIA (debuting 2024 with 20A node) and TSMC's BPDN (N2P node, 2026) are industry implementations.

The article notes that **system technology co-optimization (STCO)** requires rethinking design by modeling system needs and target applications, often resulting in 'disintegrating' functional units. SRAM scaling has slowed, making 3D stacking of cache hierarchies (L1, L2, L3) in their own layers more attractive. The roadmap also covers continued shrinking of interconnects for 3D designs, enabled by wafer-to-wafer hybrid bonding and advanced interconnect methods.

Imec serves as a neutral research hub (described as "silicon Switzerland") where industry rivals like AMD, Intel, Nvidia, TSMC, Samsung, and ASML collaborate in a non-competitive environment to define the next generation of semiconductor manufacturing tools and processes.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>

The invention relates to memory circuits, specifically read assist circuits in Static Random Access Memories (SRAM). The primary problem addressed is that as transistor feature sizes shrink, increased variability in electrical characteristics raises the likelihood of read/write failures in SRAM cells. A particular failure mode occurs during read operations when the internal node holding a zero rises due to voltage division, potentially causing the bit to flip (data loss).

The key innovation is a **word line suppression circuit** coupled to the word line of an SRAM bit cell. During write operations, it uses a two-part approach: first write operation (suppression active to protect non-selected cells on the same word line), second write operation (suppression deactivated, PMOS activated to restore full word line voltage for the write).

--- SOURCE 5: 4.2 SRAM - Noise Margin Analysis - YouTube ---
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lZw_DUvMV6Q

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a lecture from the NPTEL-NOC course "Memory Device Technology for AIML Computing" presented by Dr. Shubhadeep, focused on SRAM cell noise margin analysis, including write timing, static noise margins in hold and read operations, and butterfly curve analysis.

**Key Topics Covered:**

1. **SRAM Write Operation Timing**: The write operation occurs in two phases. Phase 1: The storage node holding value 1 (N2) discharges from 1 to 0 when the pass gate transistor turns on, driven by the bit line bar pre-charged to 0. Phase 2: As N2 approaches 0, pull-up transistor PU1 turns on, charging storage node N1 from 0 to 1. The write process is initiated from the node that previously stored 1, and the crossover point of N1 and N2 occurs close to 0V.

2. **Noise Margin Definition**: The maximum allowable disturbance in internal storage nodes that does not cause the node to flip. The analysis uses static noise analysis (assuming DC/constant disturbance sources) as a simpler introductory approach.

3. **Butterfly Loops and Noise Margin**: The size of the smallest hysteresis loop in the butterfly curve determines the noise margin. Balanced inverters with high gain produce the largest loops and best noise margins.

4. **Ranking of SRAM Cell VTC Characteristics (highest to lowest noise margin)**: A (balanced, ideal/high gain) > B (balanced, poor gain) > C (unbalanced, ideal) > D (unbalanced, non-ideal).

5. **Hold Static Noise Margin (HSNM) Estimation**: Measured by the side of the largest square that can be nested inside the butterfly loop. Practically, this is done by rotating the coordinate axes by 45 degrees, finding the maximum difference between VTC1 and VTC2 (D1 and D2), and computing the side as min(D1/√2, D2/√2).

6. **Read Static Noise Margin (RSNM)**: Significantly smaller than HSNM because during read operations, pass gate transistors are active, disturbing internal storage nodes. The NMOS portion of the VTC gets distorted due to current flow, while the PMOS portion remains relatively unaffected. The internal node never reaches a true 0V (it is 0 + ΔV'), further shrinking the butterfly loop.

7. **Impact of Voltage Scaling**: As supply voltage (VDD) scales down, the butterfly loop shrinks, reducing RSNM. For example, at 400mV VDD, the nested square was 105mV; at 250mV VDD, it shrinks to 45mV. Improving the cell ratio (beta factor) from 2 to 3 can help boost noise margins, but this creates trade-offs with the pull ratio required for write operations, leading to read-write conflicting requirements.
</summary>

The worst-case approach is infeasible for meeting conflicting read-write constraints in scaled technologies.

**Why Nanosheet over FinFET:** FinFET scaling faces challenges as fin depopulation reduces drive current. Nanosheet architectures vertically stack conduction channels, providing larger drive current per footprint, variable device width, and improved gate control via a gate-all-around structure.

**Forksheet Architecture:** Proposed by imec (2017 for SRAM, 2019 for logic), forksheet introduces a dielectric wall between n- and pMOS devices, enabling tighter n-p spacing, larger effective channel width, and potential scaling to 4T standard cells. Imec demonstrated dual work function metal gates at 17nm n-p spacing (VLSI 2021) with comparable electrostatic control to nanosheet devices.

**CFET Architecture:** The ultimate nanosheet family member stacks n- and pMOS vertically, removing n-p spacing from cell height considerations. Two integration schemes exist: monolithic (complex vertical integration, lower cost) and sequential (simpler processing, supports hybrid channel materials, but challenged by thermal budget constraints and wafer bonding). Imec demonstrated the first monolithically integrated CFET on 300mm wafers (VLSI 2020) and continues developing solutions for sequential integration challenges including low-temperature gate-stack reliability and dopant activation.
</summary>

The paper investigates the design space of FinFET SRAMs, including fin thickness (T_fin), fin height (H_fin), fin ratio of bit-cell transistors, and surface orientation, to optimize stability, leakage current, array dynamic energy, and read/write delay under layout area constraints.

URL: https://lirias.kuleuven.be/retrieve/109654

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The paper "Read Stability and Write-Ability Analysis of SRAM Cells for Nanometer Technologies" (IEEE JSSC, Nov. 2006) by Grossar et al. analyzes the N-curve metrics for SRAM cell read stability and write-ability in nanometer CMOS technologies. The authors compare N-curve metrics with the traditional static noise margin (SNM) and write-trip point definitions, and introduce new write-ability metrics derived from the same N-curve.

Key findings include:
1. The N-curve provides both voltage and current information (SVNM/SINM for read stability, WTV/WTI for write-ability), while the traditional SNM only provides voltage information. This current information is critical—two cells with identical SNM can have different stability, only distinguishable by SINM.
2. The N-curve overcomes the scaling limit of Vdd/2 for read stability, as SINM can be improved by upsizing transistors.
3. Analytical models of the N-curve metrics are derived using deep-submicron transistor models, showing good agreement with HSPICE simulations (deviation <10%).
4. Tradeoffs are analyzed: increasing cell ratio improves read stability (SINM improves ~50% when ratio increases from 1.33 to 2) but degrades write-ability. Decreasing pull-up ratio improves write-ability but degrades read stability.
5. A statistically-aware optimization approach is applied to 130nm and 65nm technologies, demonstrating significant advantages over worst-case design. --- SOURCE 11: 4.2 SRAM - Noise Margin Analysis - YouTube ---
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lZw_DUvMV6Q

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a lecture from the NPTEL-NOC course "Memory Device Technology for AIML Computing" presented by Dr. Shubhadeep, focused on SRAM cell noise margin analysis, including write timing, static noise margins in hold and read operations, and butterfly curve analysis.

**Key Topics Covered:**

1. **SRAM Write Operation Timing**: The write operation occurs in two phases. Phase 1: The storage node holding value 1 (N2) discharges from 1 to 0 when the pass gate transistor turns on, driven by the bit line bar pre-charged to 0. Phase 2: As N2 approaches 0, pull-up transistor PU1 turns on, charging storage node N1 from 0 to 1. The write process is initiated from the node that previously stored 1, and the crossover point of N1 and N2 occurs close to 0V.

2. **Noise Margin Definition**: The maximum allowable disturbance in internal storage nodes that does not cause the node to flip. The analysis uses static noise analysis (assuming DC/constant disturbance sources) as a simpler introductory approach.

3. **Butterfly Loops and Noise Margin**: The size of the smallest hysteresis loop in the butterfly curve determines the noise margin. Balanced inverters with high gain produce the largest loops and best noise margins.

4. **Ranking of SRAM Cell VTC Characteristics (highest to lowest noise margin)**: A (balanced, ideal/high gain) > B (balanced, poor gain) > C (unbalanced, ideal) > D (unbalanced, non-ideal).

5. **Hold Static Noise Margin (HSNM) Estimation**: Measured by the side of the largest square that can be nested inside the butterfly loop. Practically, this is done by rotating the coordinate axes by 45 degrees, finding the maximum difference between VTC1 and VTC2 (D1 and D2), and computing the side as min(D1/√2, D2/√2).

6. **Read Static Noise Margin (RSNM)**: Significantly smaller than HSNM because during read operations, pass gate transistors are active, disturbing internal storage nodes. The NMOS portion of the VTC gets distorted due to current flow, while the PMOS portion remains relatively unaffected. The internal node never reaches a true 0V (it is 0 + ΔV'), further shrinking the butterfly loop.

7. **Impact of Voltage Scaling**: As supply voltage (VDD) scales down, the butterfly loop shrinks, reducing RSNM. For example, at 400mV VDD, the nested square was 105mV; at 250mV VDD, it shrinks to 45mV. Improving the cell ratio (beta factor) from 2 to 3 can help boost noise margins, but this creates trade-offs with the pull ratio required for write operations, leading to read-write conflicting requirements.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from Electronic Design's 2024 Technology Forecast series explains the semiconductor industry's transition from FinFET transistors to nanosheet (gate-all-around, or GAA) transistors at the 3nm and 2nm process nodes. Major chipmakers like Intel (with RibbonFET at its 20A node in 2024), TSMC (at 2nm by early 2025), and Samsung (with MBCFET at 3nm in 2022) are racing to adopt this new architecture.

The article features an interview with Julien Ryckaert, VP of logic technologies at imec, who explains:
- The FinFET succeeded planar transistors due to better electrostatic control and short-channel effects, with the fin's vertical height allowing drive current scaling in a compact footprint.
- The FinFET is reaching its limits because fin profiles are never perfectly straight, causing leakage at the bottom. As scaling forces a move from two-fin to single-fin devices, the single fin would need to be impractically tall (e.g., 100nm vs. 50nm), introducing excessive parasitics.
- The nanosheet solution involves "chopping" a single fin into stacked horizontal slabs (20-25nm tall) with gate wrapping around all four sides, offering better electrostatic control and effective width while minimizing parasitics.
- The transition is driven more by the need to continue scaling (maintaining performance/area gains) than by dramatic performance leaps over the FinFET. The crossover point where FinFET "tanks" is around 3nm-2nm nodes.
- Nanosheet offers a unique advantage: the ability to modulate sheet width (e.g., 25nm to 10nm) for finer power-versus-performance optimization, though this will take time to implement.
- Challenges include integrating I/Os and other CMOS platform devices, designing new IP, and the concurrent transition to backside power delivery (BSPD) at similar nodes.
- Ryckaert notes that the era of the transistor dominating the entire semiconductor roadmap is over; innovations in chiplets, 3D stacking, advanced packaging, and system technology co-optimization (STCO) are increasingly important. SRAM will not scale well with nanosheet, forcing designers to find alternative solutions.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This document is a Master's thesis by Aravind Rajendran (Case Western Reserve University, August 2011) titled "Noise Margin, Critical Charge and Power-Delay Tradeoffs for SRAM Design Space Exploration." The thesis addresses the challenge of stability reduction in SRAM designs as CMOS technology scales into nanometer levels.

**Key Content:**

- **Problem:** Aggressive technology scaling has reduced SRAM stability due to increased susceptibility to noise (during read operations) and radiation-induced soft errors (during standby). SRAM cell area has shrunk to 0.171 µm² at 32 nm, making cells more vulnerable to single event upsets (SEUs).

- **Approach:** The author presents a design tradeoffs approach to improve SRAM characteristics by modulating the transistor sizing ratio (β-ratio, i.e., pull-down to access transistor ratio). Increasing β from 1 to 3 improves Static Noise Margin (SNM) and critical charge (Qcrit) at the expense of write time and power consumption.

- **Key Metrics:** For a 6T-SRAM cell in 32 nm technology:
  - β=1: SNM=27.4 mV, Qcrit=1.64 fC, Write time=35.38 ps, Power=6.54 µW
  - β=2: SNM=79.7 mV, Qcrit=1.86 fC, Write time=47.48 ps, Power=9.38 µW
  - β=3: SNM=102.8 mV, Qcrit=2.04 fC, Write time=57.17 ps, Power=12.03 µW

- **Methodology:** The approach enables constraint-driven optimization where designers can select β-ratios that satisfy constraints on Qcrit, write time, and power while maximizing SNM. The solution is expressed as: βq ≤ βi ≤ min{βt, βp}, where βq, βt, βp are the minimum β satisfying Qcrit, write time, and power constraints respectively.

- **Test Circuits:** Four SRAM designs were tested: standard 6T-SRAM, SRAM-C (capacitor-based), SRAM-T (tristate), and SRAM-NSP (tristate with separate read port), all in 32 nm technology using Berkeley Predictive Technology Model (BPTM).

- **Background:** The thesis provides comprehensive coverage of SRAM architecture (cell operation, address decoders, precharge circuits, sense amplifiers, write drivers), stability measurement methods (butterfly curve method, N-curve analysis), and soft error mechanisms (SEU, critical charge, charge collection models).

- **Conclusion:** The tradeoff approach successfully demonstrates that SRAM designs can be optimized for various constraints in power consumption, performance, radiation tolerance, and data stability through systematic β-ratio modulation.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper by Adam Teman (EPFL, 2014) provides an overview of SRAM stability analysis in nanoscaled technologies. It argues that traditional Static Noise Margin (SNM) metrics—the longstanding standard for measuring SRAM stability—are no longer sufficient under scaled supply voltages and increased process variations. The paper first explains SNM and its limitations, covering Hold, Read, and Write SNM. Key shortcomings include: SNM's static nature fails to capture the temporal dynamics of real operations (e.g., pulsed wordline signals during read/write); SNM assumes opposite-polarity DC noise, while real disturbances (e.g., particle strikes) are often same-polarity and temporal; RSNM is pessimistic (assumes infinite read time, over-predicting failures); WSNM is optimistic (assumes infinite write time, missing write failures due to insufficient pulse duration). The paper then introduces dynamic stability and Dynamic Noise Margin (DNM) concepts, which analyze SRAM behavior using state-space analysis, phase portraits, and the separatrix (the stability boundary separating regions of attraction). Key DNM definitions include: DNM_read = Tacross - Tread (time to cross separatrix minus read access time) and DNM_write = Twrite - Tacross. The paper concludes that while dynamic stability methods are essential for modern SRAM design, no single de-facto standard for DNM has yet emerged.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 5: 4.2 SRAM - Noise Margin Analysis ---
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lZw_DUvMV6Q

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a lecture from the NPTEL-NOC IITM course "Memory Device Technology for AIML Computing," presented by Dr. Shubhadeep, focusing on SRAM noise margin analysis, particularly static noise margins in hold and read operations.

**Key points covered:**

1. **SRAM Write Operation Review**: The write operation occurs in two phases. Phase 1: Storage node holding value 1 (e.g., N2=1) discharges through the pass gate transistor due to bit line bar being pre-charged to 0. Phase 2: As N2 approaches 0, pull-up transistor PU1 turns on, charging storage node N1 from 0 to 1.

2. **Write Timing**: The crossover point where N1 and N2 are equal occurs close to 0 value because N2 transitions from 1→0 first, initiated before N1 transitions from 0→1. This is controlled by transistor sizing (pull ratio and cell ratio).

3. **Noise Margins Definition**: The maximum allowable disturbance in internal storage nodes that does not cause the node to flip. The analysis uses static noise analysis (assuming DC/constant disturbance) for simplicity.

4. **Butterfly Curves & Noise Margin**: The noise margin depends on the size of the hysteresis loops in the VTC characteristics of the cross-coupled inverters. The smallest loop determines the overall noise margin. Key factors: balanced inverters (PMOS/NMOS strength) and high gain (sharp transition slope).

5. **Ranking of SRAM cells by noise margin**: A (balanced, ideal/high gain) > B (balanced, poor gain) > C (unbalanced, ideal) > D (unbalanced, non-ideal).

6. **Hold Static Noise Margin (HSNM)**: Measured by fitting the maximum possible nested square inside the butterfly loop. The side of this square (D/√2, where D is the maximum distance between VTC curves after 45° rotation) gives the HSNM. The minimum of D1/√2 and D2/√2 is the static noise margin.

7. **Read Static Noise Margin (RSNM)**: Smaller than HSNM because during read operation, pass gate transistors are active, causing disturbance (delta V') to internal storage nodes. The PMOS part of VTC remains unaltered, but the NMOS part gets distorted. The butterfly loop shrinks, reducing the maximum nested square size.

8. **VDD Scaling Impact**: Reducing supply voltage (e.g., from 400mV to 250mV) significantly reduces RSNM (from 105mV to 45mV). Improving cell ratio (beta factor from 2 to 3) can boost noise margins, but increasing cell ratio affects pull ratio, creating read-write conflicting requirements (to be covered in next class).
</summary>

URL: https://spectrum.ieee.org/buried-power-lines-make-memory-faster

SUMMARY:
<summary>
Researchers at the Belgian nanotech research center imec have developed a technique to bury power lines inside the silicon of SRAM memory cells, rather than placing them in the interconnect layers above. This frees up space in the interconnect layers, allowing bit lines and word lines to be made wider and thus less resistant. In simulations, the read speed of the resulting memory cells was about 31 percent faster than conventional SRAM, and writing required 340 millivolts less voltage.

The approach addresses a growing problem with interconnect resistance as chip features shrink. SRAM is particularly sensitive because its bit lines and word lines are relatively long and narrow. The imec team etched deep, narrow trenches between transistor fins and filled them with ruthenium to create the buried power lines. Wider bit lines were nearly 75 percent less resistant and word lines cut resistance by more than 50 percent.

Next steps include applying the technique to logic portions of microprocessors, and potentially extending it to "backside power delivery," where vertical connections reach the buried power lines from the back of the chip, potentially shrinking circuit area by 15 percent and saving additional power. The research was published in IEEE Electron Device Letters (July 2019).

This document (from Integrated Circuit Engineering Corporation, "Memory 1997") provides a comprehensive overview of SRAM (Static Random Access Memory) technology. SRAMs serve two primary roles: providing high-speed cache memory interfacing between CPUs and DRAMs, and enabling low-power applications in portable equipment due to negligible standby current compared to DRAM refresh requirements.

**How SRAM Works:** The SRAM cell uses a bi-stable flip-flop connected via two access transistors. Data is volatile (lost when power is removed) but does not require refresh cycles like DRAM. Read/write operations involve word lines (rows) and bit lines (columns) connected to sense amplifiers and write circuitry. Data retention requires stable VCC (within 5-10%), though lower voltage (~2V) suffices for retention mode.

**Memory Cell Types:**
1. **4T Cell** (4 NMOS transistors + 2 poly load resistors) - Most common due to small size; limitations include high standby current, noise/soft error sensitivity, and slower speed.
2. **6T Cell** (6 transistors - 4 NMOS + 2 PMOS) - Better electrical performance (speed, noise immunity, standby current) but larger size. Increasingly used in fast SRAMs.
3. **TFT Cell** (4 NMOS + 2 thin film transistor loads) - Improves on 4T cell limitations but requires complex manufacturing.

**SRAM Configurations (4 main categories):**
- **Asynchronous SRAMs** - Managed by chip select, output enable, and write enable signals.
- **Synchronous SRAMs (SSRAMs)** - Synchronized with microprocessor clock; include burst mode, flow-through, pipelined, late-write, ZBT (Zero Bus Turnaround), and DDR (Double Data Rate) variants.
- **Special SRAMs** - Cache Tag RAMs, FIFO SRAMs (synchronous and asynchronous), Multiport SRAMs (e.g., 4-port for shared memory).
- **Non-Volatile SRAMs** - Shadow RAMs (NVRAMs integrating SRAM + EEPROM) and Battery-Backed SRAMs (BRAMs with lithium battery for sleep mode).

**Key Trends:** Self-aligned contact (SAC) process improved cell size reduction. At 1997 ISSCC, all fast SRAM papers used 6T cell architecture. SRAM cell size trends show 4T/TFT cells at ~10-20µm² and 6T cells at ~20-30µm² for 0.25-0.35µm processes. The majority of analyzed parts used 4T architecture; only Intel's Pentium Pro L2 Cache used 6T.

**Reliability:** 4T cells are sensitive to alpha particle radiation (soft errors) due to high load resistance. TFT cells reduce this susceptibility but are not widely used due to process complexity.

# Metal Gate Granularity and Threshold Voltage Variability at 5nm

This PatSnap Insights article analyzes how metal gate granularity (MGG) has become the dominant source of threshold voltage (Vt) variability in advanced semiconductor nodes (5nm and below). As transistor gate dimensions shrink, the number of metal grains under the gate drops to single digits, transforming MGG from a statistical nuisance into a quasi-deterministic mismatch source that limits CMOS scaling.

## Key Findings:

- **The Problem:** Different crystal planes of work-function metals (TiN, TaN, TiAl, TiAlC) expose different surface free energies, making the effective work function spatially non-uniform. This causes statistical dispersion in threshold voltage (σVt) known as work function variation (WFV).
- **The "Few-Grain Regime":** Below 5nm, the gate volume accommodates only a handful of metal grains, invalidating central-limit-theorem averaging and making σVt non-Gaussian.
- **POSTECH (2022) Study:** In silicon nanowire FETs with gate lengths of 15–22nm and channel diameters of 7, 9, and 12nm, WFV from metal grain orientation was the dominant variability contributor across all geometries.
- **GAA Intensification:** Gate-all-around nanosheet architectures at 2nm-class nodes intensify MGG because metal must fill nanoscale slits between stacked sheets, constraining grain growth.

## Process Engineering Strategies:

1. **Equiaxed grain deposition by RF-PVD** (STMicroelectronics, 2019) — produces geometrically uniform grains
2. **Amorphous interlayer insertion** (Shanghai Huali) — 5–50Å silicon layer between TiN and TaN, annealed to form amorphous TiSiN/TaSiN
3. **Oxygen vacancy passivation in HfO₂ via compressive strain** (Vellore Institute of Technology, 2024)
4. **Amorphous top-cap barrier layers** to block oxygen diffusion (Shanghai Huali, 2022) — addressing TiAl oxidation that shifts work function by 66–157%

## Key Players:
- **Academic:** IIT Bombay (analytical MGG models), POSTECH (experimental decomposition), National Chiao Tung University (circuit-level variability), University of Santiago de Compostela (metrology)
- **Industrial:** Shanghai Huali Microelectronics (highest patent count), STMicroelectronics, IBM, Vellore Institute of Technology, IMECAS, Texas Instruments

## Circuit-Level Impact:
WFV-induced Vt fluctuations directly modulate propagation delay and dynamic power dissipation in inverter chains, making MGG a circuit-design constraint for SRAM bitcells and flip-flops at advanced nodes.
</summary>

The chapter, authored by Elke Erben, Klaus Hempel (GLOBALFOUNDRIES Fab1, Germany), and Dina Triyoso (GLOBALFOUNDRIES, USA), examines work function setting in high-k metal gate (HKMG) devices for CMOS technology.

As transistor scaling has reduced gate lengths below 20nm, traditional SiO2/polysilicon gates have been replaced by high-k dielectrics (e.g., HfO2, k=20) and metal gates to avoid issues like Fermi pinning. Two main integration approaches are used: gate first and gate last (replacement gate). Both require precise work function (WF) tuning for NMOS (~4.1 eV) and PMOS (~5 eV) to achieve correct threshold voltages.

**Gate First Technology:** The gate stack is formed before patterning and must withstand high thermal budgets (>500°C). WF is set via dipole formation at the interface between the SiON interfacial layer and high-k dielectric, using La for NMOS and Al for PMOS, driven in by high-temperature anneal. SiGe channels can further tune PMOS Vt (10mV shift per 1% Ge). Oxygen scavenging and interfacial layer regrowth are key challenges.

**Gate Last Technology:** A polysilicon dummy gate is used through high-temperature steps, then removed and replaced with metal gates. NMOS uses Al (WF 4.1 eV) with TiN/TaN protection layers to prevent Al spiking; PMOS uses TiN (WF tunable ~5 eV). WF is defined by metal-metal interdiffusion in a multilayer stack rather than a single metal.

**Analytical Characterization:** LEIS (Low Energy Ion Scattering) is used for gate first to analyze surface coverage of dipole-forming metals. For gate last, high-resolution EELS combined with EDX and TEM is used to profile elemental composition (oxygen, nitrogen, Ti, Al, Ta, Hf) through the gate stack on real device structures. Key findings include: higher Al reflow temperatures (50°C increase) cause leakage via Al penetration; optimum TaN thickness balances leakage vs. Vt; PMOS Vt depends strongly on oxygen/nitrogen profiles at the high-k/capping layer interface.

**Conclusion:** Gate first technology is targeted for low-power, low-leakage applications (e.g., FDSOI), while gate last is used in FINFET for high-performance products. Both require complex, carefully optimized stacks and advanced analytical techniques.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from SemiFlows Blog provides a comprehensive technical overview of High-K Metal Gate (HKMG) technology in semiconductor manufacturing. HKMG replaces the traditional SiO₂ gate dielectric with a high-dielectric-constant material (typically HfO₂) and polysilicon gate electrodes with metallic conductors, enabling continued transistor scaling beyond the 45nm node.

**Key Physics & Mechanisms:**
- SiO₂ quantum tunneling crisis: As gate dielectrics thinned to atomic scales, quantum tunneling caused unacceptable leakage current. High-k materials (HfO₂ has ~6× the dielectric constant of SiO₂) allow physically thicker layers with equivalent electrical capacitance, reducing leakage by orders of magnitude.
- Equivalent Oxide Thickness (EOT) is the metric comparing different dielectrics.
- Metal gates eliminate polysilicon depletion and Fermi-level pinning problems, and work function is engineered through metal alloy composition (e.g., TiN-based compounds) to set correct threshold voltages for both nFETs and pFETs.
- A critical finding: effective work function (EWF) is influenced by gate trench geometry, becoming increasingly significant at sub-28nm dimensions.

**Process Integration:**
- Two strategies: gate-first (deposited before high-temperature steps) and gate-last/replacement metal gate (RMG, where sacrificial polysilicon is removed after high-temperature steps and HKMG deposited into the trench). Gate-last became dominant at the 14nm FinFET node.
- Key process parameters affecting outcomes: thermal budget, high-k composition/stoichiometry, metal gate work function layer deposition (via ALD), interface passivation quality, and gate trench fill quality.

**Challenges & Failure Modes:**
- Threshold voltage instability (Bias Temperature Instability), Fermi-level pinning, EOT creep from interfacial SiO₂ growth, channel mobility degradation from enhanced phonon scattering, work function metal fill issues in narrow gates, and trap-assisted tunneling through oxygen vacancies in HfO₂.

**Technology Node Evolution:**
- 28nm: First widespread foundry adoption, both gate-first and gate-last approaches used.
- 14nm FinFET: Gate-last approach dominant; 3D fin geometry demanded high conformality from ALD processes.
- 7nm and beyond: Intensified scaling pressures with size-dependent EWF effects, EOT limits approaching interfacial SiO₂ constraints, and severe thermal budget management.

**Future Outlook:**
- Alternative high-k dielectrics (La₂O₃), gate-all-around (GAA) nanosheet transistors requiring even more aggressive HKMG deposition, negative capacitance ferroelectric HfO₂ for sub-60mV/decade subthreshold swing, and 2D material channels (MoS₂, WS₂) with HKMG integration.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 11: Laser Spike Anneal (LSA) | SemiFlows Blog ---
URL: https://semiflows.com/blog/what-is-laser-spike-anneal-in-semiconductor-manufacturing

SUMMARY:
<summary>
Laser Spike Anneal (LSA) is an advanced semiconductor thermal processing technology that uses short, intense laser pulses to rapidly heat only the near-surface region of a silicon wafer to ultra-high temperatures for sub-millisecond to nanosecond durations. This solves the fundamental thermodynamic conflict in semiconductor manufacturing: dopants must be activated at high temperatures, but these same temperatures cause unwanted diffusion. LSA's massive vertical thermal gradient allows near-perfect dopant activation without lateral dopant movement.

**Physics & Mechanism:** LSA operates via optical absorption, quantum carrier excitation, and transient heat conduction. Photons with energy greater than the semiconductor bandgap excite electrons, which transfer energy to the lattice via electron-phonon scattering. The brief pulse duration constrains thermal diffusion, enabling solid-phase epitaxial regrowth and dopant activation before Fickian diffusion occurs.

**Process Principles:** Key parameters are laser wavelength (determines penetration depth), energy density (dictates peak temperature), and pulse duration (controls time-at-temperature). Energy density must remain below the melting threshold to prevent liquid-phase transitions. Shorter pulses minimize thermal diffusion length, virtually eliminating lateral dopant spread.

**Challenges & Failure Modes:** Localized melting from excessive energy causes structural defects and dopant redistribution. Insufficient energy leaves residual defects and high-resistance phases. Pattern density variations cause uneven optical absorption and heating. Sophisticated capping layers are needed to homogenize optical coupling.

**Technology Node Evolution:** LSA became essential at 65nm CMOS, standard at 28nm planar for source/drain extensions, and evolved for 14nm FinFETs to provide conformal activation across high-aspect-ratio fins. At 7nm and beyond, sub-millisecond to nanosecond regimes are required to preserve delicate strain engineering.

**Related Processes:** LSA is coupled with ion implantation (healing crystallographic damage) and high-k metal gate technology (selective heating protects sensitive dielectrics).

**Future Outlook:** LSA is expanding to enable monolithic 3D integration (localized crystallization without damaging lower-tier interconnects), advanced non-volatile memory, and tunnel field-effect transistors requiring ultra-abrupt doping profiles.
</summary>

Key metrics and findings:

The instructor explains that SNM is derived from the butterfly curve (two inverter VTCs flipped at 45 degrees), and the largest square that fits in the curve gives the noise margin. A poorly designed inverter (e.g., one with an overly strong NMOS) results in an asymmetric VTC and a smaller SNM, making the SRAM more susceptible to noise. The lecture distinguishes between Hold SNM (when the word line is off) and Read Access SNM (when reading occurs). The Read SNM is typically worse because during a read operation, voltage division between the pull-down and access transistors prevents the output from reaching zero, resulting in a smaller square in the butterfly curve. The instructor emphasizes that the SNM represents how much noise can shift the VTC curve before regenerative feedback fails, potentially corrupting data. The read operation is reviewed: pre-charge bit lines to Vdd, turn on word line, then one bit line discharges while the other stays high, and a sense amplifier detects the difference. A key concern during read is that the voltage at the storage node (VL) must stay below the threshold voltage of the other inverter's pull-down transistor to avoid flipping the stored data.
</summary>

TSMC revealed additional details about its [N2 (2nm-class)](https://www.tomshardware.com/tech-industry/tsmcs-2nm-nodes-get-nanoflex-n2p-loses-backside-power-delivery) fabrication process at the IEEE International Electron Device Meeting (IEDM) earlier this month. The new production node promises a 24 to 35% power reduction or 15% performance improvement at the same voltage, and 1.15X higher transistor density than the prior-gen 3nm process. The vast majority of these advantages are enabled by TSMC's new gate-all-around (GAA) nanosheet transistors along with N2 NanoFlex design-technology co-optimization capability and some other enhancements detailed at IEDM.

Gate-all-around nanosheet transistors allow designers to adjust their channel width to balance performance and power efficiency. On top of that, TSMC's N2 adds N2 NanoFlex DTCO, enabling designers to develop short cells with minimum area and enhanced power efficiency, or tall cells optimized for maximum performance. The technology also includes six voltage threshold levels (6-Vt) spanning a 200mV range, achieved using TSMC's third-generation dipole-based integration with both n-type and p-type dipoles.

N2's innovations introduced at the process and device levels target not only boosting transistor drive currents by refining sheet thickness, junctions, dopant activation, and stress engineering but also reducing effective capacitance (Ceff) to achieve class-leading energy efficiency. Collectively, these refinements yield I/CV speed gains of about 70% and 110% for N-type and P-type nanosheet transistors, respectively.

Latest Videos FromTom's Hardware

Watch full video here:

Compared to FinFETs, N2 nanosheet transistors deliver noticeably better performance per watt at low supply voltage ranges of 0.5V to 0.6V, where process and device optimizations boost clocks by around 20% and cut standby power consumption by about 75% at 0.5V operation. Moreover, integrating N2 NanoFlex and multiple threshold voltage (multi-Vt) options enables additional design flexibility for energy-efficient processors at high logic densities.

Transistor architecture and DTCO advantages directly affect SRAM scalability, which was [tough to achieve with leading-edge nodes in recent years](https://www.tomshardware.com/news/no-sram-scaling-implies-on-more-expensive-cpus-and-gpus). With N2, TSMC has managed to achieve a record 2nm SRAM density of about 38Mb/mm^2. In addition to hitting record SRAM density, TSMC also lowered its power consumption. As GAA nanosheet transistors feature tighter threshold voltage variation (Vt-sigma), N2 achieves about a 20mV reduction in minimum operational voltage (Vmin) for High Current (HC) macros and a 30–35mV reduction for High Density (HD) macros compared to FinFET-based designs. These improvements enable stable SRAM read and write functionality down to approximately 0.4V while maintaining robust yields and reliability.

In addition to new transistors, TSMC's N2 employs all-new middle-of-line (MoL), back-end-of-line (BEOL), and far-BEOL wiring to cut resistance by 20% and improve performance efficiency. N2's MoL now uses barrier-free tungsten wiring, which reduces vertical gate contact (VG) resistance by 55% and increases the ring oscillator's frequency by about 6.2%. Additionally, the first metal layer (M1) is now created in one EUV exposure pass followed by a single etch step (1P1E), reducing complexity, lowering mask counts, and improving overall process efficiency. TSMC says that using EUV 1P1E for M1 cuts standard cell capacitance by nearly 10% and saves several EUV masks. In addition, N2 cuts metal (My) and via (Vy) resistance by 10%.

In addition, N2's extra features for HPC applications include super high-performance MiM ([SHP-MiM](https://www.anandtech.com/show/18884/tsmc-shares-more-details-about-n2-and-n2p-production-nodes)) capacitors providing around 200fF/mm² of capacitance, which helps achieve higher maximum operating frequencies (Fmax) by reducing transient voltage droop.

Finally, TSMC's N2 technology features a new Cu RDL option with flat passivation and TSVs that is optimized for face-to-face and face-to-back 3D stacking with an SoIC bond pitch of 4.5 μm, which is set to become a usable feature for AI, HPC, and even mobile designs, according to TSMC.

args.summary:
TSMC revealed detailed specifications about its N2 (2nm-class) fabrication process at the IEEE International Electron Device Meeting (IEDM) in December 2024. The new node delivers 24-35% less power consumption or 15% more performance at the same voltage, along with 1.15X higher transistor density compared to the prior-gen 3nm process. These gains are enabled by gate-all-around (GAA) nanosheet transistors, N2 NanoFlex design-technology co-optimization (DTCO), and six voltage threshold levels (6-Vt) spanning a 200mV range.

Key technical improvements include: I/CV speed gains of ~70% (N-type) and ~110% (P-type) nanosheet transistors; ~20% clock boost and ~75% standby power reduction at 0.5V-0.6V low voltage ranges; record 2nm SRAM density of ~38Mb/mm²; 20-35mV reduction in minimum operational voltage (Vmin) for SRAM; barrier-free tungsten wiring cutting vertical gate contact resistance by 55%; new EUV 1P1E process for M1 reducing standard cell capacitance by nearly 10%; and super high-performance MiM capacitors providing ~200fF/mm² for HPC applications. The node also supports 3D stacking with SoIC bond pitch of 4.5μm. TSMC is set to begin N2 production in the latter half of 2025.

# TSMC @ IEDM 2024

## Semiconductor Industry Outlook and New Technology Frontiers

At the 70th International Electron Devices Meeting (IEDM) this year, TSMC Executive VP and Co-COO, Dr. Y.J. Mii, delivered a visionary keynote highlighting the semiconductor industry’s promising future and exploring new technological frontiers in device architecture, lithography, and system integration. In addition to Dr. Mii’s keynote, TSMC presented 19 papers on topics such as 2nm nanosheet technology, CFET device architecture, alternative channel materials, 3D integrated circuit technology, transition metal dichalcogenides, 2D material device advancements, and semiconducting oxides. As AI continues to transform every aspect of human existence, it enhances people’s daily lives by driving efficiency, enabling smarter decision-making, and fostering unprecedented innovation across industries. These advancements underscore the mission-critical role of semiconductor technology in powering AI solutions. At TSMC, we are committed to pushing the boundaries of semiconductor technology to create a smarter, more sustainable, and more beautiful world.

[Semiconductor Industry Outlook and New Technology](/english/collaborations/events/event/invited-talks-18.html)

Dr. Y.J. Mii, EVP & Co-COO, TSMC

The semiconductor industry is a dynamic landscape of innovation, where new materials, advanced processing techniques, and cutting-edge design converge to shape the future of technology. Powered by the principle of technology scaling, this field continues to push boundaries, enabling transformative applications in AI, HPC, 5G/6G, autonomous driving, IoT, and more. As we progress through time, scaling evolves, unlocking new levels of chip efficiency and performance. The horizon shines bright with the promise of breakthroughs in EUV lithography, new device architectures like CFETs, novel low-dimensional channel materials, and the strategic synergy of DTCO, paving the way for exciting new technology eras. Additionally, advanced packaging techniques enhance system-level performance, blending computational power to surpass current limitations. The growth in specialty technology segments such as RF, non-volatile memory, power management, CMOS image sensors, and Si photonics expands the range of innovative devices. This keynote paper will explore the latest advancements and emerging trends in the semiconductor industry, offering insights into how these cutting-edge frontiers will drive smart technology integration and create a brighter future for society.

# IEDM 2025 – TSMC 2nm Process Disclosure – How Does it Measure Up?

[IEDM 2025 – TSMC 2nm Process Disclosure – How Does it Measure Up?](https://semiwiki.com/semiconductor-services/techinsights/352972-iedm-2025-tsmc-2nm-process-disclosure-how-does-it-measure-up/)  
by [Scotten Jones](javascript:void(0)) on 02-10-2025 at 6:00 am  

[View Profile](/forum/members/7697)

[View Forum Posts](/forum/search/member?user_id=7697)

[View Articles](https://semiwiki.com/author/scotten-jones/)

[Private Message](/forum/conversations/add?to=Scotten+Jones)

Categories: [Semiconductor](https://semiwiki.com/category/semiconductor-manufacturers/), [TechInsights](https://semiwiki.com/category/semiconductor-services/techinsights/), [TSMC](https://semiwiki.com/category/semiconductor-manufacturers/tsmc/)  
[14 Comments](https://semiwiki.com/semiconductor-services/techinsights/352972-iedm-2025-tsmc-2nm-process-disclosure-how-does-it-measure-up/#comments "View Comments")

  

**Initial thoughts**

At IEDM held in December 2024, TSMC presented: “2nm Platform Technology featuring Energy-efficient Nanosheet Transistors and Interconnects co-optimized with 3DIC for AI, HPC and Mobile SoC Applications,” the authors are:

Geoffrey Yeap, S.S. Lin, H.L. Shang, H.C. Lin, Y.C. Peng, M. Wang, PW Wang, CP Lin, KF Yu, WY Lee, HK Chen, DW Lin, BR Yang, CC Yeh, CT Chan, JM Kuo, C-M Liu, TH Chiu, MC Wen, T.L. Lee, CY Chang, R. Chen, P-H Huang, C.S. Hou, YK Lin, FK Yang, J. Wang, S. Fung, Ryan Chen, C.H. Lee, TL Lee, W. Chang, DY Lee, CY Ting, T. Chang, HC Huang, HJ Lin, C. Tseng, CW Chang, KB Huang, YC Lu, C-H Chen, C.O. Chui, KW Chen, MH Tsai, CC Chen, N. Wu, HT Chiang, XM Chen, SH Sun, JT Tzeng, K. Wang, YC Peng, HJ Liao, T. Chen, YK Cheng, J. Chang, K. Hsieh, A. Cheng, G. Liu, A. Chen, HT Lin, KC Chiang, CW Tsai, H. Wang, W. Sheu, J. Yeh, YM Chen, CK Lin, J. Wu, M. Cao, LS Juang, F. Lai, Y. Ku, S.M. Jang, L.C. Lu- with Jeffrey Yeap presenting the work.

This paper continued TSMC’s trend over the last several years of presenting marketing papers at IEDM instead of technical papers. In fact, this paper took the trend even further, there are no pitches in the paper, no SRAM cell size, and that graphs are all relative performance graphs without real units. Although the paper doesn’t present the kind of technical details that would typically be included in an IEDM paper, it does paint a picture of a process ready for 2025 production and the session was packed.

In this review we will take the few substantive details that are in the paper as well as our own analysis and present how the process compares to competing 2nm class processes.

In terms of the overreaching Power, Performance, and Area (PPA), the paper states that the process delivers a 30% power improvement or 15% performance gain and >1.15x density versus the previous 3nm node. Note: the 3nm paper reference suggests this is in comparison to N3E, not N3.

###### **Power**

At the 14nm (Samsung)/16nm (TSMC) node Samsung and TSMC both produced the Apple A9 processors. Measurements by Tom’s hardware found the Samsung version had slightly better power performance compared to TSMC. We believe the A9 was designed for Samsung first so that may simply reflect a design that is more optimized for Samsung that was ported to TSMC, nevertheless, the power was very close between the two. Going forward from 14nm/16nm, to 10nm, 7nm, 5nm, 3nm, and now 2nm Samsung and TSMC have both provided relative power improvement for each node versus the previous node.

We have been able to compare the Samsung and TSMC at 3 different nodes since the 14/16nm comparison and our extrapolations have been consistent with those values.

At 10nm TSMC provided a larger power reduction than Samsung and maintained that lead until 3nm where Samsung Gate All Around (GAA) provided a large enough improvement to mostly close the gap to TSMC’s 3nm FinFET process in power (GAA versus FinFET is expected to provide a greater power improvement).

TSMC 2nm announced power improvement of 30% versus 3nm is greater than Samsung’s 25% improvement and TSMC once again maintains a lead.

During the presentation of the paper, graphs were shown of power efficiency and performance per watt versus node. The power efficiency graph was in one version of the paper although it is not in the “final” version of the paper published in the proceeding. Thankfully we captured the power efficiency graph because it is very interesting to analyze, see figure 1.

![tsmc iedm](https://semiwiki.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/Figure-1.jpg "Figure 1")

Figure 1. TSMC Power Efficiency.

We took the graph image, pulled it into Excel and created an Excel graph overlaying it with the 28nm bar normalized to 1 and then entering values for the other bars until they matched the graph. If we then build a set of bars starting at 28nm = 1 scaled up based on the TSMC announced node to node power improvements we get a total improvement of less than 9x. Nodes from N28 to N10 match well but from N7 on the bars on the graph show more improvement per node than TSMC has announced. Just the N3 to N2 bars on the graph show a 55% improvements versus the announced 30% improvement.

It isn’t clear what may be driving this difference, but it is a big disconnect. This may be why the graph was removed from the final paper.

###### **Performance**

Similar to the power analysis above, at Samsung 14nm/TSMC 16nm the Apple A9 processor had identical performance on the 2 processes. Normalizing both processes to 1 and applying the announced node to node performance improvements from both companies it is possible to compare performance per node. It has also been possible to use an Intel 10SF versus AMD processors on TSMC 7nm process, to add Intel to the analysis and forward calculate based on Intel performance by node announcements.

We have been able to check our extrapolations at 3 nodes for Samsung and TSMC since the 16/14nm nodes as well as Intel at 2 nodes and those checks have confirmed our extrapolations are tracking correctly.

Based on this analysis it is our belief that Intel 18A has the highest performance for a 2nm class process with TSMC in second place and Samsung in third place.

Our performance index values are in the full article available with free registration on the TechInsights platform [here](https://bit.ly/42B3DDE).

###### **Area**

The third part of PPA is area. We analyze two “area” related factors, one is high density logic cell transistor density and the second is SRAM cell size. TechInsights has done detailed reverse engineering work on TSMC N3E process and we have all the pitches necessary to calculate our standard high density logic cell transistor density. Similarly, we have analyzed Samsung SF3E and SF3. Both TSMC in this paper and Samsung in public statements have provided density improvement values for 2nm. In the case of Intel we have used our own estimated pitches to do a density comparison. For high density logic cells TSMC is well ahead of Samsung and Intel on density, Intel is second, and Samsung is third.

The high density logic cell transistor density is in the full article available with free registration on the TechInsights platform [here](https://bit.ly/42B3DDE).

As previously mentioned, the TSMC paper does not include SRAM cell sizes, however there is a graph of SRAM density versus node, see figure 3.

![Figure 3](https://semiwiki.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/Figure-3.jpg "Figure 3. SRAM Array Density Versus Node.")

Figure 3. SRAM Array Density Versus Node.

The problem with this is an SRAM array includes not only the SRAM cell but also overhead, for example 7nm has 25.0 Mb/mm2, the SRAM cell size at 7nm was 0.0270um2. If you multiply 25.0Mb by the SRAM cell size, you get 0.675mm2. The difference between 1.000 and 0.675mm2 is the overhead and it isn’t constant from node to node, see table 1.

###### **Yield**

Yield is a hot topic these days with lot of reports about Samsung struggling with yield at 3nm and losing customers due to low yield, there have also been some recent reports that Intel’s 18A yield is 10%.

In the paper TSMC reports that a 256Mb SRAM array has >80% average yield and >90% peak yield. These yields at this point in development indicate excellent defect densities. There are other yield components beside those tested in an SRAM array, but these are impressive results.

With respect to Intel’s 10% yield report, we have had two separate credible sources that tell us that simply isn’t true, that yields are much better than that. The other things about a report of 10% yield is how big/what is the die and at what point in development was that yield seen if it is even true. Our belief based on our sources is the 10% reported yield is either wrong or old data.

###### **Wafer price**

Another number that has been widely circulated is that TSMC is going to charge $30,000 per wafer for 2nm.

TechInsights produces the world’s leading cost and price models for semiconductors. Prior to 3nm entering production we were projecting <$20,000 per wafer and a few customers contacted us insisting 3nm prices would be $20,000 to $25,000 per wafer. Once 3nm entered production we were able to run our proprietary forensics on TSMC’s financials and determine we were correct, and the volume price was <$20,000/wafer by thousands of dollars.

To go from a price of <$20,000/wafer for 3nm wafers to $30,000/wafer for 2nm wafers is a >1.5x price increase for a 1.15x density improvement, that is a dramatic increase in transistor cost and it raises the question of who would pay that, our price estimates are <$30,000/wafer. There have also been reports that Apple who is typically TSMC’s lead customer for each node may be forgoing initial 2nm use due to price although we have also heard push back on that.

Another element to this discussion is what volumes the pricing is for TSMC’s high volume wafer price is a lot lower than their low volume wafer price, so volume needs to be considered in any discussion. In general, we believe $30,000 is higher than the average to high volume pricing will be.

If TSMC prices 2nm wafers at $30,000/wafer they will create a lot of pressure for customers to switch to Intel and Samsung for 2nm class wafer supplies.

###### **Backside Power Delivery**

The TSMC paper does not address backside power delivery but competing 2nm processes will be implementing backside power delivery.

Intel 18A will have backside power delivery – with a 2025 ramp Intel will be the first to implement this technology. In 2026 Samsung SF2P process is due to also implement backside power delivery. Finally, TSMC is not expected to implement backside power delivery on their 2nm process variants at all and will wait until 2027 (recent reports are that this is being pulled in to 2026) to implement it on their A16 process. The A16 backside power delivery is expected to be a direct backside connection that can provide smaller track heights than Intel’s and likely Samsung’s implementation.

Since Intel is the most performance focused of the three companies it makes sense, they are implementing backside power delivery first.

Another interesting thing we are hearing about backside power delivery is that foundry HPC customers want it but mobile customers don’t due to cost.

For multiple nodes we may see nodes with and without backside power delivery and given the effect it has on metal 0 the design rules would likely be different. In addition to this for the highest performance we expect molybdenum to be introduced first for vias and later from critical interconnect. This could lead to nodes splitting between backside power delivery and molybdenum metallization for HPC and no backside power and copper metallization for mobile.

###### **Other**

One final interesting item in the paper is the comment about “flat passivation”. Many processes have a top aluminum metal layer and passivation follows the metal contours, if something like hybrid bonding is desired the wafer surface must be flat. Flat passivation is presumably a planarized top layer to enable bonding.

###### **Conclusion**

TSMC has disclosed a 2nm process likely to be the densest available 2nm class process. It also appears to be the most power efficient at least when compared to Samsung. In terms of performance, we believe Intel 18A is the leader. The early yield reports appear promising, but the reports of $30,000/wafer pricing do not in our opinion represent acceptable value for the process and may present an opportunity for Intel and Samsung to capture market share . TSMC 2nm should be in production in the second half of this year.

This article by Scotten Jones on SemiWiki analyzes TSMC's 2nm process disclosure presented at IEDM 2024 (December). The paper, titled "2nm Platform Technology featuring Energy-efficient Nanosheet Transistors and Interconnects co-optimized with 3DIC for AI, HPC and Mobile SoC Applications," was presented by Jeffrey Yeap. The author notes the paper lacked technical details (no pitches, SRAM cell size, or real units in graphs), continuing a trend of "marketing papers" at IEDM.

Key PPA claims: 30% power improvement or 15% performance gain and >1.15x density versus N3E (3nm node). 

**Power:** TSMC 2nm claims 30% power improvement vs 3nm, exceeding Samsung's 25% improvement. However, the author found a discrepancy in a power efficiency graph (later removed from the final paper) showing a 55% N3-to-N2 improvement instead of the announced 30%.

**Performance:** Based on analysis, the author believes Intel 18A has the highest performance among 2nm-class processes, followed by TSMC in second and Samsung in third.

**Area/Density:** TSMC leads in high-density logic cell transistor density, followed by Intel and Samsung. No SRAM cell size was disclosed.

**Yield:** TSMC reports >80% average yield and >90% peak yield on a 256Mb SRAM array, indicating excellent defect densities. The author disputes reports of Intel 18A yield at 10%, citing credible sources that yields are "much better than that."

**Wafer Pricing:** The widely reported $30,000/wafer for 2nm is disputed. The author notes 3nm wafers were priced at less than $20,000/wafer, and a >1.5x price increase for 1.15x density improvement would dramatically increase transistor cost. The author believes pricing will be less than $30,000/wafer.

**Backside Power Delivery:** TSMC's 2nm does not address this. Intel 18A (2025 ramp) will be first with backside power, Samsung SF2P (2026) will implement it, and TSMC's A16 (expected 2026-2027) will use a direct backside connection. HPC customers want backside power delivery while mobile customers do not due to cost.

**Conclusion:** TSMC's 2nm appears to be the densest 2nm-class process and likely the most power efficient vs Samsung. Intel 18A leads in performance. Early yield reports are promising, but $30,000/wafer pricing would not represent acceptable value and may create opportunity for Intel and Samsung. TSMC 2nm is expected to be in production in the second half of 2025.

# IEDM: TSMC N3 Details

![facebook sharing button](https://platform-cdn.sharethis.com/img/facebook.svg)
![twitter sharing button](https://platform-cdn.sharethis.com/img/twitter.svg)
![linkedin sharing button](https://platform-cdn.sharethis.com/img/linkedin.svg)
![copy sharing button](https://platform-cdn.sharethis.com/img/copy.svg)

[![ breakfast bytes logo](https://community.cadence.com/resized-image/__size/940x0/__key/communityserver-blogs-components-weblogfiles/00-00-00-01-06/8015683.Breakfast_5F00_Bytes_5F00_small_5F00_withPadding.jpeg "breakfast bytes logo")](https://community.cadence.com/cadence_blogs_8/b/breakfast-bytes)![iedm logo](https://community.cadence.com/resized-image/__size/400x960/__key/communityserver-blogs-components-weblogfiles/00-00-00-01-06/0572.iedm_2D00_logo_2D00_68.png)As you know from previous blog posts, I attended IEDM in San Francisco in December. There were two presentations about TSMC's N3 process. This is actually a bit of a misnomer since TSMC has two N3 processes, one simply called N3. The other (the second generation) is called N3E. The two papers were:

![ breakfast bytes logo](https://community.cadence.com/resized-image/__size/940x0/__key/communityserver-blogs-components-weblogfiles/00-00-00-01-06/8015683.Breakfast_5F00_Bytes_5F00_small_5F00_withPadding.jpeg "breakfast bytes logo")
![iedm logo](https://community.cadence.com/resized-image/__size/400x960/__key/communityserver-blogs-components-weblogfiles/00-00-00-01-06/0572.iedm_2D00_logo_2D00_68.png)

![ ](https://community.cadence.com/resized-image/__size/1280x960/__key/communityserver-blogs-components-weblogfiles/00-00-00-01-06/Screen-Shot-2023_2D00_01_2D00_20-at-12.04.20-PM.png)

![ ](https://community.cadence.com/resized-image/__size/1280x960/__key/communityserver-blogs-components-weblogfiles/00-00-00-01-06/Screen-Shot-2023_2D00_01_2D00_20-at-12.04.20-PM.png)

N3 is TSMC's last FinFET node. N2 will be nanosheet technology (TSMC's name for gate-all-around GAA technology).

The first paper covers N3, and the second (a late-news paper) covers N3E. You may have heard that N3 turned out to be challenging to yield, and the schedule slipped, but that's not true. It was always scheduled for 2H 2022, which is a slightly longer development cycle than previous process nodes. It entered production on schedule last quarter, Q4. 2022. N3E should enter production in the second half of this year. There are two more N3 processes in the pipe. N3P is the third generation of N3, and N3X is optimized for HPC. As far as I know, nothing has been revealed about these processes other than the name. It is clear that N3E, once it is available later this year, will be the main N3 process, and N3 will not be used for designs beyond the initial tapeouts.

Here is TSMC's official position from their recent earnings call:

Somewhat surprisingly, the second-generation N3E is a more relaxed process than N3, presumably to improve yields and reduce costs by requiring fewer EUV layers. In particular, N3E has the same SRAM bit-cell size as the N5 family of nodes. To me, the big implication of this is that it makes no sense to put any large SRAM cache on the same die as a processor. Much better to use a cheaper N5 process to build the SRAM and then use advanced packaging to assemble the system. Since analog gains nothing from very advanced processes, I would not be surprised to see designs with a processor die in N3E, an SRAM die in N5, and an I/O die in either N5 or even N7, all either stacked or side-by-side in a system-in-package.

![finflex graph](https://community.cadence.com/resized-image/__size/1280x960/__key/communityserver-blogs-components-weblogfiles/00-00-00-01-06/3286.finflexpic.png)

![finflex graph](https://community.cadence.com/resized-image/__size/1280x960/__key/communityserver-blogs-components-weblogfiles/00-00-00-01-06/3286.finflexpic.png)

The N3 processes use what TSMC calls FINFLEX, which allows for variable numbers of fins to have different power/performance/area points in the same process. I covered this (and quite a bit more about N3) in my blog post reporting on OIP, [TSMC OIP: FINFLEX, Analog Migration, mmWave, and Awards](https://community.cadence.com/cadence_blogs_8/b/breakfast-bytes/posts/oip2022a). The graph above comes from TSMC's own blog post by Godfrey Cheng, [TSMC FINFLEX – Ultimate Performance, Power Efficiency, Density and Flexibility](https://www.tsmc.com/english/news-events/blog-article-20220616), which takes a deeper dive. Most of the key numbers are in the above diagram.

I had planned to cover the two papers from IEDM in more detail. But, to be honest, since I am writing this over a month after IEDM, others have gone before me:

I recommend that you go and read all three of those posts.

## Demand

On TSMC's last earnings call, it said that there is available 7nm capacity. Of course, even if we are not in a recession, certainly some end markets are struggling. But there is also a possible issue with the most advanced nodes. Are there enough design teams and volume to keep the fab full once mobile and the other early adopters have moved on to the next node? I was talking to Handel Jones at some event recently, saying how I thought that more automotive manufacturers would follow Tesla's lead and design their own chips. He said he thought it unlikely; it is both too expensive and too challenging for them to do. He thought most automotive manufacturers would have little option but to buy chips from the likes of Qualcomm and NVIDIA, even though that doesn't give them differentiation. But if mobile and HPC will always want to be on the most advanced nodes, and automotive is not flooding in behind, then who is going to use all the 5nm capacity once the most advanced companies have moved on to 3nm? Especially as chips are more expensive per transistor in these advanced nodes, a further discouragement.

On the other hand, something similar to this gets said at each process node. As the old joke goes, the number of people predicting the end of Moore's Law doubles every two years.

## Fabs

TSMC announced last year that N3 would be manufactured in Fab 18 in the Tainan Science Park. They recently also announced further investment in Fab 21 Phase 2. With my magic decoder ring, I can see that Fab 21 is in Arizona, and this expansion will be used to produce N3x wafers. This means Arizona will have both 5nm and 3nm, with 20,000 wafer-starts-per-month (wpm) in 5nm and 30,000 wpm in 3nm.

## GUC

Earlier this week, Cadence announced that:

Global Unichip Corporation (GUC) successfully delivered an advanced HPC design and a CPU design using Cadence digital solutions. The HPC design was created using the Cadence Innovus Implementation System on TSMC’s advanced N3 process and featured a 3.5 million instance count that reached clock speeds of up to 3.16GHz. The CPU design was created using the AI-enabled Cadence Cerebrus Intelligent Chip Explorer and the digital full flow on the TSMC N5 process technology, delivering 8% reduced power and a 9% area improvement while significantly improving engineering productivity.

Since this is a post about N3, let's pull out another couple of sentences from the press release:

The Innovus Implementation System’s highly accurate GigaPlace engine provided GUC with support for TSMC FinFlex cell row placement and consideration for pin access throughout the flow for N3 design rule checking (DRC) closure. The state-of-the-art GigaOpt engine delivered improved optimization by enabling the most optimal configuration from the TSMC N3 library while balancing different cell row utilization. The Innovus Implementation System also includes a massively parallel architecture and incorporates the well-established NanoRoute engine, which enabled GUC to address signal integrity early in the design flow while improving post-route correlation.

The key takeaway, I think, is that Innovus fully supports the flexibility that comes with the FinFLEX approach (actually, not just Innovus but the whole digital full flow).

# Gate-All-Around Transistors Show up at ISSCC

***By Dick James***

The [International Solid-State Circuits Conference](http://isscc.org/)*was held virtually last month from February 13th – 22nd, 205 papers in 35 sessions, with industrial participation from Analog Devices, Broadcom, Huawei Technologies, IBM, Intel, Qualcomm, Realtek Semiconductor, Renesas, Samsung, Sony, SK Hynix, STMicroelectronics, TSMC, Texas Instruments, and more.*

Gate-All-Around (GAA, otherwise known as nanowire or nanosheet) transistors have been showing up in quantity in more process-related conferences such as [IEDM](https://ieee-iedm.org/program/) and the [VLSI symposia](https://vlsisymposium.org/2020/), but rarely if at all at ISSCC. In a sign that they are becoming mainstream, TSMC chairman Mark Liu showed off GAA-SRAM results in his opening keynote [1], and Samsung gave a conference paper on the same topic [2].

GAAFETs have inherently better channel control than finFETs, since the gate is wrapped around all the channel surfaces. FinFETs have improved performance over planar FETs, but they have the disadvantage that the gate width is quantized to the gate wrap-over distance on the fin.

One could argue that a GAAFET gate width is quantized to the gate wrap-around on the nanosheet and is dependent on the number of sheets; but it is easier to adjust sheet width than it is to alter fin height within a design, giving more flexibility.

**TSMC**

The TSMC data [1] was first shown at the TSMC Technology Symposium last August, and it has appeared a couple of times since, though I cannot find a conference reference for it.

Mark Liu said:

“This nanosheet transistor achieved smaller drain-induced barrier lowering and sub-threshold swing to boost circuit performance as compared to previous technology generations. Transistor performance improvement translates directly into lower Vdd operation of SRAM. The shmoo plot shows fully functional SRAM at 0.46 V.”

At the Symposium it was stated that the data were from a 32 MB SRAM, though no other technical details were given. However, if we take the wild guess that the M0 pitch shown is 28 nm as in the 5N process, then the nanosheets are ~35 nm wide and ~6 nm thick. That gives us a channel width of 240 – 250 nm, or the equivalent of a 2+-fin transistor at current fin heights.

If the parallel with the 5N technology continues, CPP will be ~51 nm. We can also see that we have PMOS and NMOS transistors and contact on active gate has been used.

**Samsung**

In Session 24 of the conference Samsung presented “*3nm Gate-All-Around SRAM Featuring an Adaptive Dual-BL and Adaptive Cell-Power Assist Circuit*“. They seem to have gone with the acronymic flow in the business and changed their nomenclature from MBCFET (Multi-Bridge Channel FET) to GAAFET.

Samsung takes advantage of the ability to adjust nanosheet width to tune the SRAM bitcell transistors to improve performance margins, an option not available with a finFET cell. In a six-transistor bitcell we have three types of transistor, pass-gate (PG), pull-up (PU), and pull-down (PD):

In a finFET, the PU:PG:PD gate width ratio is inevitably set to 1:1:1 for a high-density bitcell, while in their GAA-SRAM Samsung tried a different WPD:WPG ratio in the same footprint:

This improved the disturb margin quite noticeably, and even gave a slight improvement in the write margin:

Write margin is dependent on RVDDC (bitcell power-line resistance), RBL (bitcell bitline resistance), RPU (PU transistor on-resistance), and RPG (PG transistor on-resistance); RPU and RPG are already fixed by cell layout, so higher-level design was used to increase margin.

RBL was reduced by adding an Adaptive Dual-Bitline (ADBL) – essentially adding a second switchable bitline in parallel to the original bitline:

ADBL is ON for write, and OFF for read:

With ADBL ON, RBL is reduced by 70%; in read, with ADBL OFF, RBL goes back to normal, and CBL is not affected by CAUX-BL, so read margin stays the same.

Write margin is also improved by raising RVDDC, so “Adaptive Cell-Power” (ACP) is used to increase it selectively. RVDDC for each cell is different depending on its position in the array, so ACP uses two power-switches at the bottom and top of the array, which is selectively switched dependent on the address. When a lower bitcell is activated, the upper switch is selected, and vice versa. Since power is supplied by the switch furthest away, and thus has a larger RVDDC, the write margin increases. In read, both switches are closed.

As you would expect, with this scheme, RVDDC reaches a minimum in the middle of the array, but overall the write margin is improved, compared with a conventional single power switch:

If we take ADBL and ACP into the design, we get this macro view:

And without knowing the starting VMIN, the cumulative VMIN reduction is up to 230 mV:

With a corresponding improvement in the Shmoo plot:

The GAA-SRAM was implemented in a 6T-cell, 56 mm2, 256-Mb test chip, and to finish the presentation we were shown a die photo and a TEM cross-section in the plane of the nanosheets. All the images are fuzzy, but we can see that there are at least ten copper metallization layers, and a stack of three nanosheets, similar to the TSMC device.

There have been numerous publications on GAAFETs from collaborative institutes such as imec and SUNY Albany, but now we are seeing more focused work from the foundries, and GAAFETs are on the roadmaps at 3 nm (Samsung), 2 nm (TSMC), and no doubt at Intel (5 nm?).

**References**

* M. Liu, “*Unleashing the Future of Innovation*” ISSCC 2021, paper 1.1, pp. 9 – 12
* T. Song et al., “*3nm Gate-All-Around SRAM Featuring an Adaptive Dual-BL and Adaptive Cell-Power Assist Circuit*“, ISSCC 2021, paper 24.3, pp. 338 – 340

This article from Semiconductor Digest, authored by Dick James, reports on the appearance of Gate-All-Around (GAA) transistors at the International Solid-State Circuits Conference (ISSCC), held virtually from February 13–22, 2021. GAAFETs (also called nanowire or nanosheet transistors) offer inherently better channel control than finFETs because the gate wraps entirely around the channel surfaces, providing greater design flexibility.

**TSMC:** Chairman Mark Liu presented GAA-SRAM results in his opening keynote, showing a 32 MB SRAM with fully functional operation at 0.46 V. The nanosheets are estimated to be ~35 nm wide and ~6 nm thick, with a channel width of 240–250 nm (equivalent to a 2+-fin transistor). PMOS and NMOS transistors with contact on active gate were used.

**Samsung:** Presented a 3nm GAA SRAM featuring an Adaptive Dual-Bitline (ADBL) and Adaptive Cell-Power (ACP) assist circuit. Samsung exploited the ability to adjust nanosheet width to tune SRAM bitcell transistors (improving the PU:PG:PD ratio beyond the 1:1:1 limitation of finFETs). ADBL adds a switchable second bitline to reduce write resistance by 70%, while ACP uses two power switches at the array top and bottom to selectively increase write margin. The cumulative VMIN reduction was up to 230 mV. The test chip was a 6T-cell, 56 mm², 256-Mb design with at least ten copper metallization layers and a stack of three nanosheets.

GAAFETs are now on foundry roadmaps: Samsung at 3 nm, TSMC at 2 nm, and likely Intel at 5 nm.

args.summary:
This is a Samsung Semiconductor foundry webpage detailing the company's Logic Node process technology offerings. The page lists Samsung's semiconductor manufacturing nodes across two wafer sizes (12-inch and 8-inch), organized by production start dates and key technology characteristics.

**12-inch Nodes (cutting-edge processes):**
- **SF2** (2nm-class GAA): Started mass production in 2025. Second-generation MBCFET(GAA) node for mobile, HPC, AI, and automotive applications.
- **SF3** (3nm GAA): Started mass production in 2022. Uses gate-all-around architecture with nanosheet channels for improved PPA.
- **SF4** (4nm FinFET): Started mass production in 2021. First 4nm process for mobile applications.
- **SF5** (5nm FinFET): Started mass production in 2021. Enables HPC systems with better performance and power efficiency.
- **SF7** (7nm FinFET): Started mass production in 2019. First to introduce EUV lithography.
- **8nm** (FinFET): Started mass production in 2018. RF-focused one-chip solution for 5G.
- **28FDS** (FD-SOI): Started mass production in 2015. Overcomes bulk CMOS limitations.
- **14nm** (FinFET): Started mass production in 2014. First integration of 3D FinFET in foundry.
- **28nm** (Planar): Started mass production in 2012. RF process for connectivity applications.

**8-inch Nodes (mainstream, proven reliability):**
- **70nm**: Started mass production in 2011.
- **90nm**: Started mass production in 2006. Entry into nanotechnology.
- **130nm**: Started mass production in 2002. For wearable and IoT devices.
- **180nm**: Started mass production in 2000. For analog applications.

The page also notes that as of July 31, 2025, it is no longer available.
