International Journal of Computer Applications (0975 – 8887) Volume 134 – No.5, January 2016 29 Optimized High Performance 10T SRAM Cell Characterization Arjun Singh Yadav Ph.D. Scholar Electronics and Communication Department M.A.N.I.T, Bhopal (M.P.) Sangeeta Nakhte Assistant Professor Electronics and Communication Department M.A.N.I.T, Bhopal (M.P.) ABSTRACT In this work, optimized Low power and high speed SRAM architecture based on ten transistor (10T) bit-cell is proposed. This cell obtains low static power and high speed read due to two independent read access mechanisms, which offers cascading of read driver. It also estimates read/write delay, read stability, write stability and compare the result with that of standard 6T, 9T and LP10T SRAM cell. The comparative study based on VDD and Temperature variation using simulation exhibits appreciable improvement in read delay and write SNM. General Terms VLSI Circuit Keywords Standby Powers, Read Operation Delay, Write Operation Delay, Monte Carlo Simulation and Static Noise Margin. 1. INTRODUCTION To support faster read and write operations, need large size SRAM Cache memories in multi-core architecture. This large size cache has occupied 90% of total chip area (Montecito processor)[1]. Since the total leakage power is proportional to transistor count and its W/L ratio, a reduction of the SRAM cache leakage is therefore inevitable for low power design. Large sizes of pull-up and pull-down MOS device are responsible for sub-threshold leakage or static power dissipation as well as occupy more area on the total chip area. But large size of pull up and pull down MOS is required for reliable read and write operation. Standard 6T SRAM cell suffer from that problem. As observed in the 8Kbyte instruction cache of the M32R processor at 45nm technology, in idle state leakage power dissipation in SRAM cache can exceed the dynamic power dissipation [2]. The another issue considered in design is to ensure a reasonable noise margin, which is measured in term of Static Noise Margin (SNM) and the Write Trip Point [3], [4]. According to [3], SNM degrade when threshold voltage variation increases. Furthermore, the SNM is linearly dependent on the supply voltage, reducing which to save power has a negative impact on the cell stability. As a result, it is extremely difficult to maintain the cell stability as technology enters the sub-100 nm regime. For scaled VLSI devices, sub threshold leakage current, junction leakage current and gate leakage current are becoming important leakage component, for applications such as embedded cache and battery operated systems where leakage currents must be kept extremely low. Therefore, leakage is a serious issue in scaled technology. A single bit line based 6T SRAM cell [5] offers higher write operation delay. A low power differential 6T SRAM cell [6] provide significant improvement in read operation delay and write power (energy) but can‟t improve read static noise margin (RSNM). To improve RSNM, a differential 9T SRAM cell [7] was proposed with increase in read operation delay. The low power 10T SRAM cell in[8] provide performance like 9T along with improved leakage due to tail transistor. This paper proposes an optimized high performance 10T SRAM cell (hereafter called OHP10T) and compare the result with differential 6T, 9T and low power 10T SRAM (hereafter called LP10T). The remaining paper is organized in the following order. Section II presents the Existing and proposed 10T SRAM cell design and device sizing, Section III presents simulation result and its analysis and Section IV presents the concluding remarks. 2. EXISTING AND PROPOSED 10T SRAM CELL This section presents a novel optimized high performance 10T SRAM cell (OHP10T) as shown in fig. 4 and compared the result with 6T, 9T, LP10T as shown in fig.2, fig.3 and fig.4 respectively. Here, minimum width devices are used to for fair comparison of read SNM, write SNM and feedback pull-up strength. These strict constraints on the device sizing of conventional 6T cell are maintained for fair comparison with the existing and proposed design (cell ratio = pull-up = 1.33). 2.1 Device Dimension of 6T SRAM cell The size ratio of pull-down device to the access device, referred to as the cell ratio is critical in case of 6T SRAM cell due to its direct read mechanism. The cell ratio determines how high the node QB that stores „„0‟‟ rises during read access due to voltage dividing effect between driver and access MOSFETs. Typically, cell ratio 1.2–3 is required to avoid read upset in conventional 6T SRAM cell [9]. Write-ability of SRAM cell is determined by the pull-up ratio. Generally, pull-up ratio less than 1.8 is required to maintain good write-ability [10]. Therefore, for maintaining appreciable read stability, write-ability and feed-back pull-up strength minimum width devices are typically not used in standard 6T SRAM cell. International Journal of Computer Applications (0975 – 8887) Volume 134 – No.5, January 2016 30 Fig :1 Conventional 6T SRAM cell 2.2 Device Dimension of 9T SRAM cell This design is based on indirect read and direct write mechanism. The content of 9T cell remains unchanged after each read operation [7]. So, it is called indirect read mechanism. The 6T cell can‟t offer appreciable read stability. Therefore, this design added extra devices MN5/MN6/MN7 in 6T cell to improve the read stability. WWL VDD BLB BL QB MP1 MP2 MN1 MN2 MN3 MN4 MN5 MN6 MN7 RWL InvL InvR Q Node3 > 0 Fig 2: 9T SRAM Cell 2.3 Device Dimension of LP10T SRAM cell Existing 6T and 9T still suffer with severe leakage. To minimize the leakage power furthers the tail transistor MN8 is added in stack between pull down transistor and ground. This transistor enables during read and writes [8]. Therefore, in idle mode LP10T operate in sub threshold region. WWL VDD BLB BL QB MP1 MP2 MN1 MN2 MN3 MN4 MN5 MN6 MN7 RWL InvL InvR Q MN8 WWL RWL Fig 3: LP10T SRAM Cell 2.4 Device Dimension of OHP10T SRAM cell This design offer two read driver one for direct read and another for indirect read while only one way of direct write operation. The critical design strategy of our cell is the access transistor MN3/MN4 and tail transistor MN8 are controlled by XOR gate, which is driven by RWL and WWL. The read driver transistors MN6/MN7/MN8 are controlled by RWL as shown in Fig. 4. XWL VDD BLB BL QB MP1 MP2 MN1 MN2 MN3 MN4 MN5 MN6 MN7 RWL InvL InvR Q MN8 WWL RWL XWL Fig 4: OHP10T SRAM cell 3. SIMULATION RESULT AND ITS ANALYSIS This section cover the read delay, write delay, read NM , write SNM, standby power and layout area comparison among various existing 6T, 9T, LP10T and Proposed SRAM cell. Complete results are simulated in HSPICE at 22nm technology node [11]. 3.1 Read delay The proposed bit cell exhibits 40% (12%) smaller read delay as compare to LP10T (6T) at nominal VDD prior to read operation. In case of 6T, bit lines are pre charged MN1 is ON, storage node “QB” stores a “0” and “Q” stores a “1”(assumed) when WL(word line) is activated BLB drops through MN3/MN1.Prior to read operation, in proposed OHP10T storage node “QB” store “0” and “Q” store “1” (assumed). Additional indirect read driver performs slower read but offer higher RSNM while direct read driver performs faster read along with smaller RSNM. The combination of both driver offers faster read than existing 6T, 9T and LP10T. Fig 5: Read delay comparison at different VDD WL=0 VDD BLB BL QB Q MP1 MP2 MN1 MN2 MN3 MN4 ‘0’ ‘1’ 0.72 0.78 0.84 0.90 60 80 100 120 140 160 Read Delay (in ps) VDD 6T 9T, LP10T OHP10T International Journal of Computer Applications (0975 – 8887) Volume 134 – No.5, January 2016 31 As shown in Fig.5, Proposed design offers higher read current hence it take smaller time to discharge BL/BLB. The proposed cell offers smaller read delay due to double read driver. 3.2 Read delay Similar LP10T write, the proposed write delay is estimated as the time required for flipping the state of node that store „1‟ after activating XOR output XWL. As PU and access devices are mainly responsible for the write delay and they are of same sizes in all the four cells, hence, only marginal 2% penalty in the write delay is observed due to the tail transistor in OHP10T as like LP10T compared with the 6T and the 9T cell shown in Fig.6. Fig 6: Write delay comparison at different VDD 3.3 Write SNM The write ability of an SRAM cell is gauged by WSNM (write static noise margin) as shown in fig.4 .The WSNM is a measure of ability of the cell to pull down the node storing „„1‟‟ to a voltage less than the VM (switching threshold) of the other inverter storing „„0‟‟ so that flipping of the cell state occurs. There is a rationed fight between the pull-up PMOS that tries to maintain a „„1‟‟ and the access NMOS that tries to pull it down [12]. As mentioned, earlier the write-ability of the cell depends on pull up transistor MP1 & MP2 to access transistor MN3 & MN4 strength ratio called pull-up ratio. The write-ability of a cell is estimated using read and write VTCs (voltage transfer curves) [13]. When WSNM falls below zero, write VTC intersects read VTC, indicating positive write margin and signifying write failure[14,15]. As can be seen in Fig. 7, standard OHP10T offers 1.15X higher WSNM as compared with LP12T. Fig 7: WSNM comparison at different VDD 3.4 Read SNM The SRAM cell is most vulnerable to noise during read operation since the node storing”0” rises to a voltage higher than ground due to the voltage dividing effect between the access transistor and inverter pull down NMOS driver. The size ratio of pull down transistor to the access transistor, referred to as the cell ratio, determines how high the “0” storing node rises during read access. The smaller cell ratio translates into higher voltage drop across the pull down transistor, requiring a smaller noise voltage at the node storing “0” to trip the cell [16]. Therefore, RSNM is more critical design metric of SRAM cell than Write SNM. Fig.7 show that OHP10T offers 48% higher RSNM as compared with 6T. Fig 8: WSNM comparison at different VDD 3.5 Standby Leakage Power The standby leakage in embedded cache is an alarming issue in deep-submicrometer technology since several ten of million identical cells are common in today‟s caches. The leakage current is one of the major contributors to the total power dissipation in an embedded SRAM cell because a major part of the cache remains idle most of the time except for the row being accessed. The total leakage current in an SRAM cell mainly (neglecting other minor leakage components such as GIDL leakage and punch through leakage) consists of the subthreshold leakage current (Isub), the gate leakage current (Ig), and Junction leakage current (IJN) through different devices. 0.72 0.78 0.84 0.90 160 170 180 190 200 Write Delay (ps) VDD 6T 9T LP10T OHP10T 6T 9T LP10T OHP10T 200 250 300 350 400 358 312 286 WSNM (mV) Various Design WSNM (in mV) at VDD= 0.8V 320 6T 9T LP10T OHP10T 80 120 160 200 240 214 81 120 Read SNM (mV) Various design RSNM (in mV) at VDD=0.8V 214 International Journal of Computer Applications (0975 – 8887) Volume 134 – No.5, January 2016 32 Fig 9: Standby leakage power comparison at different VDD As subthreshold leakage in hold mode is the major leakage component that is reduced due to tail transistor[17,18]. The proposed design dissipates 40% smaller leakage power compared with 6T and 9T while similar as LP10T(see Fig10). As observed, the proposed bitcell reduces leakage power at all considered VDD. The comparison of leakage power at different VDD is shown in Fig.9. 3.6 Comparison of leakage power versus temperature Since VLSI circuits often operate at elevated temperature, we have simulated the cell varying temperature in the range from 250C to 1500C for estimation of leakage power, because leakage power becomes incremental at higher temperature as shown in fig.10. This is because the Isub (threshold current) controlled by the carrier diffusion, increase exponentially with temperature. Fig 10: Standby leakage power comparison at different temperature 3.7 Layout Area Due to lack of unavailability of 22-nm layout tool for a precise layout area comparison of 6T, 9T, LP10T and OHP12T, layouts are generated using 45-nm design rules. The area of the generated proposed bit cell OHP10T (shown in Fig.13) is found to be 54 λ × 32 λ (column height × column pitch) against 6T 53 λ × 24 λ. Thus, our bitcell occupies 38% area overhead compared to 6T SRAM cell. The estimated area overhead is 5% if the area occupied by XOR gate is shared among the cells of the single row. If the word size is increased, the area overhead per cell will be reduced as the XOR gate need not be upsized[19]. Thus, the area occupied by OHP10T is similar as LP10T and 38% larger than 6T. Fig 11: Layout diagram of OHP10T 4. CONCLUSION This work proposes an optimized high performance 10T SRAM cell. It analyzes the impact of PVT improvement in the most of the design parameters over standard 6T, 9T and LP10T SRAM cell demonstrating its reliability, smaller read delay and moderate RSNM. This design occupies similar layout area like LP10T instead of appreciable improvement on read access time as compared with 6T, 9T and LP10T. This cell obtain 40% smaller read delay and 15% higher WSNM as compared with LP10T. 5. args.summary:
This academic paper from the International Journal of Computer Applications (January 2016) proposes an Optimized High Performance 10T (OHP10T) SRAM cell for low power and high speed cache memory applications. The design features two independent read access mechanisms (direct and indirect read drivers) controlled by an XOR gate driven by read and write word lines, along with a tail transistor for leakage reduction. The cell was simulated at 22nm technology node using HSPICE and compared against standard 6T, 9T, and LP10T SRAM cells.

Key results:
- 40% smaller read delay compared to LP10T, 12% smaller than 6T
- 15% higher Write Static Noise Margin (WSNM) compared to LP10T (286mV vs 312mV)
- 48% higher Read SNM (RSNM) compared to 6T (214mV vs 81mV at VDD=0.8V)
- 40% smaller standby leakage power compared to 6T and 9T (similar to LP10T)
- 38% area overhead compared to 6T (54λ × 32λ vs 53λ × 24λ), but similar to LP10T

The proposed design achieves faster read operations through dual read drivers while maintaining low leakage power via the tail transistor. The paper concludes the OHP10T cell demonstrates reliability with smaller read delay and moderate RSNM, making it suitable for high-performance cache applications.

<webpage_content>
Leakage Power Reduction and Stability Analysis of 5nm node GAA CNTFET SRAMs Devesh Soni and Sumit Saha Dept. Electronics and Communication Engineering National Institute of Technology Rourklea, India deveshsoni999@gmail.com;sahas@nitrkl.ac.in Abstract. In modern system-on-chips (SoCs), embedded static random access memory (SRAM) units are vital components that facilitate on-chip memory for fast data storage and access. However, traditional SRAM cells based on metal oxide semiconductor (MOS) designs consume relatively high power, making them less suitable for power-constrained devices. Researchers are tackling the constraints of SRAM technology by investigating refined approaches rooted in carbon nano-tube field-effect transistors (CNTFETs) which includes fine-tuning of model Pa-rameters like nanotube diameter, flat band voltage, and CNT density to enhance SRAM cell performance and efficiency and to create more advanced and power-efficient memory solutions. The objective of this work is to design, evaluate and predict the performance of different SRAM cell by incorporating low-power strategies within 5nm node CNTFET 6T SRAM cell. These strategies encompass the Sleepy approach, Header approach, Footer approach, Zigzag approach, Leak-age feedback approach, Stack approach, Leakage feedback with stack approach, Sleepy keeper approach, Sleepy stack approach, and Sleepy stack with keeper approach. To evaluate their effectiveness, the research paper uses performance met-rics such as noise margin, delay, and leakage power. Keywords: 5nm node CNTFET SRAM, Low Power techniques, Delay, SNM, Leakage power. 1 Introduction The rapid advancement of portable devices such as smartphones and smartwatches has exerted significant pressure on engineers to design electronic devices that can extend battery life. With the increasing demand for these devices the challenges related to power dissipation, stability, and performance have become major focal points in their design. Indeed, a multitude of techniques have been suggested to address these chal-lenges at the algorithm, the circuit, and the system levels. Examples include dynamic voltage and frequency scaling, integration of variable threshold voltage circuits with logic circuits, utilization of multi-threshold voltage logic circuits, implementation of clock gating, and the incorporation of system-level pipelining [1]. In recent years, sig-nificant growth has been observed in memory electronics. This growth has generated a need for systems that can substantially reduce cost and density. In response, developers have introduced system on chip (SoC) designs, where a substantial portion (around 70%) of the area is dedicated to static memory (SRAM) cells [2]. Hence, the develop-ment of energy-efficient SRAM architecture has become imperative for enhancing the overall system performance. As modern technology continues to shrink to deep submi-cron scales, traditional SRAM cell designs are encountering difficulties that result in in-sufficient performance. The primary obstacles include: 1.1 Static Power Traditional SRAM cells suffer from static power consumption (leakage power), wherein current flows through the logic block even when they are turned off, particu-larly significant for shorter channel devices. 1.2 Dynamic Power SRAM cells consume dynamic power during data read or write operations, with power consumption proportional to the frequency of access, supply voltage, and load capaci-tance. The demand for faster access and higher data throughput in mobile devices in-tensifies concerns about dynamic power usage. To address these issues, various ad-vanced SRAM cell designs and memory management techniques have been devised. Effectively decreasing dynamic power involves techniques such as body biasing and voltage scaling [3]. These approaches dynamically modify the supply voltage according to workload and performance needs, leading to significant reductions in power con-sumption [3]. However, this approach can impact leakage power, a significant contrib-utor to static power consumption. Generally, the leakage power dominates overall power consumption as MOS de-vices scale down, with the subthreshold leakage current being a major factor in lower technology nodes. While lowering the voltage reduces power consumption, it increases delay due to decreased on-current. To alleviate this delay, low-voltage threshold tran-sistors can be utilized, but this raises subthreshold conduction current and compromises stability at lower voltages. This underscores the need to balance performance enhance-ment with device stability, relying on parameters like pull-up ratio, and cell ratio. To counteract this impact, numerous techniques have been put forth to efficiently diminish leakage power, with one of them being power gating techniques. These techniques in-volve deactivating unused SRAM banks or memory sections when they are not in use. Consequently, researchers and semiconductor companies have devised a novel SRAM cell that reduce leakage power while maintaining acceptable performance and stability. These designs often employ specialized transistors or additional circuitry to mitigate power consumption. “Ternary SRAM cell using GAA CNTFET” by Bhavna Muley and Sumit Saha [4], "Sleepy stack" by Park J.C and Mooney [5], "Sleep with keeper" by S.H. Kim [6], "stack with leakage feedback" and "keeper hybrid with sleep stack" by P.K. Pal [7] , and "Stacked keeper with body bias" by Bhargav KN [8] are some of the techniques proposed for low power achievement. As the device feature size scaling has limits, ex-cessive scaling can detrimentally impact the performance of conventional MOS-based designs. Nanoscale technologies like Single Electron Transistors (SET), Fin-Shaped Field Effect Transistors (Fin-FET), and CNTFET can surpass these limitations. CNTFET, with its strong performance, high thermal stability, low-static current, and superior electrical characteristics, stands out for digital system design [9-10]. In this paper, our work revolves around the 5nm node GAA CNTFET (Gate All Around CNTFET), a three-terminal device made using intrinsic CNTs covered by gate oxide founded upon the utilization of the Stanford University Virtual-Source model. This partially experimental model simulates MOSFET-like CNTFETs that use intrinsic nanotubes as channel materials[11]. Our simulations utilize the VSCNTFET Stanford model, and the Verilog-A model file of this VSCNTFET has been integrated into Ca-dence Virtuoso for circuit simulations. While CNTFET can enhance the design metrics of SRAM cells, for further reductions in power, delay, and stability enhancement are achievable by utilizing various circuit-level low-power techniques, while carefully con-sidering the trade-offs between the cell area and delay. These approaches can be cate-gories as: state-destructive techniques, where the existing output state could be for-feited, and non-state-destructive techniques, which ensure the preservation of the state. Numerous studies have been conducted in the realm of CNTFET-based SRAM cell design. For instance, Kavin Kumar[12] et. al. proposed “DTMOS based SRAM cell”, Rajendra Prasad[13] proposed the “sleep technique” based SRAM cell for low-power applications with minimum delay. Similarly, R. Prasad et. al. [14] has introduced the “stack sleep approach” as a state-saving technique that reduces the power leakage but increases the delay and area. Amit Singh Rajput[15] has proposed a “CMOS SRAM cell utilizing Schmitt trigger” to increase stability and decrease leakage power. Bal-winder Singh et. al. [16] formulated the"4 -trit adder-subtractor using CNTFET tech-nologies”. Subsequently, a comprehensive comparison was conducted, revealing the superiority of the CNTFET-based design. However, an evaluation of these circuit level low-power techniques remains pending. Hence, this research introduces a range of low-power techniques applied to the 5nm node CNTFET SRAM memory cell, followed by a comparative analysis, all aimed at enhancing overall system performance. Following, Section II outlines the fundamental description and operation of the 5nm node GAA CNTFET-based 6T SRAM cell. Section III elaborates on the low-power tech-niques proposed for the 5nm node GAA CNTFET SRAM cell. Following that, Section IV encompasses the simulations conducted using Cadence Virtuoso and offers a compar-ative performance analysis. The paper concludes with a summary. 2 5nm Node GAA CNTFET Based SRAM Cell The architecture of a 6T SRAM cell involves the integration of CNTFETs where the channel material is replaced by carbon nanotubes (CNTs) unlike MOSFET where sili-con is used as channel material. The structure closely resembles the traditional MOS-based SRAM as shown in Fig. 1, which comprises six transistors. Connecting two inverters in sequence constructs the cell, with each inverter consisting of a PCNTFET and an NCNTFET. The PCNTFET source is linked to the supply voltage, while NCNTFET source is connected to the ground. Furthermore, two NCNTFET access transistors are integrated to facilitate data reading and writing through bit lines at the storage node. Regarding SRAM cells, the sizing of transistors holds a crucial role in ensuring the effective execution of both read and write operations. Pull down transistors must be more robust than the access transistors to prevent data corruption during read operations, thereby enhancing RSNM. Fig. 1. Schematic of 6T SRAM cell 3 5nm Node GAA CNTFET Based Low Power SRAM Cell This section describes the various CNTFET based SRAM cell in which low power techniques have been embraced to further reduce the leakage power consumption. Here, we present the set of techniques classified as non-state destructive (state preserving) technique and state destructive technique. 3.1 State Destructive Techniques The technique described in this context accomplishes low power consumption, it does affect the output state during idle mode due to the alignment of bit lines with output. This set of techniques encompasses the sleep approach, the variation in sleep (header and footer), and zigzag approach. Fig. 2. (a) Schematic of sleep approach. (b) Header approach. (c) Footer approach. (d) Zigzag approach In the sleepy technique [17], an extra transistor referred to as a sleep transistor as depicted in Fig. 2(a) is introduced between the pull-up and supply terminals, as well as between the pull-down and ground paths. The core idea is to activate these sleep tran-sistors during the normal mode of operation and deactivate them during the sleep mode. This interruption in the current flow reduces leakage current, consequently lowering static power consumption. However, this approach comes with trade-offs, including increased area and delay. To mitigate the area overhead an advanced version of the sleep approach involves employing sleep with header and sleep with footer switches approach is introduced as shown in Fig. 2(b), 2(c). These variations offer reduced area compared to the sleep transistor approach, enhancing the overall efficiency of SRAM operation. An alternative technique is the zigzag approach as depicted in Fig. 2(d), where sleep transistors are alternately placed on the pull-down and pull-up networks. (a) (b) (c) (d) This configuration aids in mitigating the issue of floating output voltage concerning the ground, which is present in the sleep approach. In summary, the header and footer var-iations enhance efficiency, and the zigzag approach aims to address floating output voltage concerns. Fig. 3. (a) Schematic of stack approach. (b) sleepy stack approach. (c) leakage feedback approach. (d) sleepy keeper approach. (e) leakage feedback stack approach. (f) sleepy stack keeper approach 3.2 Non-State Destructive Techniques The major limitations of the above schemes are data retention as SRAM cells can be susceptible to various sources of data corruption, such as leakage currents, process var-iations, and voltage fluctuations. Therefore, we go towards non-state destructive tech-niques. These techniques include stack, leakage feedback (LF), leakage feedback with stack (LFS), sleepy stack (SS), sleepy keeper (SK) approach, and sleepy stack with keeper (SSK) approach. (a) (b) (c) (d) (e) (f) The fundamental concept behind the stack approach depicted in Fig. 3(a), revolves around the utilization of a stacking effect. By incorporating stacking transistors, the effective threshold voltage of the transistors is increased, leading to a reduction in static power consumption within the SRAM cell [17-18]. An evolved version of the stack approach is the sleepy stack [19], as depicted in Fig. 3(b). It employs the stack approach through vertical stacking of transistors and then introduces additional transistors re-ferred to as sleep transistors. This combination strives to uphold state information, a goal that is not easily attainable through the sleepy technique alone. Another notable low-power technique depicted in Fig. 3(c) is the leakage feedback scheme [20]. The core of this approach includes introducing PCNTFET connected in parallel to the PCNTFET sleep transistor, along with the integration NCNTFET in parallel with NCNTFET sleep transistor. These additional transistors provide feedback from the out-put during idle states, preventing the destruction of the circuit's logic state—a limitation observed in conventional sleepy approaches. A variant of the leakage feedback scheme demonstrated in Fig. 3(d) is the combination of keeper and sleepy approach [21]. This technique introduces two extra transistors known as "keepers" to preserve the logic state during idle modes. This addresses the possibility of the logic state being lost during idle mode. The Leakage feedback as shown in Fig. 3(e) incorporated with stacking effect (LFS) [17] is a combination of the leakage feedback and stack approaches. The feedback loop detects the level of leakage current and adjusts the transistor stack accordingly. This dynamic adjustment optimizes power consumption by reducing leakage current through modifications to the transistor stack configuration. Lastly, the sleepy stack and keeper approach [7], depicted in Fig. 3(f), combines the stacking effect with sleepy and keeper approaches. By utilizing sleep transistors, inactive SRAM cells are disconnected from the power supply, significantly reducing power consumption during standby mode. The integration of the keeper technique ensures the retention of the SRAM cell's logic state while in sleep mode, preventing any loss of information. 4 Performance and Stability Evaluation of Various Low Power Approaches 4.1 Performance Analysis This paper introduces a diverse range of the low-power circuit-level techniques inte-grated into the SRAM cell, with a comprehensive evaluation of their respective perfor-mances. The comparative analysis of these various low-power techniques encompasses parameters such as write delay, read delay, and leakage power. As a starting point, write, read delays, and power leakage of the fundamental 6T SRAM cell is measured, establishing a baseline for comparison. Subsequently, a comparison is drawn between these baseline values and the values obtained for the techniques that are integrated into the CNTFET SRAM cell, as presented in Table 1. Examining the read delay, it's worth noting that, among these configurations, the header, stack, sleepy stack, leakage feed-back, leakage feedback with stack, and sleepy stack with keeper showcases the least reduction 8.95%, 7.46%, 11.94%, 1.49%, 4.47%, and 2.98% respectively. However, in terms of write delay, it's significant to highlight that the sleepy and zigzag configura-tions stand out with substantial reductions when compared to the baseline 6T setup. These configurations achieve reductions of 3.89% and 5.03%, respectively. Shifting the focus to leakage power dissipation, we observe the sleepy approach exhibiting the low-est leakage power as during idle mode interruption in the current flow can be seen, reducing leakage current. Further, the comparative analysis of the aforementioned approaches is outlined in Table 2. This comparison entails a contrast between our optimized low-power tech-niques tailored for the 5nm node GAA CNTFET SRAM cell and low-power techniques optimized for the 32nm CNTFET 6T SRAM cell, as researched by Hemanth Kumar [22]. The analysis highlights specific trends within these approaches. Notably, in terms of write delay, the sleepy stack, sleepy and zigzag approaches exhibit significant reduc-tions of 30.37%, 28.81%, and 18%, respectively, when compared to the 32nm counter-part. This indicates a considerable improvement in terms of write delay efficiency for these techniques in the context of the 5nm node GAA CNTFET SRAM cell. Further-more, when considering leakage power, the sleepy approach stands out with a remark-able decrease in leakage power compared to the counterpart 32nm optimized CNTFET SRAM cell. This significant reduction underscores the efficacy of the sleepy approach in minimizing leakage power in the context of the 5nm node GAA CNTFET SRAM cell. Table 1. SNM is utilized as a metric for stability measurement, representing the ability of the cell to preserve its state when exposed to DC noise variations. The butterfly curve method, commonly used to assess the stability of SRAM cells, is employed in this work. It computes SNM by plotting VTC curve for both the inverter under different opera-tional modes and measuring the length of the edge of the biggest square that fits within the curve. The stability analysis, which includes comparison of various low-power ap-proaches employed in SRAM cell, is displayed in Fig. 4(a),4(b), and Table 1. Notably, WSNM demonstrates an increasing trend for all the employed low-power techniques. Among them, the footer and header approaches stand out with significant increases in WSNM, approximately 21.58% and 20.95% respectively. In the case of HSNM, signif-icant enhancements are noticed in the footer and sleepy methods, in comparison to the standard cell as the data at respective node remains at same level despite of noise dis-ruption thus enhancing HSNM. However, in terms of RSNM, no significant im-provement is observed due to the inherent trade-off between RSNM and WSNM. Fig. 4. (a) RSNM plot for various low power techniques. (b) WSNM plot for various low power techniques Additionally, a comparison is provided in Table 3 among the optimized low-power techniques for the 5nm node GAA CNTFET SRAM cell, specifically focusing on the footer, header, and sleepy approaches with K. Hemanth [22] previously explored and optimized low-power techniques specific to the 32nm CNTFET 6T SRAM cell. Nota-bly, the analysis reveals that there are no significant changes observed in WSNM val-ues. However, when examining the RSNM, interesting trends emerge. The footer, sleepy, and header approaches exhibit notable increases of 53.57%, 70.29%, and (b) (a) 18.11% respectively, in comparison to the corresponding values from the 32nm CNTFET SRAM cell. The footer and header approaches notably stand out with substantial increases in WSNM. Additionally, various techniques, such as sleepy stack, header, stack, leakage feedback stack, sleepy stack keeper, and leakage feedback, have been observed to lead to reduc-tions in delays when compared to the base 6T configuration. Moreover, an interesting trend in leakage power is observed, where the sleepy approach demonstrates the lowest leakage power, surpassing the efficiency of the base 6T SRAM cell, with a trade-off of increased area overhead. Furthermore, a performance comparison is made between our 5nm node low-power SRAM cell and the 32nm low-power SRAM cells, focusing on the aforementioned approaches. Remarkably, the sleepy and zigzag techniques exhibit significant reductions in terms of write delay, while sleepy approach shows substantial decreases in terms of leakage power when contrasted with their 32nm counterparts. Similarly, a stability (SNM) comparison is performed for the identified approaches. In terms of RSNM, the footer, sleepy, and header approaches showcase notable increases. Interestingly, there are no significant changes observed in WSNM values. However, concerning the HSNM metric, both the footer and sleepy approaches exhibit significant increases in stability. args.summary:
This research paper by Devesh Soni and Sumit Saha (National Institute of Technology Rourkela, India) investigates leakage power reduction and stability analysis of 5nm node Gate-All-Around (GAA) Carbon Nanotube Field-Effect Transistor (CNTFET) SRAM cells. The study addresses the challenge of high power consumption in traditional MOS-based SRAM cells used in system-on-chips (SoCs) for portable devices.

The authors designed and evaluated multiple low-power circuit-level techniques applied to a 5nm node GAA CNTFET 6T SRAM cell, categorized as:
- **State-destructive techniques**: Sleepy approach, Header approach, Footer approach, Zigzag approach
- **Non-state destructive techniques**: Stack approach, Leakage feedback approach, Leakage feedback with stack approach, Sleepy keeper approach, Sleepy stack approach, Sleepy stack with keeper approach

Key performance metrics evaluated include noise margin (SNM), delay, and leakage power, using Cadence Virtuoso with the Stanford University Virtual-Source CNTFET model.

**Key Findings:**
- **Leakage Power**: The Sleepy approach demonstrated the lowest leakage power (8.56E-8 pW), significantly outperforming the basic 6T cell (378.6 pW).
- **Write Delay**: Sleepy and Zigzag approaches showed the best reductions (3.89% and 5.03% respectively vs. baseline).
- **Read Delay**: Header, Stack, Sleepy stack, Leakage feedback, Leakage feedback with stack, and Sleepy stack with keeper showed minimal reduction (1.49% to 11.94%).
- **Stability (WSNM)**: Footer and Header approaches showed significant WSNM increases (~21.58% and 20.95% respectively).
- **RSNM**: No significant improvement was observed due to inherent trade-offs between RSNM and WSNM.

**Comparison with 32nm CNTFET SRAM**: The 5nm node designs showed substantial improvements, particularly in write delay (Sleepy stack: 30.37% reduction) and leakage power (Sleepy approach: dramatic decrease vs. 101.9 pW in 32nm).

The paper concludes that while low-power techniques offer significant benefits, there are trade-offs in area overhead and delay that must be carefully considered.

# SRAM Read, Write & Stability Explained: SNM, Sense Amps, Sizing & Vmin
## Abhijit Pethe
1210 subscribers
28 likes

### Description
2981 views
Posted: 2 Nov 2024
SRAM is the fastest memory inside every modern chip — cache, register file, scratchpad. But unlike DRAM, it doesn't just passively hold data. Every read operation actively fights the cell trying to flip its stored value. And every write operation has to win a tug-of-war against the same feedback loop that makes the cell stable in the first place.

This lecture covers the complete SRAM design picture from the 6T bit cell all the way to sense amplifiers, decoders, and scaling limits.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
WHAT YOU'LL LEARN
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

► The 6T SRAM bit cell: how back-to-back inverters create a bistable latch, and why the wordline, bitline, and bit_b together form a complete read/write interface

► SRAM Read operation: why D1 must be stronger than A1 to prevent Q from rising during read — the read stability problem explained with waveforms

► SRAM Write operation: why the write driver must overpower the PMOS pull-up P2 — and why bit_b pulling Q_b low is the key to flipping the cell

► Static Noise Margin (SNM): what it physically means, how the butterfly diagram is constructed, and why the largest inscribed square defines the stability margin for hold, read, and write modes

► Why read margin and write margin are in direct conflict: making D stronger helps read but hurts write — and the transistor sizing rules (β and γ ratios) that balance both

► Cell sizing hierarchy: NMOS pull-down (D) strongest, access transistors (A) intermediate, PMOS pull-up (P) weakest — and why getting this wrong causes yield loss

► Vmin: why VT mismatch from RDF, WF variation, and LG variation creates a distribution of margins — and why any cell with negative SNM is inoperable

► Bitline conditioning and precharge: PMOS precharge to VDD, the equalizer transistor, and why both bit and bit_b must be at identical voltages before a read

► Sense amplifiers — large signal vs small signal: when to let the bitline swing all the way, and when a clocked differential sense amp is needed for speed and power efficiency

► The clocked sense amp: how cross-coupled inverters use regenerative feedback to amplify a tiny differential bitline voltage, and the role of isolation transistors

► Sense amp design pitfalls: differential noise, coupling from adjacent bitlines, offset voltage from process variation and BTI, and the critical timing window

► Row circuitry and decoders: NAND2 + INV implementation, pitch matching to the bitcell, wordline buffering, and why simple decoders only work for 5–6 rows

► Predecoders: how factoring common NAND logic reduces branching effort for large arrays — the 16-word decoder example worked through in detail

► Hierarchical wordlines: global wordline in upper metal for low RC, local wordline in lower metal for short segments — how this manages delay in large arrays

► Leakage in SRAM arrays: all six transistors contribute leakage paths, differential VDD schemes to shut off idle cells, and the worst-case leakage scenario during a read

► 8T SRAM cell: how adding a dedicated read port eliminates the read-stability vs cell-current conflict, and the boosted RWL/RBL advantages

► 10T SRAM cell: how two additional transistors create independent read and write paths, allowing β and γ to be optimized independently without compromising SNM

► SRAM scaling limits: why area scaling has stalled — limited dimensional scaling, Vmin stuck due to process variation, and reliability degradation requiring larger ECC periphery

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
THE CENTRAL INSIGHT
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

The 6T SRAM cell has one fundamental tension: the same feedback strength that makes it stable during hold makes it hard to read without disturbing the state, and hard to write against its own resistance. Every circuit in the SRAM periphery — the access transistors, write drivers, sense amps, and cell sizing ratios — exists to manage this single trade-off.

This is a technical lecture transcript (posted Nov 2, 2024, by Abhijit Pethe, 2,981 views) covering complete SRAM design from the 6T bit cell to sense amplifiers, decoders, and scaling limits.

**Key Concepts:**

- **6T SRAM Bit Cell:** Consists of two back-to-back inverters (pull-up PMOS P1/P2, pull-down NMOS D1/D2) plus two access transistors (A1/A2) controlled by wordline, connected to bitline (bit) and bitline bar (bit_b).

- **Read Operation:** Bitlines are precharged to VDD. Wordline goes high, enabling access transistors. If Q=0, A1 and D1 pull bit down. Critical design constraint: D1 must be stronger than A1 to prevent Q from rising and flipping the cell (read stability).

- **Write Operation:** Write driver forces bit=1, bit_b=0 (to write a 1). Access transistor A2 must overpower PMOS pull-up P2 to pull Q_b low, which then flips Q via positive feedback. Writeability requires P2 weaker than A2.

- **Transistor Sizing Hierarchy:** Pull-down (D) strongest > Access (A) intermediate > Pull-up (P) weakest. The β ratio (W/L of D divided by W/L of A) determines read margin; γ ratio affects write margin.

- **Read vs. Write Conflict:** Making D stronger helps read but hurts write; larger access transistors help write but hurt read. This is the fundamental tension of the 6T SRAM.

- **Static Noise Margin (SNM):** Measured using butterfly diagram (V2 vs. V1 transfer curves). The largest inscribed square defines the stability margin. Three modes: hold SNM, read SNM (reduced compared to hold), and write SNM.

- **Vmin:** The minimum reliable operating voltage. VT mismatch from random dopant fluctuations, work function variation, and gate length variation creates a distribution of margins. Any cell with negative SNM is inoperable. Vmin is driven by process quality, not design.

- **Periphery:** PMOS precharge to VDD with equalizer transistor; clocked differential sense amplifiers using regenerative feedback; NAND2+INV decoders; predecoders for large arrays; hierarchical wordlines (global in upper metal, local in lower metal).

- **Advanced Cells:** 8T SRAM adds dedicated read port to eliminate read-stability vs. cell-current conflict; 10T SRAM allows independent read/write paths for independent β/γ optimization.

- **Scaling Limits:** Area scaling has stalled due to limited dimensional scaling, Vmin stuck from process variation, and reliability degradation requiring larger ECC periphery.

- **Leakage:** All six transistors contribute leakage paths; differential VDD schemes shut off idle cells; worst-case leakage occurs during read.

#### Abstract

Aggressive technology scaling has resulted in stability reduction for classic SRAM designs. This is especially problematic for large integrated circuits. The stability of SRAM cells can be affected by noise during a read operation and by radiation during the standby mode. In this paper, we present an approach to address the gradual stability reduction in SRAM designs. We present an SRAM design tradeoffs approach to improve the characteristics of SRAM by modulating the transistor sizing ratio, ß. We test our approach on various SRAM designs in 32nm technology. We optimize the SRAM designs with ß for various constraints in power consumption, performance, radiation tolerance and data stability. We discuss different design trends produced by the extensive approach analysis.

--- SOURCE 1: Static Noise Margin of 6T SRAM Cell in 90-nm CMOS ---
URL: https://www.academia.edu/107793121/Static_Noise_Margin_of_6T_SRAM_Cell_in_90_nm_CMOS

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an Academia.edu page for a 2011 research paper titled "Static Noise Margin of 6T SRAM Cell in 90-nm CMOS" by Christian Roque, published in the 2011 UkSim 13th International Conference on Computer Modelling and Simulation. The paper examines factors affecting the Static Noise Margin (SNM) of a 6T Static Random Access Memory (SRAM) cell designed in 90-nm CMOS technology. The SRAM cell is simulated to obtain noise margins while varying several parameters: temperature, threshold voltage, supply voltage, cell ratio, pull-up ratio, and process corner variations. Simulation results were found to agree with the model derived by Seevinck et al. (1987) based on the square law device model.

Key findings include:
- SNM is crucial for SRAM stability, determining sensitivity to noise and ensuring data retention.
- Higher cell and pull-up ratios improve read and write noise margins respectively, enhancing stability.
- Temperature variations minimally affect SNM.
- Threshold voltage and process corners notably impact cell performance.
- Noise margins are directly proportional to supply voltage levels; lower voltages lead to greater noise susceptibility.
- SNM is determined using voltage transfer characteristics (VTC) to form a 'butterfly curve', from which the side of the largest square that fits in the curve is defined.

The page also lists 6 references and provides links to approximately 20 related research papers on SRAM cell stability, noise margin analysis, and various SRAM topologies (6T, 8T, 9T, 10T) across different CMOS technology nodes. The author, Christian Roque, has 21 papers and 5 followers on Academia.edu.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"This paper examines the factors that affect the Static Noise Margin (SNM) of a 6T Static Random Access Memory (SRAM) cell designed in 90-nm CMOS.", "The paper evaluates factors affecting Static Noise Margin (SNM) in 6T SRAM cells using 90-nm CMOS technology. Various parameters such as temperature, supply voltage, and ratios significantly influence SNM measurements.", "Higher cell and pull-up ratios improve read and write noise margins, respectively, enhancing stability.", "Temperature variations minimally affect SNM, while threshold voltage and process corners notably impact cell performance.", "The study shows that factors such as supply voltage, pull-up ratio, and threshold voltage significantly impact the static noise margin, highlighting their dependence on operational conditions."
</key_excerpts>



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------


--- SOURCE 2: CN102915771A - SRAM noise margin measuring method - Google Patents ---
URL: https://patents.google.com/patent/CN102915771A/en

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This patent (CN102915771A) describes a method for measuring the Static Noise Margin (SNM) of SRAM memory cells. The SNM is defined as the amplitude of the maximum DC noise signal a memory cell can endure before its stored state is erroneously flipped, making it a critical parameter for evaluating the anti-jamming capability and stability of memory cells, especially under deep-submicron conditions where device parameter fluctuations cause threshold mismatches.

The proposed method improves upon traditional noise margin measurement by:
1. Forming a butterfly diagram from overlapping inverter transfer characteristics under two coordinate systems (F1 curve and F2' symmetric curve).
2. Rotating the x-y coordinate system 90 degrees clockwise to become a u-v coordinate system, where noise margin is the side length of the largest square.
3. Under the u-v coordinate system, subtracting the v value of F2' from F1 yields a curve where |v|max represents the diagonal value of the largest square.
4. Converting this mathematical approach into a circuit simulation using voltage-controlled voltage sources with specific gains (0.7071, 1.4142, -0.7071, -1) connected to inverters within the SRAM.
5. The curveA is obtained from V1-V2, and multiplying by 0.7071 gain yields the accurate noise margin value.

The patent includes simulation results under 40nm technology across various process corners (TT, SS, FF, SF, FS) at different voltages (0.8V, 1.0V) and temperatures (25°C, -40°C, 125°C), with measured noise margin values ranging from 35.7mV to 152.1mV. The invention is assigned to Nanjing University of Science and Technology Changshu Research Institute Co Ltd, with inventors Zhang Zhen and Qi Yong, filed November 1, 2012.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 5: 4.2 SRAM - Noise Margin Analysis - YouTube ---
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lZw_DUvMV6Q

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a lecture from the NPTEL-NOC course "Memory Device Technology for AIML Computing" presented by Dr. Shubhadeep, focused on SRAM cell noise margin analysis, including write timing, static noise margins in hold and read operations, and butterfly curve analysis.

**Key Topics Covered:**

1. **SRAM Write Operation Timing**: The write operation occurs in two phases. Phase 1: The storage node holding value 1 (N2) discharges from 1 to 0 when the pass gate transistor turns on, driven by the bit line bar pre-charged to 0. Phase 2: As N2 approaches 0, pull-up transistor PU1 turns on, charging storage node N1 from 0 to 1. The write process is initiated from the node that previously stored 1, and the crossover point of N1 and N2 occurs close to 0V.

2. **Noise Margin Definition**: The maximum allowable disturbance in internal storage nodes that does not cause the node to flip. The analysis uses static noise analysis (assuming DC/constant disturbance sources) as a simpler introductory approach.

3. **Butterfly Loops and Noise Margin**: The size of the smallest hysteresis loop in the butterfly curve determines the noise margin. Balanced inverters with high gain produce the largest loops and best noise margins.

4. **Ranking of SRAM Cell VTC Characteristics (highest to lowest noise margin)**: A (balanced, ideal/high gain) > B (balanced, poor gain) > C (unbalanced, ideal) > D (unbalanced, non-ideal).

5. **Hold Static Noise Margin (HSNM) Estimation**: Measured by the side of the largest square that can be nested inside the butterfly loop. Practically, this is done by rotating the coordinate axes by 45 degrees, finding the maximum difference between VTC1 and VTC2 (D1 and D2), and computing the side as min(D1/√2, D2/√2).

6. **Read Static Noise Margin (RSNM)**: Significantly smaller than HSNM because during read operations, pass gate transistors are active, disturbing internal storage nodes. The NMOS portion of the VTC gets distorted due to current flow, while the PMOS portion remains relatively unaffected. The internal node never reaches a true 0V (it is 0 + ΔV'), further shrinking the butterfly loop.

7. **Impact of Voltage Scaling**: As supply voltage (VDD) scales down, the butterfly loop shrinks, reducing RSNM. For example, at 400mV VDD, the nested square was 105mV; at 250mV VDD, it shrinks to 45mV. Improving the cell ratio (beta factor) from 2 to 3 can help boost noise margins, but this creates trade-offs with the pull ratio required for write operations, leading to read-write conflicting requirements.
</summary>

5. A statistically-aware optimization approach is applied to 130nm and 65nm technologies, demonstrating significant advantages over worst-case design. The worst-case approach results in ~25% over-design for 130nm and ~40% for 65nm in read stability, and ~15% and ~26% area over-design respectively. SUMMARY:
<summary>
This scientific article, published in Scientific Reports (volume 16, article 16857, 2026), proposes and evaluates a novel 3-Tier CFET (Complementary FET) 6T-SRAM cell architecture that incorporates 2D Transition Metal Dichalcogenides (TMDs) as channel materials for the Angstrom technology node. The key innovations are: (1) replacing silicon channel materials with 2D TMDs (MoS₂ for n-type, WSe₂ for p-type) and (2) advancing from a conventional 2-Tier to a 3-Tier stacked structure.

**Key Findings:**
- The 3-Tier architecture achieves a ~29.5% reduction in bitcell area (8,892 nm² vs. 12,616 nm²) compared to the conventional 2-Tier structure.
- Internal node (Q) capacitance is reduced by 13–22%, leading to >39% lower write energy.
- The write-specialized (2P3N) model achieves over 50.3% energy savings.
- The final optimized design (3-Tier 2P4N+3N_Access) delivers 11.9% improvement in Read Access Time and a 24.9% reduction in Energy-Delay Product (EDP).

**Methodology:**
The research used a hierarchical simulation workflow: 3D structure design in Synopsys Sentaurus TCAD, calibration against experimental data from IMEC's 2D GAA-FET devices, parasitic RC extraction using Synopsys Raphael, and SPICE circuit simulation with HSPICE. The supply voltage was 0.6V (per IRDS 2023 for 1nm node). Four configurations were compared: Conv. (3P3N), 3-Tier (3P3N), 3-Tier (2P3N), and 3-Tier (2P4N+3N_Access).

**Advantages of 2D TMDs:**
- Atomically thin (~0.7 nm) channels enable vertical stacking without significant height increase.
- Low-temperature processing allows multi-layer stacking without thermal damage.
- Excellent electrostatic control and interface properties.

**Advantages of 3-Tier Architecture:**
- Enables independent optimization of PU, PD, and PG transistors.
- Allows tuning of nanosheet stack ratios to control stability-speed trade-offs.
- Reduces parasitic capacitance through structural miniaturization.

**Limitations/Considerations:**
- The 3-Tier structure shows ~87% increase in Q/QB node resistance (156.4Ω vs. 83.6Ω).
- The optimized 3-Tier (2P4N+3N_Access) model exhibits 4.8% HSNM reduction and 6.5% RSNM reduction compared to the symmetric baseline.
- Static stability (HSNM/RSNM) is identical between Conv. 2-Tier and 3-Tier with the same transistor ratios, indicating the structural change alone does not affect stability.

Benchmarking showed a 22% area reduction for outer wall forksheet-based SRAM cells compared to A14 nanosheet designs. SUMMARY:

The paper "Read Stability and Write-Ability Analysis of SRAM Cells for Nanometer Technologies" (IEEE JSSC, Nov. 2006) by Grossar et al. analyzes the N-curve metrics for SRAM cell read stability and write-ability in nanometer CMOS technologies. The authors compare N-curve metrics with the traditional static noise margin (SNM) and write-trip point definitions, and introduce new write-ability metrics derived from the same N-curve.

Key findings include:
1. The N-curve provides both voltage and current information (SVNM/SINM for read stability, WTV/WTI for write-ability), while the traditional SNM only provides voltage information. This current information is critical—two cells with identical SNM can have different stability, only distinguishable by SINM.
2. The N-curve overcomes the scaling limit of Vdd/2 for read stability, as SINM can be improved by upsizing transistors.
3. Analytical models of the N-curve metrics are derived using deep-submicron transistor models, showing good agreement with HSPICE simulations (deviation <10%).
4. Tradeoffs are analyzed: increasing cell ratio improves read stability (SINM improves ~50% when ratio increases from 1.33 to 2) but degrades write-ability. Decreasing pull-up ratio improves write-ability but degrades read stability.
5. A statistically-aware optimization approach is applied to 130nm and 65nm technologies, demonstrating significant advantages over worst-case design. The worst-case approach results in ~25% over-design for 130nm and ~40% for 65nm in read stability, and ~15% and ~26% area over-design respectively. The worst-case approach is infeasible for meeting conflicting read-write constraints in scaled technologies.

The paper concludes that N-curve current information is critical for nanometer SRAM design, and statistically-aware optimization is imperative for future technology nodes.

Phase 1: The storage node holding value 1 (N2) discharges from 1 to 0 when the pass gate transistor turns on, driven by the bit line bar pre-charged to 0. Phase 2: As N2 approaches 0, pull-up transistor PU1 turns on, charging storage node N1 from 0 to 1. The write process is initiated from the node that previously stored 1, and the crossover point of N1 and N2 occurs close to 0V.

2. **Noise Margin Definition**: The maximum allowable disturbance in internal storage nodes that does not cause the node to flip. The analysis uses static noise analysis (assuming DC/constant disturbance sources) as a simpler introductory approach.

3. **Butterfly Loops and Noise Margin**: The size of the smallest hysteresis loop in the butterfly curve determines the noise margin. Balanced inverters with high gain produce the largest loops and best noise margins.

4. **Ranking of SRAM Cell VTC Characteristics (highest to lowest noise margin)**: A (balanced, ideal/high gain) > B (balanced, poor gain) > C (unbalanced, ideal) > D (unbalanced, non-ideal).

5. **Hold Static Noise Margin (HSNM) Estimation**: Measured by the side of the largest square that can be nested inside the butterfly loop. Practically, this is done by rotating the coordinate axes by 45 degrees, finding the maximum difference between VTC1 and VTC2 (D1 and D2), and computing the side as min(D1/√2, D2/√2).

6. **Read Static Noise Margin (RSNM)**: Significantly smaller than HSNM because during read operations, pass gate transistors are active, disturbing internal storage nodes. The NMOS portion of the VTC gets distorted due to current flow, while the PMOS portion remains relatively unaffected. The internal node never reaches a true 0V (it is 0 + ΔV'), further shrinking the butterfly loop.

7. **Impact of Voltage Scaling**: As supply voltage (VDD) scales down, the butterfly loop shrinks, reducing RSNM. For example, at 400mV VDD, the nested square was 105mV; at 250mV VDD, it shrinks to 45mV. Improving the cell ratio (beta factor) from 2 to 3 can help boost noise margins, but this creates trade-offs with the pull ratio required for write operations, leading to read-write conflicting requirements.

--- SOURCE 5: 4.2 SRAM - Noise Margin Analysis - YouTube ---
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lZw_DUvMV6Q

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a lecture from the NPTEL-NOC course "Memory Device Technology for AIML Computing" presented by Dr. Shubhadeep, focused on SRAM cell noise margin analysis, including write timing, static noise margins in hold and read operations, and butterfly curve analysis.

**Key Topics Covered:**

1. **SRAM Write Operation Timing**: The write operation occurs in two phases. Phase 1: The storage node holding value 1 (N2) discharges from 1 to 0 when the pass gate transistor turns on, driven by the bit line bar pre-charged to 0. Phase 2: As N2 approaches 0, pull-up transistor PU1 turns on, charging storage node N1 from 0 to 1. The write process is initiated from the node that previously stored 1, and the crossover point of N1 and N2 occurs close to 0V.

2. **Noise Margin Definition**: The maximum allowable disturbance in internal storage nodes that does not cause the node to flip. The analysis uses static noise analysis (assuming DC/constant disturbance sources) as a simpler introductory approach.

3. **Butterfly Loops and Noise Margin**: The size of the smallest hysteresis loop in the butterfly curve determines the noise margin. Balanced inverters with high gain produce the largest loops and best noise margins.

4. **Ranking of SRAM Cell VTC Characteristics (highest to lowest noise margin)**: A (balanced, ideal/high gain) > B (balanced, poor gain) > C (unbalanced, ideal) > D (unbalanced, non-ideal).

5. **Hold Static Noise Margin (HSNM) Estimation**: Measured by the side of the largest square that can be nested inside the butterfly loop. Practically, this is done by rotating the coordinate axes by 45 degrees, finding the maximum difference between VTC1 and VTC2 (D1 and D2), and computing the side as min(D1/√2, D2/√2).

6. **Read Static Noise Margin (RSNM)**: Significantly smaller than HSNM because during read operations, pass gate transistors are active, disturbing internal storage nodes. The NMOS portion of the VTC gets distorted due to current flow, while the PMOS portion remains relatively unaffected. The internal node never reaches a true 0V (it is 0 + ΔV'), further shrinking the butterfly loop.

7. **Impact of Voltage Scaling**: As supply voltage (VDD) scales down, the butterfly loop shrinks, reducing RSNM. For example, at 400mV VDD, the nested square was 105mV; at 250mV VDD, it shrinks to 45mV. Improving the cell ratio (beta factor) from 2 to 3 can help boost noise margins, but this creates trade-offs with the pull ratio required for write operations, leading to read-write conflicting requirements.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper presents a black box method for stability analysis of arbitrary SRAM cell structures, developed by researchers at the University of Michigan and ARM R&D. The technique uses vector field analysis to extract both static and dynamic stability characteristics of SRAM cells without requiring transient simulations or DC convergence operations.

**Key Contributions:**
1. The method quantizes the SRAM cell state-space into a grid (e.g., 50x50), instantiating multiple cells in a netlist with fixed DC voltage sources, then computes time derivatives from current and capacitance values using model equations (no transient simulation needed).
2. Demonstrates that traditional Seevinck butterfly curves are equivalent to closed-loop dynamical nullcline traces from the proposed method.
3. Introduces a separatrix tracing algorithm that interpolates vectors from the metastable point to the state-space boundary.
4. Proposes a new "separatrix affinity" metric for cell robustness, which integrates dV/dt vectors from each stable node to its closest separatrix point.

**Results:**
- Total execution time for a 50x50 grid analysis of a 6T cell is ~33 seconds (84% model solution, 15% separatrix tracing), representing a several thousand times speedup over brute-force transient approaches.
- Over 500 runs, standard butterfly SNM and nullcline SNM showed high correlation.
- 20,000 Monte Carlo runs with importance sampling showed that the separatrix affinity metric is more sensitive to cell robustness (200% range) compared to traditional SNM (~10% range), making it better for optimization.
- The method works for arbitrary cell topologies including asymmetric cells, 5T, 8T, and Portless SRAM cells (first reported butterfly curve for Portless 5T cell).

**Conclusions:** The technique enables qualification of transient operations (write, wordline boosting, data retention voltage) without explicit transient simulations, and is compatible with standard design tools.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This IEEE Spectrum article reports on record SRAM memory densities unveiled at the IEEE International Solid State Circuits Conference (ISSCC) on February 26, 2025. Intel and TSMC detailed SRAM built using their newest nanosheet transistor technologies (Intel 18A and TSMC N2), achieving 38.1 megabits per square millimeter with a 0.021 square micrometer memory cell—a 23% density boost for Intel and 12% for TSMC. Synopsys separately achieved the same density using older 3nm FinFET technology but at less than half the speed (2.3 GHz vs. 4.2 GHz for TSMC and 5.6 GHz for Intel).

Nanosheet transistors, which replace fin-shaped channels with adjustable silicon ribbons, allow more flexible transistor sizing, enabling SRAM scaling improvements. Intel's 18A technology also incorporates backside power delivery networks (though not inside the bit cell itself), while TSMC's N2 extended bit-line length from 256 to 512 bits for a ~10% density gain. Synopsys achieved density parity through an interface dual-rail architecture and extended-range level shifters that allow wider voltage separation (bit cells: 0.54-1.4V, periphery: as low as 0.38V), though at lower speed.
</summary>

SUMMARY:

Samsung is moving to nanosheet/MBCFET transistors at its 3-nanometer node (expected 2022), while TSMC plans to stay with FinFETs for 3nm. The key advantage: nanosheets allow tuning of transistor "effective width" (Weff) by varying the width of silicon sheets, whereas FinFETs only allow doubling or tripling Weff by adding fins. Samsung engineers exploited this flexibility to design SRAM cells with improved write margin — the minimum voltage needed to switch the cell's state. --- SOURCE 7: Read Stability and Write-Ability Analysis of SRAM Cells for ... ---
URL: https://lirias.kuleuven.be/retrieve/109654

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The paper "Read Stability and Write-Ability Analysis of SRAM Cells for Nanometer Technologies" (IEEE JSSC, Nov. 2006) by Grossar et al. analyzes the N-curve metrics for SRAM cell read stability and write-ability in nanometer CMOS technologies. The authors compare N-curve metrics with the traditional static noise margin (SNM) and write-trip point definitions, and introduce new write-ability metrics derived from the same N-curve.

Key findings include:
1. The N-curve provides both voltage and current information (SVNM/SINM for read stability, WTV/WTI for write-ability), while the traditional SNM only provides voltage information. This current information is critical—two cells with identical SNM can have different stability, only distinguishable by SINM.
2. The N-curve overcomes the scaling limit of Vdd/2 for read stability, as SINM can be improved by upsizing transistors.
3. Analytical models of the N-curve metrics are derived using deep-submicron transistor models, showing good agreement with HSPICE simulations (deviation <10%).
4. Tradeoffs are analyzed: increasing cell ratio improves read stability (SINM improves ~50% when ratio increases from 1.33 to 2) but degrades write-ability. Decreasing pull-up ratio improves write-ability but degrades read stability.
5. A statistically-aware optimization approach is applied to 130nm and 65nm technologies, demonstrating significant advantages over worst-case design. The worst-case approach results in ~25% over-design for 130nm and ~40% for 65nm in read stability, and ~15% and ~26% area over-design respectively. The worst-case approach is infeasible for meeting conflicting read-write constraints in scaled technologies.

The paper concludes that N-curve current information is critical for nanometer SRAM design, and statistically-aware optimization is imperative for future technology nodes.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
The N-curve contains information both on the read stability and on the write-ability, thus allowing a complete functional analysis of the SRAM cell with only one N-curve, "This extension in using the N-curve for the write-ability is reported here for the first time.", "Two different SRAM cells can have identical values for both the SNM and SVNM, but this does not mean that they are equally stable... This difference is only visible in the factor 2 improvement of the SINM of cell 2 with respect to cell 1, while the SNM and SVNM values are the same for both cell designs.", "With the worst-case design approach, meeting the SINM constraint results in over-designing for the actual read stability (~25% for 130nm and ~40% for 65nm) and for the area (~15% for 130nm and ~26% for 65nm).", "The increasing over-design and the hard-to-meet design criteria make the statistically-aware circuit optimization very promising for SRAM cell designs in future technology nodes."

--- SOURCE 8: SRAM cache power leakage solutions below 3nm | Patsnap ---
URL: https://www.patsnap.com/resources/blog/articles/sram-cache-power-leakage-solutions-below-3nm

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This PatSnap Insights article examines SRAM cache power leakage challenges at sub-3nm process nodes. At these advanced nodes, four leakage mechanisms (sub-threshold, gate, GIDL, and junction leakage) converge simultaneously, making single-mechanism solutions insufficient. Even 100 picoamperes of leakage per cell aggregates to 100 milliamperes at the chip level across a billion-cell array.

The article analyzes over 50 patents across five jurisdictions, identifying key techniques:

**Device-Level Techniques:** High-Vt transistors with thicker gate oxides or high-k dielectrics (IBM, 2004-2006) suppress sub-threshold leakage exponentially. Asymmetric transistor engineering (Texas Instruments, 2009) selectively suppresses GIDL. Multi-Vt intra-chip strategies (Panasonic, 2004) balance leakage and performance.

**Body Biasing:** Oki Electric (2007) demonstrated dual biasing (substrate bias for PMOS, source bias for NMOS) during standby. However, below 90nm, parasitic RC makes rapid Vt switching impractical (Renesas, 2008).

**Power Gating & Virtual Rails:** IBM (2008-2009) introduced virtual voltage rails with sensing elements to regulate potential without floating ground nodes. TSMC (2017) implemented pulsed dynamic low cell voltage circuits. ARM (2021) introduced per-bank dynamic power gating based on hit bandwidth vs. leakage cost.

**System-Level Strategies:** Fudan University (2016) uses ECC-assisted iterative voltage reduction to find minimum retention voltage. Qualcomm (2016) developed 5T SRAM topologies. Chinese institutions (Tianjin University, CAS) target compute-in-memory leakage recycling.

**Key Players:** IBM is the most prolific assignee, followed by Renesas, Samsung, TSMC, Qualcomm, Fujitsu, and Oki. Chinese academic institutions represent a growing cohort. A temporal trend shows pre-2010 patents focused on device-level Vt engineering and body biasing, while post-2015 patents increasingly integrate PVT-tracking adaptive control, ECC-assisted standby, and system-level power gating.

The defining characteristic of state-of-the-art sub-3nm SRAM leakage management is convergence on multi-technique approaches combining high-Vt cells, adaptive body biasing, power gating with virtual rails, dynamic retention voltage scaling, and asymmetric device doping.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"At below-3nm nodes, no single technique is sufficient. State-of-the-art implementations combine high-Vt cell transistors, adaptive body biasing, power gating with virtual rails, dynamic retention voltage scaling, and asymmetric device doping to simultaneously address sub-threshold, gate, GIDL, and junction leakage.", "Sub-threshold leakage current grows exponentially with decreasing threshold voltage (Vt) and with increasing drain-to-source voltage (Vds)—meaning that in an SRAM array with millions or billions of transistors, even 100 picoamperes of leakage per cell aggregates to 100 milliamperes at the chip level", "Body biasing for SRAM leakage reduction becomes RC-limited at process nodes below 90nm: large parasitic capacitance and resistance of well nodes make rapid threshold voltage switching impractical for high-speed SRAMs with 1 nanosecond access times", "A clear temporal trend emerges from the dataset: early patents (pre-2010) focus predominantly on device-level Vt engineering and body biasing... Post-2015 patents increasingly integrate PVT-tracking adaptive voltage control, ECC-assisted minimum-voltage standby, and system-level power gating as the dominant paradigms", "IBM is the single most prolific assignee, with patents covering multi-threshold device selection, SOI/bulk hybrid SRAM structures, virtual power rail leakage control, dynamic leakage reduction integrated with write assist, high-k dielectric interconnects for SNM and leakage improvement, and cell layout optimisation for pass-gate leakage."

--- SOURCE 10: 3-Tier CFET 6T-SRAM with 2D-TMDs channels for Angstrom technology node | Scientific Reports ---
URL: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37881-5

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This scientific article, published in Scientific Reports (volume 16, article 16857, 2026), proposes and evaluates a novel 3-Tier CFET (Complementary FET) 6T-SRAM cell architecture that incorporates 2D Transition Metal Dichalcogenides (TMDs) as channel materials for the Angstrom technology node. The key innovations are: (1) replacing silicon channel materials with 2D TMDs (MoS₂ for n-type, WSe₂ for p-type) and (2) advancing from a conventional 2-Tier to a 3-Tier stacked structure.

**Key Findings:**
- The 3-Tier architecture achieves a ~29.5% reduction in bitcell area (8,892 nm² vs. 12,616 nm²) compared to the conventional 2-Tier structure.
- Internal node (Q) capacitance is reduced by 13–22%, leading to >39% lower write energy.
- The write-specialized (2P3N) model achieves over 50.3% energy savings.
- The final optimized design (3-Tier 2P4N+3N_Access) delivers 11.9% improvement in Read Access Time and a 24.9% reduction in Energy-Delay Product (EDP).

**Methodology:**
The research used a hierarchical simulation workflow: 3D structure design in Synopsys Sentaurus TCAD, calibration against experimental data from IMEC's 2D GAA-FET devices, parasitic RC extraction using Synopsys Raphael, and SPICE circuit simulation with HSPICE. The supply voltage was 0.6V (per IRDS 2023 for 1nm node). Four configurations were compared: Conv. (3P3N), 3-Tier (3P3N), 3-Tier (2P3N), and 3-Tier (2P4N+3N_Access).

**Advantages of 2D TMDs:**
- Atomically thin (~0.7 nm) channels enable vertical stacking without significant height increase.
- Low-temperature processing allows multi-layer stacking without thermal damage.
- Excellent electrostatic control and interface properties.

**Advantages of 3-Tier Architecture:**
- Enables independent optimization of PU, PD, and PG transistors.
- Allows tuning of nanosheet stack ratios to control stability-speed trade-offs.
- Reduces parasitic capacitance through structural miniaturization.

**Limitations/Considerations:**
- The 3-Tier structure shows ~87% increase in Q/QB node resistance (156.4Ω vs. 83.6Ω).
- The optimized 3-Tier (2P4N+3N_Access) model exhibits 4.8% HSNM reduction and 6.5% RSNM reduction compared to the symmetric baseline.
- Static stability (HSNM/RSNM) is identical between Conv. 2-Tier and 3-Tier with the same transistor ratios, indicating the structural change alone does not affect stability.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The proposed 3-Tier CFET architecture demonstrates a significant cell area reduction of approximately 29.5% compared with the Conventional 2-Tier structure.", "This miniaturization lowers the internal-node capacitance by 13–22%, yielding markedly better write performance (e.g. >39% lower write energy).", "The optimized design (2P4N+3N_Access) improves read-access time by 11.9% while maintaining robust write characteristics. This synergistic optimization results in a 24.9% reduction in the Energy-Delay Product (EDP).", "The structural transition from a 2-Tier to a 3-Tier architecture, in itself, has a negligible effect on the cell's static stability, provided that the relative transistor strengths are maintained.", "The 3-Tier structure, with its scaled footprint achieved through vertical stacking, reduces interaction with the WL and Q nodes, lowering the WL-BL coupling."

--- SOURCE 15: Outer wall forksheet: bridging nanosheet and CFET | imec ---
URL: https://www.imec-int.com/en/articles/outer-wall-forksheet-bridge-nanosheet-and-cfet-device-architectures-logic-technology

SUMMARY:
<summary>
Imec introduced the "outer wall forksheet" device architecture at VLSI 2025 as an improved evolution of their earlier "inner wall" forksheet design. The forksheet architecture was originally introduced in 2017 to extend the gate-all-around (GAA) nanosheet-based logic roadmap to the A10 technology node, bridging the gap before complementary FET (CFET) technology becomes viable for mass production starting at the A7 node.

The original inner wall forksheet placed a dielectric wall between nMOS and pMOS devices, enabling tighter n-to-p spacing and cell area scaling down to 90nm cell height. However, it faced manufacturability challenges: the wall needed to be extremely thin (8-10nm), was exposed to aggressive front-end-of-line (FEOL) etching steps, required precise p/n mask alignment, obstructed p-n connected gates, and used a tri-gate structure with limited channel control.

The new outer wall forksheet places the dielectric wall at the standard cell boundary (as a p-p or n-n wall), allowing it to be thicker (~15nm) and shared with neighboring cells. Key improvements include: (1) a wall-last integration approach using mainstream silicon dioxide, (2) relaxed wall width for process simplification, (3) easily connected n-p gates, (4) superior gate control via a Ω-gate structure (achieved by 5nm wall etch-back, boosting drive current by ~25%), and (5) the ability to achieve full channel strain through effective source/drain stressors, enabled by a Si spine that acts as a seed crystal template.

Benchmarking showed a 22% area reduction for outer wall forksheet-based SRAM cells compared to A14 nanosheet designs. Ring oscillator simulations indicated the outer wall forksheet maintains frequency performance at the A10 node, provided full channel stress can be enabled. Imec is now investigating compatibility of the outer wall design with CFET architecture.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 18: Entering the nanosheet transistor era | imec ---
URL: https://www.imec-int.com/en/articles/entering-nanosheet-transistor-era-0

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This longread article from imec, authored by Naoto Horiguchi (Director of CMOS Device Technology), reviews the transition from FinFET to nanosheet transistor architectures for 3nm and 2nm logic chip production, as announced by Samsung, Intel, TSMC, and IBM from 2022/2023 onward.

**Why Nanosheet over FinFET:** FinFET scaling faces challenges as fin depopulation reduces drive current. Nanosheet architectures vertically stack conduction channels, providing larger drive current per footprint, variable device width, and improved gate control via a gate-all-around structure.

**Critical Process Challenges:** Four key innovations were required: (1) epitaxial Si/SiGe multilayers for channel definition with shape control, (2) inner spacer formation (most complex step), (3) nanosheet channel release requiring highly selective etching, and (4) replacement metal gate (RMG) integration with scalable work function metals.

**Forksheet Architecture:** Proposed by imec (2017 for SRAM, 2019 for logic), forksheet introduces a dielectric wall between n- and pMOS devices, enabling tighter n-p spacing, larger effective channel width, and potential scaling to 4T standard cells. Imec demonstrated dual work function metal gates at 17nm n-p spacing (VLSI 2021) with comparable electrostatic control to nanosheet devices.

**CFET Architecture:** The ultimate nanosheet family member stacks n- and pMOS vertically, removing n-p spacing from cell height considerations. Two integration schemes exist: monolithic (complex vertical integration, lower cost) and sequential (simpler processing, supports hybrid channel materials, but challenged by thermal budget constraints and wafer bonding). Imec demonstrated the first monolithically integrated CFET on 300mm wafers (VLSI 2020) and continues developing solutions for sequential integration challenges including low-temperature gate-stack reliability and dopant activation.
</summary>
