Sleight†, Robert H. Dennard, Robert K. Montoye, Lidija Sekaric, Sharee J. McNab, Anna W. Topol, Charlotte D. Adams, Kathryn W. Guarini, and Wilfried Haensch IBM Semiconductor Research and Development Center (SRDC) T. J. Watson Research Center, Yorktown Heights, NY 10598, †Microelectronics Division, Hopewell Junction, NY 12533 *e-mail: lelandc@us.ibm.com phone: (914) 945-2329 Abstract SRAM cell stability will be a primary concern for future technologies due to variability and decreasing power supply volt-ages. 6T-SRAM can be optimized for stability by choosing the cell layout, device threshold voltages, and the ß ratio. 8T-SRAM, however, provides a much greater enhancement in stability by eliminating cell disturbs during a read access, thus facilitating continued technology scaling. We demonstrate the smallest 6T (0.124μm2 half-cell) and full 8T (0.1998μm2) cells to date.
Introduction As memory begins to dominate chip area in high performance applications, SRAM has become the focus of technology scaling [1,2]. Traditionally, SRAM cell size has scaled in accordance with technology ground rules; however, with the growing impor-tance of variability, it is feared that this may no longer be possi-ble. Because minimum gate length and width devices are used to minimize cell area, SRAM is most susceptible to both process-induced variations in device geometry as well as threshold volt-age variability due to dopant fluctuations [3]. In addition, the impact of variability is most pronounced in SRAM because cell operation, which depends upon well-matched FETs, must be sat-isfactory for each individual cell (no averaging across multiple stages as in logic). The fundamental concern of cell stability [4], which determines minimum array operating voltage and yield, has thus become increasingly difficult to address.
In this work, SRAM (half) cells with areas down to 0.124μm2 [1] provide the unique opportunity to study device set points to maximize cell stability. The device structure (25nm SOI, 15nm spacer, single-implant S/D, 12nm CoSi2) is chosen to accommo-date aggressively scaled SRAM. Ground rules are scaled in ac-cordance with process capabilities to achieve different cell areas.
As SRAM is scaled, sufficient static noise margin (SNM) be-comes difficult to maintain (Fig. 1) due both to increased varia-tion and shifting of device characteristics from design targets (conceptually, these are equivalent to noise). In particular, mis-match between the reflected SNMs of the two halves of a cell is enhanced (Fig. 2) due to aggressive ground rules and dopant fluc-tuations. In addition, narrow-width or short-channel effects de-grade SNM by distorting inverter transfer characteristics.
6T-SRAM Cell Optimization SRAM cell layout can be optimized to minimize variability by converting the “Thincell” [5] active pattern to a straight line layout (eliminating jogs and corners, thereby increasing reliance on metal interconnect). This facilitates lithography and reduces sensitivity to overlay errors, which improves mismatch and criti-cal dimension control, thus increasing SNM (Fig. 3).
The cell ß ratio (Fig. 4) balances performance, stability, and area. For stability, increasing ß (thus growing the cell size) re-duces the disturb voltage on the “0” node of the cell and lowers the switch point of the cross-coupled inverters (Fig. 5). The two mechanisms have opposing effects on SNM and result in an op-timum stability for ß~2-3 (Fig. 6). Since ß has very little impact on SNM in this range, ß~2 may be desired to minimize cell area.
A low pFET VT for the pull-up device and high nFET VT for the pass-gate device are desirable to maximize SNM (Fig. 7), though both result in degraded performance. By setting ß=2, fur-ther adjustment of the nFET pull-down VT has little impact on SNM (Fig. 8). Thus, it is practical to set it to be the same as the nFET pass-gate VT (i.e. to minimize nFET narrow-width effect).
Functional SRAM cells down to 0.143μm2 [1] and half-cells down to 0.124μm2 (Fig. 9) in cell area were fabricated. Ground rules for 0.124μm2 cells are similar to [1], except for shorter gate lengths (35nm) and tighter overlay margins. ß=1 minimizes cell size, but degrades SNM by increasing the read disturb voltage.
An 8T-SRAM Cell with Improved Stability The fundamental stability problem in 6T cells is that in the read condition, a pass-gate pulls the “0” storage node up to a non-zero value (circled in Fig. 10a). Adding two FETs to a 6T cell provides a read mechanism that does not disturb the internal nodes of the cell (Fig. 10b), thereby eliminating the worst-case stability condition. This requires separate read and write word lines and can accommodate dual-port operation with separate read and write bit lines. Without read disturbs, the worst-case stability condition for an 8T cell is that for two cross-coupled inverters, which provides a significantly larger SNM (Fig. 11). A dramatic stability improvement can thus be achieved without a tradeoff in performance since a read access is still performed by two stacked nFETs. An efficient layout for this cell is achieved by extending the gate shape for one inverter in a ß=1 6T cell (Fig. 12). This accommodates the additional FET stack at an area pen-alty of only ~30% as compared with a compact ß=2 6T cell.
While other 8T configurations are possible, this cell is very lay-out efficient, provides the maximum SNM by decoupling cell nodes during read and write operations, and can even provide a performance advantage over 6T if the pass-gates and read stack are designed to be strong devices. 8T-SRAM cells have been fabricated down to 0.1998μm2 in area with improved SNM (Fig. 13). The 8T cell provides especially pronounced benefits at low VDD (Fig. 14) even when 6T ground rules are relaxed.
Summary SRAM cell design strategies have been discussed to maxi-mize cell stability. While 6T-SRAM can be optimized for stabil-ity, much larger gains can be realized with 8T-SRAM cell. A ~30% area penalty is incurred with the addition of two extra FETs, but 8T-SRAM can allow for continued scaling beyond that which is possible with traditional 6T-SRAM.

args.summary:
This paper from the 2005 Symposium on VLSI Technology, authored by Leland Chang and colleagues at IBM Semiconductor Research and Development Center, addresses SRAM cell stability for the 32 nm node and beyond. It highlights that SRAM cell stability is a primary concern due to increasing variability and decreasing power supply voltages. The authors explore two approaches: 6T-SRAM optimization and 8T-SRAM design.

For 6T-SRAM, cell stability (static noise margin or SNM) can be improved through: (1) straight-line active layout (replacing Thincell patterns) to reduce lithography sensitivity; (2) optimizing the ß ratio (pull-down to pass-gate strength), with optimal SNM at ß~2-3; and (3) selecting device threshold voltages (low pFET VT for pull-up, high nFET VT for pass-gate). The smallest demonstrated 6T half-cell was 0.124 μm².

The 8T-SRAM cell adds two extra FETs to decouple read and write operations, eliminating read disturbs entirely. This provides significantly larger SNM compared to 6T cells, especially at low VDD, at only ~30% area penalty over a compact 6T cell. The smallest fabricated 8T cell was 0.1998 μm². The paper concludes that while 6T-SRAM can be optimized, 8T-SRAM enables continued scaling beyond what is possible with traditional 6T-SRAM.

Device structure used: 25nm SOI, 15nm spacer, single-implant S/D, 12nm CoSi₂, with gate lengths down to 35nm for the smallest cells.

# SRAM Read, Write & Stability Explained: SNM, Sense Amps, Sizing & Vmin
## Abhijit Pethe
1210 subscribers
28 likes

### Description
2981 views
Posted: 2 Nov 2024
SRAM is the fastest memory inside every modern chip — cache, register file, scratchpad. But unlike DRAM, it doesn't just passively hold data. Every read operation actively fights the cell trying to flip its stored value. And every write operation has to win a tug-of-war against the same feedback loop that makes the cell stable in the first place.

This lecture covers the complete SRAM design picture from the 6T bit cell all the way to sense amplifiers, decoders, and scaling limits.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
WHAT YOU'LL LEARN
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

► The 6T SRAM bit cell: how back-to-back inverters create a bistable latch, and why the wordline, bitline, and bit_b together form a complete read/write interface

► SRAM Read operation: why D1 must be stronger than A1 to prevent Q from rising during read — the read stability problem explained with waveforms

► SRAM Write operation: why the write driver must overpower the PMOS pull-up P2 — and why bit_b pulling Q_b low is the key to flipping the cell

► Static Noise Margin (SNM): what it physically means, how the butterfly diagram is constructed, and why the largest inscribed square defines the stability margin for hold, read, and write modes

► Why read margin and write margin are in direct conflict: making D stronger helps read but hurts write — and the transistor sizing rules (β and γ ratios) that balance both

► Cell sizing hierarchy: NMOS pull-down (D) strongest, access transistors (A) intermediate, PMOS pull-up (P) weakest — and why getting this wrong causes yield loss

► Vmin: why VT mismatch from RDF, WF variation, and LG variation creates a distribution of margins — and why any cell with negative SNM is inoperable

► Bitline conditioning and precharge: PMOS precharge to VDD, the equalizer transistor, and why both bit and bit_b must be at identical voltages before a read

► Sense amplifiers — large signal vs small signal: when to let the bitline swing all the way, and when a clocked differential sense amp is needed for speed and power efficiency

► The clocked sense amp: how cross-coupled inverters use regenerative feedback to amplify a tiny differential bitline voltage, and the role of isolation transistors

► Sense amp design pitfalls: differential noise, coupling from adjacent bitlines, offset voltage from process variation and BTI, and the critical timing window

► Row circuitry and decoders: NAND2 + INV implementation, pitch matching to the bitcell, wordline buffering, and why simple decoders only work for 5–6 rows

► Predecoders: how factoring common NAND logic reduces branching effort for large arrays — the 16-word decoder example worked through in detail

► Hierarchical wordlines: global wordline in upper metal for low RC, local wordline in lower metal for short segments — how this manages delay in large arrays

► Leakage in SRAM arrays: all six transistors contribute leakage paths, differential VDD schemes to shut off idle cells, and the worst-case leakage scenario during a read

► 8T SRAM cell: how adding a dedicated read port eliminates the read-stability vs cell-current conflict, and the boosted RWL/RBL advantages

► 10T SRAM cell: how two additional transistors create independent read and write paths, allowing β and γ to be optimized independently without compromising SNM

► SRAM scaling limits: why area scaling has stalled — limited dimensional scaling, Vmin stuck due to process variation, and reliability degradation requiring larger ECC periphery

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
THE CENTRAL INSIGHT
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

The 6T SRAM cell has one fundamental tension: the same feedback strength that makes it stable during hold makes it hard to read without disturbing the state, and hard to write against its own resistance. Every circuit in the SRAM periphery — the access transistors, write drivers, sense amps, and cell sizing ratios — exists to manage this single trade-off.

args.summary:
This is a technical lecture on SRAM (Static Random-Access Memory) design, covering the complete picture from the 6T bit cell to sense amplifiers, decoders, and scaling limits. The lecture was presented by Abhijit Pethe on November 2, 2024.

**Key Topics Covered:**

- **6T SRAM Bit Cell:** Two back-to-back inverters create a bistable latch, with access transistors (A1, A2), pull-down NMOS (D1, D2), and pull-up PMOS (P1, P2) forming the read/write interface via wordline, bitline, and bit_b.

- **Read Operation:** During read, bitlines are pre-charged to VDD. If Q=0, A1 and D1 pull the bitline down. The key challenge is read stability: D1 must be stronger than A1 to prevent Q from rising enough to flip the cell's state.

- **Write Operation:** To write, the write driver must overpower the PMOS pull-up (P2). For a write-1, bit_b is pulled low; A2 must be stronger than P2 to pull Q_b down, triggering the feedback loop to flip the cell.

- **Static Noise Margin (SNM):** Quantified using butterfly diagrams (V2 vs V1). The largest inscribed square defines the stability margin. SNM is evaluated for hold, read, and write modes separately.

- **Sizing Conflict:** Read margin and write margin are in direct conflict. Making D stronger helps read but hurts write. The sizing hierarchy is: NMOS pull-down (D) strongest, access transistors (A) intermediate, PMOS pull-up (P) weakest. This is captured by the β ratio (W/L of pull-down divided by W/L of access transistor).

- **Vmin:** VT mismatch from RDF (Random Dopant Fluctuation), work function variation, and gate length variation creates a distribution of margins. Any cell with negative SNM is inoperable. Vmin is the minimum voltage at which the SRAM can reliably operate.

- **Periphery Circuits:** Bitline precharge with PMOS to VDD and equalizer; clocked differential sense amplifiers using cross-coupled inverters with regenerative feedback; row decoders (NAND2+INV) with pitch matching; predecoders for large arrays; hierarchical wordlines (global in upper metal, local in lower metal).

- **Advanced Cells:** 8T SRAM adds a dedicated read port to eliminate the read-stability vs. cell-current conflict. 10T SRAM adds independent read and write paths, allowing β and γ ratios to be optimized independently.

- **Scaling Limits:** Area scaling has stalled due to limited dimensional scaling, Vmin stuck due to process variation, and reliability degradation requiring larger ECC periphery.

**Central Insight:** The 6T SRAM cell has a fundamental tension: the same feedback strength that makes it stable during hold makes it hard to read without disturbing the state and hard to write against its own resistance. Every circuit in the SRAM periphery exists to manage this single trade-off.

## Abstract

The critical charge of sensitive nodes decreases as transistors scale down with the advancement of CMOS technology, making SRAM cells more susceptible to soft errors in the space industry. When a radiation particle strikes a sensitive node of a conventional 6T SRAM cell, a single event upset (SEU) can occur, flipping in the stored data in the cell. Additionally, charge sharing between transistors can cause single-event multi-node upsets (SEMNUs), where data in multiple nodes are flipped simultaneously due to a single particle strike. Therefore, this paper proposes a radiation-hardened high stability 16T (RHHS16T) cell for space applications. The characteristics of RHHS16T are evaluated and compared with previously proposed radiation-hardened SRAM cells such as QUCCE12T, WEQUATRO, RHBD10T, RHD12T, RSP14T, RHPD14T, and RHBD14T. Simulation results for RHHS16T indicated that the proposed cell demonstrates improved performance in read stability, write access time, and write stability compared to all comparison cells. These improvements in the proposed cell are achieved with higher power consumption and a minor area penalty. Notably, isolating the storage node from the bit line during read operations and the feedback loop between nodes during write operations enables the proposed RHHS16T to achieve enhanced read stability and write stability, respectively. The proposed integrated circuit was implemented using a 90 nm CMOS process and operates at a supply voltage of 1V. Furthermore, RHHS16T provides high immunity against SEUs and SEMNUs. Through its enhanced read and write stability, it ensures reliable data retention for space applications.

## 1. Introduction

With the advancement of space exploration and the space industry, satellite communication technology has been used in various fields such as disaster monitoring, broadcasting, and military operations. Satellite communication technology provides wide-area service regardless of the ground network structure, offering significant advantages [[1](#B1-applsci-14-11940)]. For these satellites to function, memory devices are required, and static random-access memory (SRAM) is evaluated as suitable memory for satellite communication technology due to its high density and enhanced logic performance [[2](#B2-applsci-14-11940),[3](#B3-applsci-14-11940)]. However, the presence of numerous high-energy particles in space can cause a significant threat to the operation of memory devices that store data. When high-energy particles strike the sensitive nodes of integrated circuits, electron–hole pairs are formed, resulting in a short pulse current of voltage known as single event transient (SET) [[4](#B4-applsci-14-11940)]. This can lead to soft errors of a single event upset (SEU). SRAM is composed of a cross-coupled inverter structure, which inherently involves a feedback mechanism. In such a configuration, radiation exposure can lead to alterations in the data stored not only in the sensitive node but also in the interconnected nodes [[5](#B5-applsci-14-11940)]. With the advancement of CMOS technology, a single ion strike can affect multiple nodes simultaneously due to charge sharing between transistors, leading to single-event multi-node upsets (SEMNUs) [[6](#B6-applsci-14-11940),[7](#B7-applsci-14-11940)]. Therefore, to enhance the reliability of data stored in SRAM, it is necessary to design SRAM cells to be robust against SEU and SEMNUs.

To address the malfunction of SRAM caused by an SEU, researchers have proposed various methods such as triple modular redundancy (TMR), error correction code (ECC), and SRAM cell design that can recover from the influence of SEUs. Firstly, the TMR method requires two additional redundant cells for each existing SRAM bit cell [[8](#B8-applsci-14-11940)]. This method selects the correct value through majority voting among the three cells [[9](#B9-applsci-14-11940)]. However, this method results in a significant increase in area and power consumption. Therefore, it is not suitable for SRAM cells in the space industry. Secondly, the ECC method mitigates SEUs by utilizing additional encoding and decoding circuits [[10](#B10-applsci-14-11940)]. This method is based on error correction and detection codes, requiring additional circuits, which makes it unsuitable for memory cells in satellite communication technology when considering time, power, and area [[11](#B11-applsci-14-11940)]. Compared to these two methods, using radiation-hardened SRAM cells is relatively superior in terms of time, power, and area. Therefore, it is desirable to design radiation-hardened SRAM cells that can recover from both SEUs and SEMNUs [[12](#B12-applsci-14-11940)].

Due to the advantages of radiation-hardened SRAM cells, researchers have proposed various SRAM cells with recovery capabilities from soft errors over the years. Jahinuzzaman et al. proposed the QUATRO10T [[13](#B13-applsci-14-11940)]. However, QUATRO10T has a limited recovery capability only for a ‘1’→‘0’ SEU occurring at the ‘1’-storing node and is vulnerable to write operations due to long write delays and high write failure rates. To improve the write stability of QUATRO10T, Kim et al. proposed the 12T structure WE-QUATRO [[14](#B14-applsci-14-11940)]. However, this structure also has limited recovery capability for SEUs and shows degraded read stability. Jung et al. proposed two hardened SRAM cells, NS10T and PS10T, with recovery capabilities from SEUs [[15](#B15-applsci-14-11940)]. However, NS10T and PS10T provide only partial immunity to SEUs. For example, the NMOS stack-based NS10T can recover from a ‘0’→‘1’ SEU occurring at the ‘0’-storing node but cannot recover from a ‘1’→‘0’ SEU occurring at the ‘1’-storing node. Moreover, the PMOS stack-based PS10T has a recovery capability only for a ‘1’→‘0’ SEU occurring at the ‘1’-storing node. Calin et al. proposed the 12T structure DICE, which has recovery capability for all types of SEUs [[16](#B16-applsci-14-11940)]. DICE can recover to its initial state using positive feedback when an SEU occurs due to an ion strike at any sensitive node. Therefore, DICE has recovery capability from SEUs induced at all sensitive nodes but lacks recovery capability for SEUMNUs. Jianwei et al. proposed two radiation-hardened SRAM cells, QUCCE10T and QUCCE12T, with recovery capabilities from SEUs. However, QUCCE10T and QUCCE12T have issues with read stability. Additionally, both cells cannot recover from a ‘0’→‘1’ SEU if sufficient charge accumulates at the “0”-storing node. Dohar et al. proposed the RHBD10T structure with improved write and read delays [[17](#B17-applsci-14-11940)]. However, RHBD10T does not have improved SEU tolerance, and none of the aforementioned cells have the capability to recover to their initial state from multi-node upsets.

To overcome SEMNUs, Xiao et al. proposed the RHD12T, which has recovery capabilities from multi-node upsets occurring at internal node pairs [[18](#B18-applsci-14-11940)]. However, RHD12T cannot recover from a ‘0’→‘1’ SEU occurring at the ‘0’-storing storge node. To address this issue, Peng et al. proposed the RSP14T [[19](#B19-applsci-14-11940)]. While RSP14T can recover from SEUs occurring at the ‘0’-storing storage node, it still cannot recover from a ‘0’→‘1’ SEU if sufficient charge accumulates at the ‘0’-storing storage node. Consequently, both RHD12T and RSP14T show reduced read stability because the ‘0’-storing storage node is directly connected to the bit line through the access transistor during read operations. Prasad et al. proposed the RHBD14T, which has recovery capabilities from multi-node upsets occurring at storage node pairs [[20](#B20-applsci-14-11940)]. However, RHBD14T is more vulnerable to SEMNUs because all storage nodes and internal nodes are sensitive nodes. Additionally, RHBD14T uses more PMOS transistors, which are generally known to have higher parasitic bipolar amplification compared to NMOS transistors [[21](#B21-applsci-14-11940)]. Therefore, the increased number of PMOS transistors in RHBD14T can promote charge sharing effects among PMOS transistors [[22](#B22-applsci-14-11940)]. Hao et al. proposed the RHPD14T, which has recovery capabilities from multi-node upsets occurring at storage node pairs [[23](#B23-applsci-14-11940)]. However, RHPD14T shows reduced read stability because both pairs of access transistors are accessed during read operations, directly connecting the storage node to the bit line. Therefore, it is necessary to design the SRAM cell that can recover from SEUs, demonstrate satisfactory performance in both read and write operations, and recover from multi-node upsets caused by charge-sharing effects.

In this paper, we propose a radiation-hardened high-stability 16T (RHHS16T) SRAM cell. The proposed cell demonstrates high immunity to SEUs at all sensitive nodes and can recover from multi-node upsets occurring at storage node pairs. Furthermore, the proposed cell shows the highest read stability among all comparison cells while also showing the highest write stability and the shortest write access time.

The structure of the paper is as follows: [Section 2](#sec2-applsci-14-11940) describes the basic operation of the proposed RHHS16T cell and its SEU recovery operation. [Section 3](#sec3-applsci-14-11940) presents the measurement results of read delay, write delay, word line write trip voltage (WWTV), read static noise margin (RSNM), hold power, and critical charge for the proposed cell and all comparison cells. Finally, the paper concludes in [Section 4](#sec4-applsci-14-11940).

## 2. Proposed RHHS16T SRAM Cell

### 2.1. Proposed Cell Design and Its Operation

The schematic of the RHHS16T circuit is shown in [Figure 1](#fig_body_display_applsci-14-11940-f001), and the corresponding layout is depicted in [Figure 2](#fig_body_display_applsci-14-11940-f002). The RHHS16T has two storage nodes, Q and QB, and two internal nodes, S1 and S0. Transistor N1, N2, N9, and N10 serve as access transistors, with N9 and N10 controlled by the word line (WL) and N1 and N2 controlled by the write word line (WWL). When the word lines WL/WWL are set to VDD/VDD, the nodes are connected to their respective bit lines through the access transistors. Specifically, Q and S1 are connected to BL through N9 and N10, respectively, while QB and S0 are connected to BLB through N1 and N2, respectively. If the stored data are ‘1’, the logical values at nodes Q, QB, S1, and S0 are ‘1’, ‘0’, ‘1’, and ‘0’, respectively. Furthermore, for all operations, it is assumed that the proposed cell maintains the initial state of ‘1’.

![Applsci 14 11940 g001](/applsci/applsci-14-11940/article_deploy/html/images/applsci-14-11940-g001-550.jpg)

**Figure 1.**
Schematic of the proposed RHHS16T cell.

![Applsci 14 11940 g002](/applsci/applsci-14-11940/article_deploy/html/images/applsci-14-11940-g002-550.jpg)

**Figure 2.**
The cell layout of the proposed RHHS16T cell.

(1) Hold operation: During the hold operation, WL/WWL are set to GND/GND, keeping all access transistors connected to the nodes in the off state. The bit lines are pre-charged to VDD to reduce wake-up time [[24](#B24-applsci-14-11940)]. For the assumed initial state ‘1’, transistors N4, N5, N7, P4, P5, and P6 are in the on state, while the other transistors are in the off state. Nodes Q and S1 maintain the initial state ‘1’ by being connected to the pull-up paths ‘Q-P5-P4-VDD’ and ‘S1-N7-P6-VDD’, respectively. Nodes QB and S0 maintain the initial state ‘0’ by being connected to the pull-down paths ‘QB-N5-GND’ and ‘S0-N4-GND’, respectively. Therefore, the cell remains stable in the initial state.

(2) Read operation: During the read operation, bit lines BL and BLB are pre-charged to VDD, and WL/WWL are set to VDD/GND, isolating the storage nodes Q and QB from the bit lines. Consequently, from N4, while BL remains in the pre-charged VDD state, N8 is in the off state. When the voltage difference between BL and BLB becomes sufficiently large, approximately 50 mV, the read operation can be performed by the sense amplifier [[4](#B4-applsci-14-11940)].

(3) Write operation: To change the initially stored data ‘1’ to ‘0’ in the cell, BL is pre-discharged to GND and BLB is pre-charged to VDD. Moreover, WL/WWL are set to VDD/VDD, keeping all access transistors connected to the nodes in the on state. Therefore, the voltages of QB and S0 can rise through access transistors N1 and N2, respectively. As the voltages of QB and S0 rise, the pull-up paths for Q and S1 weaken, assisting the rapid discharge of S1. When the voltage of S1 falls below the threshold voltage of the NMOS, pull-down transistors N4 and N5 turn off, accelerating the charging of QB and S0. Therefore, the states of all nodes can be flipped to the desired values through the respective access transistors. The process of simultaneously flipping the values of the storage nodes and internal nodes through the two pairs of access transistors accelerates the write operation of the proposed cell.

### 2.2. SEU Recovery Analysis

This subsection describes the characteristics of the proposed cell. A node is considered sensitive when it experiences an SEU, which occurs near the drain junction of an off-state transistor [[25](#B25-applsci-14-11940)]. Generally, PMOS and NMOS transistors are known to induce positive and negative transient pulses, respectively [[12](#B12-applsci-14-11940)]. Therefore, only the cases of ‘1’→‘0’ for PMOS and ‘0’→‘1’ for NMOS need to be considered. Assuming the initial state ‘1’ for the proposed RHHS16T cell, the internal node S0 has an initial value of ‘0’ and is surrounded only by NMOS transistors, so the only possible transient state in the event of an SEU is ‘0’→‘0’. Therefore, in the assumed case, S0 can be considered a non-sensitive node, while Q, QB, and S1 are sensitive nodes.

(1) SEU at node Q: When Q is flipped by an SEU, stored data at node Q transition from ‘1’ to ‘0’, causing N7 to turn off and P3 to turn on. However, nodes QB and S0 maintain their initial state of ‘0’ through the pull-down paths ‘QB-N5-GND’ and ‘S0-N4-GND’, respectively. Additionally, since both transistors N7 and N8 are in the off state, node S1 transitions to a high-impedance state with no pull-up or pull-down path connected. Generally, the state of a node in a high-impedance state remains unaffected [[4](#B4-applsci-14-11940)]. Therefore, node S1 maintains its initial state of ‘1’. Since nodes QB, S0, and S1, which are not directly affected by SEUs, maintain their initial state, node Q, which is affected by the SEU, can recover to its initial state ‘1’ through the pull-up path ‘Q-P5-P4-VDD’.

(2) SEU at node QB: When QB is flipped by an SEU, stored data at node QB transition from ‘0’ to ‘1’, causing P5 to turn off and N3 to turn on. Since both transistors P5 and N6 are in the off state, stored data at node Q transition to a high-impedance state, maintaining its initial state of ‘1’. As Q maintains its value, N7 remains in the on state, and S1 maintains its initial state of ‘1’ through the pull-up path ‘S1-N7-P6-VDD’. This keeps transistor P1 in the off state, blocking the pull-up path ‘S0-N4-GND’. As Q, S0, and S1 maintain their initial states, transistors P2 and P3 remain in the on state. Therefore, node QB, which is affected by the SEU, can recover to its initial state of ‘0’ through the pull-down path ‘QB-N5-GND’.

(3) SEU at node S1: When S1 is flipped by an SEU, stored data at node S1 transition from ‘1’ to ‘0’, causing transistors P1 and P2 to turn on and N4 and N5 to turn off. However, the storage nodes Q and QB maintain their initial states through the paths ‘Q-P5-P4-VDD’ and ‘QB-N5-GND’, respectively. As QB maintains ‘0’, transistor N3 remains in the off state, causing S0 to transition to a high-impedance state, maintaining its initial state of ‘0’. Therefore, S1 can recover to its initial state of ‘1’ through the pull-up path ‘S1-N7-P6-VDD’.

(4) SEMNU at node pair Q-QB: When the storage node pair Q-QB is affected by an SEMNU, stored data at node Q transition from ‘1’ to ‘0’, and stored data at node QB transition from ‘0’ to ‘1’. Consequently, transistors P5 and N7 turn off, and transistors P3 and N3 turn on. However, the internal node S1 transitions to a high-impedance state, maintaining its initial state of ‘1’. As S1 maintains its initial state, transistors P1 and N4 remain in the off and on states, respectively, and S0 maintains its initial state of ‘0’ through the pull-down path ‘S0-N4-GND’; as the voltage of QB drops sufficiently, transistor P5 turns on, allowing Q to recover to ‘1’ through the pull-up path ‘Q-P5-P4-VDD’.

Therefore, the proposed cell can fully recover to its initial state even if soft errors affect nodes Q, QB, S1, or the storage node pair Q-QB, as shown in the simulation waveform in [Figure 3](#fig_body_display_applsci-14-11940-f003). If sufficient charge accumulates at the node pairs Q-S1 or QB-S1, it can flip the state of the cell. However, it is known that charge sharing between transistors can be avoided by maintaining a distance of at least 1.62 μm and 0.6 μm between PMOS transistors or between PMOS and NMOS transistors, respectively [[21](#B21-applsci-14-11940)]. Considering this, the layout of the proposed cell, as shown in [Figure 2](#fig_body_display_applsci-14-11940-f002), maintains distances of 2.655 μm and 4.89 μm between Q-S1 and QB-S1, respectively, to avoid multi-node upsets occurring at these node pairs.

## 3. Simulation Results and Analysis

This section aims to evaluate the characteristics of the RHHS16T cell through simulations using 90 nm CMOS technology. To achieve high read stability and appropriate read speed, the widths of transistors N5 and N6 in the proposed cell are set to 2.0 times that of access transistors N1 and N9, while the widths of transistors N4 and N8 are set to 3.3 times that of access transistors N2 and N10. Moreover, to achieve high write stability and short write access time, the widths of transistors P2 and P4 in the proposed cell are set to 0.5 times that of the respective access transistors, and the widths of transistors P1 and P6 are set to 0.66 times that of the respective access transistors. This paper presents the measurement results of read delay, write delay, RSNM, WWTV, and hold power for the proposed RHHS16T cell compared with WE-QUATRO, QUCCE12T, RHBD10T, RHD12T, RSP14T, RHBD14T, and RHPD14T, conducted using the ratios presented in the respective papers. For RHD12T, which does not specify transistor sizes in the paper, appropriate sizes were used for measurement.

### 3.1. Read Delay Comparison

Read delay or read access time (RAT) is defined as the time interval from when the word line voltage reaches 50% of VDD, starting from its initial low/high level at the rising/falling edge to when a 50 mV voltage difference occurs between BL and BLB [[26](#B26-applsci-14-11940)]. RAT can be calculated as shown in [Figure 4](#fig_body_display_applsci-14-11940-f004)a. Generally, RAT is highly dependent on the read current through the access transistor and pull-down transistor, as well as the bit line capacitance [[6](#B6-applsci-14-11940)]. Certain cells, such as WE-QUATRO, RHBD14T, QUCCE12T, RHPD14T, and RHHS16T, use two access transistors per bit line, resulting in higher bit line capacitance compared to cells that use only a pair of access transistors. Typically, lower bit line capacitance tends to shorten RAT. Cells like RHBD10T, RHD12T, and RSP14T, which have a single access transistor connected to the BL, show shorter RAT than other cells. Cells like RHBD10T, RHD12T, and RSP14T, which have a single access transistor connected to the BL, show shorter RAT than other cells. Among the cells using a single access transistor, RHBD14T shows the shortest RAT due to its highest cell ratio (CR = 3). During the read operation, the voltage at the ‘0’ storage node rises due to the voltage division effect between the access transistor and pull-down transistor, which increases the source and body voltage. Consequently, the drive strength of the access transistor may decrease due to the body effect, but a higher cell ratio can improve RAT [[6](#B6-applsci-14-11940)]. Among the cells using two pairs of access transistors, QUCCE12T and RHPD14T have shorter RATs due to their high CR of 1.8 and 2, respectively. On the other hand, RHHS16T, which has the higher CR (3.3) among the cells with two access transistors per bit line, shows a longer RAT than most cells because it uses only a pair of access transistor connected to the internal node during the read operation, resulting in a single read path. Additionally, RHBD14T, despite having lower bit line capacitance due to using a single access transistor, shows the longest RAT among all the mentioned cells due to its very low CR (1) and the presence of the PMOS transistor in the read discharge path ([Figure 4](#fig_body_display_applsci-14-11940-f004)b).

### 3.2. Read Stability Comparison

During a read operation, the node storing ‘0’ is connected to the bit line pre-charged to VDD, and the voltage generated at the ‘0’ storage node due to the read current can flip the stored data [[6](#B6-applsci-14-11940)]. In conventional SRAM design metrics, read stability is evaluated through the read static noise margin (RSNM) [[27](#B27-applsci-14-11940)]. The RSNM can be simulated through the circuit presented in [Figure 5](#fig_body_display_applsci-14-11940-f005)a. To measure SNM during the read operation, the bit lines BL and BLB are pre-charged to the supply voltage VDD. Subsequently, noise is applied to each node of the SRAM cell to simulate the linear DC characteristics of each node. By overlapping the two voltage transfer curves, the butterfly curve can be obtained. As shown in [Figure 5](#fig_body_display_applsci-14-11940-f005)b, the RSNM is calculated as the diagonal length of the largest square that can fit within the butterfly curve. [Figure 5](#fig_body_display_applsci-14-11940-f005)b shows the RSNM curves for various cells at VDD = 1 V, and [Figure 6](#fig_body_display_applsci-14-11940-f006) presents the RSNM values for all cells at different VDD voltages. Generally, a higher CR results in a higher RSNM because it generates a lower voltage at the ‘0’ storage node. RHBD10T, having the highest CR except for RHHS16T, shows a higher RSNM than all other comparison cells except RHHS16T. Cells like WEQUATRO, QUCCE12T, RHBD14T, and RHPD14T, which have both the storage node and internal node accessed by the bit line through two access transistors, are more vulnerable to read upsets compared to cells such as RHD12T, RSP14T, and RHBD10T, where only the storage node is accessed by the bit line through a single access transistor. Due to the highest CR (3.3) and the read isolated characteristic of the proposed RHHS16T, the proposed cell shows the highest RSNM among all comparison cells, as shown in [Figure 6](#fig_body_display_applsci-14-11940-f006). Since only the internal node of RHHS16T is accessed by the bit line during the read operation, the storage node of RHHS16T is not directly affected by noise during a read operation. Moreover, the highest CR of RHHS16T generates the lowest voltage at the internal node S0, which stores ‘0’. Therefore, the proposed RHHS16T cell demonstrates the highest read stability among all comparison cells.

### 3.3. Write Delay Comparison

Write delay, or write access time (WAT), is measured as the time interval from when the word line reaches 50% of its full voltage swing to the point where the storage nodes Q and QB intersect [[6](#B6-applsci-14-11940)]. WAT can be calculated as shown in [Figure 7](#fig_body_display_applsci-14-11940-f007)a. The WAT values for various comparison cells at different VDD voltages are presented in [Figure 7](#fig_body_display_applsci-14-11940-f007)b. Generally, affecting both the storage node and the internal node simultaneously during a write operation tends to reduce WAT [[6](#B6-applsci-14-11940)]. Cells such as WEQUATRO, RHPD12T, RHBD14T, and RHHS16T, which flip the values both the storage node and the internal node through access transistors connected to each bit line, show shorter WATs compared to cells like RHD12T, RSP14T, and RHBD10T, which have only a pair of access transistors. In the cases of RHHS16T, RHPD14T, and RHBD14T, the NMOS pull-up transistor with a weak ‘1’ characteristic is used for one of the nodes between the storage node and the internal node. Hence, it becomes easier for the access transistor to discharge the weak ‘1’ at the ‘1’-storing node, resulting in shorter WATs for these cells than WEQUATRO and QUCCE12T. Furthermore, the proposed RHHS16T has the lowest pull-up ratio (=0.5/0.6) for the two access transistors. A lower pull-up ratio can make the strength of the access transistor discharge the ‘1’-storing node to the bit line pre-discharged to ‘0’ stronger than the strength of the corresponding pull-up transistor to pull the ‘1’-storing node to VDD. Thus, appropriate pull-up ratio adjustment results in a shorter WAT. Consequently, as shown in [Figure 7](#fig_body_display_applsci-14-11940-f007), the proposed RHHS16T exhibits the shortest WAT among all comparison cells.

### 3.4. Write Stability Comparison

Conventionally, the write ability of SRAM cells has been measured through static noise margin, similar to read operations. However, recent studies have mentioned that word line write trip voltage (WWTV) is a more reliable method to evaluate the writing ability of SRAM cells compared to write static noise margin (WSNM) [[4](#B4-applsci-14-11940)]. As shown in [Figure 8](#fig_body_display_applsci-14-11940-f008)a, WTV is measured as the voltage difference between the word line voltage and VDD at the point where the storage nodes Q and QB intersect when the word line is activated. Therefore, cells with a longer WAT require more time to change the stored data, leading to a higher voltage rise at WL at the point where Q and QB intersect. Consequently, the proposed RHHS16T, having the shortest WAT among all comparison cells, shows the highest WWTV, as shown in [Figure 8](#fig_body_display_applsci-14-11940-f008)b.

Since SRAM cells spend most of their time in hold mode, the power consumed in hold mode, known as hold power (, constitutes a significant portion of the total power consumption of SRAM cells [[28](#B28-applsci-14-11940)]. As shown in [Figure 9](#fig_body_display_applsci-14-11940-f009), has been calculated based on the average power consumption while the SRAM cell is in hold mode for various supply voltages. is primarily consumed due to bit line leakage and the leakage of inverters used in the SRAM cell. Generally, is proportional to the number of transistors used in the cell, and the excessive use of access transistors tends to increase [[6](#B6-applsci-14-11940)]. Cells like RHHS16T, RHBD14T, and RHPD14T consume higher compared to RSP14T, which uses a single access transistor due to the presence of excessive access transistors. Among these, RHHS16T consumes higher than RHBD14T and RHPD14T because it uses a larger pull-down transistor. ## 4. Conclusions

In this paper, we introduced a radiation-hardened, high-stability SRAM cell designed to meet the demanding requirements of space applications. The proposed RHHS16T cell demonstrates exceptional robustness against radiation-induced soft errors, enabling it to effectively recover to its initial state even if a radiation particle impacts a sensitive node and causes a bit flip. This level of resilience is particularly crucial for environments with high radiation exposure, where data integrity must be reliably maintained. Additionally, the RHHS16T cell is engineered to withstand and recover from SEMNU occurrences at the storage node pair, further enhancing its data retention capabilities. Moreover, the proposed RHHS16T cell offers high read stability and write stability by isolating the storage node from the bit line during read operations and maintaining feedback loops between nodes during write operations. Therefore, the RHHS16T cell can ensure reliable data through its resilience to soft errors, as well as its high read and write stability. In conclusion, radiation-hardened SRAM cells designed for space applications must provide high reliability for stored data. The high reliability of the RHHS16T cell makes it a highly suitable candidate for space SRAM applications, where long-term and stable operation is essential. We have demonstrated the RHHS16T cell’s effectiveness through extensive simulations, highlighting its potential as a reliable solution for radiation-hardened memory systems in space applications.

This is a scientific research article published in *Applied Sciences* (2024, 14(24), 11940) by Jong-Yeob Oh and Sung-Hun Jo from the Department of Nano & Semiconductor Engineering, Tech University of Korea, Republic of Korea. The paper proposes a Radiation-Hardened High Stability 16T (RHHS16T) SRAM cell designed for space applications, where high-energy particles cause single event upsets (SEUs) and single-event multi-node upsets (SEMNUs) in conventional memory cells.

**Key Details:**
- **Problem:** As CMOS technology scales down, critical charge decreases, making SRAM cells more susceptible to soft errors from radiation. Conventional 6T SRAM cells are vulnerable to SEUs and SEMNUs.
- **Proposed Solution:** The RHHS16T cell uses 16 transistors, two storage nodes (Q, QB) and two internal nodes (S1, S0), with read isolation and feedback loops for enhanced stability.
- **Methodology:** Simulated using 90nm CMOS process at 1V supply voltage. Compared against QUCCE12T, WEQUATRO, RHBD10T, RHD12T, RSP14T, RHPD14T, and RHBD14T cells.
- **Results:** The RHHS16T cell demonstrates:
  - Highest read stability (RSNM) among all compared cells due to isolating the storage node from the bit line during read operations and having the highest cell ratio (CR=3.3).
  - Shortest write access time (WAT) due to simultaneous flipping of storage and internal nodes through two pairs of access transistors and low pull-up ratio.
  - Highest write stability (WWTV) due to the shortest WAT.
  - Full recovery capability from SEUs at nodes Q, QB, S1, and SEMNUs at the storage node pair Q-QB, with immunity above 100fC accumulated charge.
  - Higher hold power consumption due to using more transistors and larger pull-down transistors.
  - Larger area footprint compared to other cells.
  - Highest overall Electrical Quality Metric (EQM), indicating superior balanced performance.
- **Conclusion:** The RHHS16T cell is highly suitable for space SRAM applications requiring reliable data retention under radiation exposure.

**Submitted:** 30 October 2024; **Revised:** 7 December 2024; **Accepted:** 16 December 2024; **Published:** 20 December 2024.

This is a Master's thesis by Aravind Rajendran (Advisor: Dr. Christos Papachristou, Case Western Reserve University, August 2011) on noise margin, critical charge, and power-delay tradeoffs for SRAM design space exploration. The thesis addresses the problem of stability reduction in SRAM cells due to aggressive CMOS technology scaling into nanometer levels, particularly issues with static noise margin (SNM) degradation during read operations and increased susceptibility to radiation-induced soft errors (single event upsets, SEU).

**Key Content:**
- **Background:** Covers SRAM architecture (6T-SRAM cell, address decoders, precharge circuits, sense amplifiers, write drivers) and SRAM stability (Static Noise Margin - SNM, measured via butterfly curves or N-curve, and soft errors involving critical charge Qcrit).
- **Approach:** A design tradeoffs approach is presented that modulates the transistor sizing ratio (β-ratio, pull-down to access transistor ratio) to improve SRAM characteristics. By varying β from 1 to 3, SNM improves over 2x (from 27.4 mV to 102.8 mV in 32nm technology), while Qcrit, write time, and power consumption also increase.
- **Methodology:** The study tests four SRAM cell designs in 32nm technology: standard 6T-SRAM, SRAM-C (capacitor-based), SRAM-T (tristate), and SRAM-NSP (tristate with separate read port). Transistor sizing and simulation setups are described.
- **Results:** Tables present performance characteristics (SNM, Qcrit, write time, average power) for each SRAM cell type at various β-ratios in 32nm technology.
- **Constraint-driven tradeoff:** A formal method is provided to select β-ratios that satisfy designer constraints on Qcrit (minimum), write time (maximum), and power (maximum) while optimizing SNM. The solution involves finding β subsets where βq ≤ βi ≤ min{βt, βp}.
</summary>

# ISSCC 2026 Roundup: Key Semiconductor Developments

This SemiAnalysis article covers major announcements from ISSCC 2026 across memory, optical networking, high-speed electrical interconnects, and processors.

## Memory

**Samsung HBM4 (Paper 15.6):** Samsung presented a 36 GB, 12-high HBM4 stack with 2048 IO pins and 3.3 TB/s bandwidth. Key innovations include:
- Process technology split: 1c (6th-gen 10nm-class) DRAM core dies paired with an SF4 logic base die (vs. DRAM process for both in HBM3E)
- Operating voltage (VDDQ) fell 32% from 1.1V to 0.75V
- Adaptive body-bias control and 4× higher TSV count enable up to 13 Gb/s per pin
- Per-channel TSV RDQS timing auto-calibration scheme improved data rates from 7.8 Gb/s to 9.4 Gb/s
- Programmable Memory Built-In Self-Test (PMBIST) architecture enabled by logic base die
- Significantly exceeds JEDEC HBM4 standard (6.4 Gb/s per pin, ~2 TB/s)
- Trade-off: SF4 base die is higher cost vs. SK Hynix (TSMC N12) and Micron (internal CMOS)

**Samsung LPDDR6 (Paper 15.8):** 2 sub-channel per die architecture with 16 banks each. Uses wide NRZ signaling with 12 DQ pins per sub-channel. Reaches 12.8 Gb/s at 0.97V and up to 14.4 Gb/s at 1.025V. Each 16 Gb die is 44.5 mm², density 0.360 Gb/mm². Read power reduced 27%, write power 22%.

**Samsung SF2 LPDDR6 PHY (Paper 37.3):** PHYs on SF2 process support up to 14.4 Gb/s, with bandwidth densities of 16.6 Gb/s/mm and 55.3 Gb/s/mm². Efficiency mode with clock-gating achieves ~50% power reduction for read/write.

**SK Hynix 1c LPDDR6 (Paper 15.7):** First 1c DRAM products, up to 14.4 Gb/s (35% faster than LPDDR5X). Estimated bit density 0.59 Gb/mm². Efficiency mode at 12.8 Gb/s over single sub-channel with 12.7% lower standby and 18.9% lower operational current.

**SK Hynix 1c GDDR7 (Paper 15.9):** Up to 48 Gb/s at 1.2V. Bit density 0.412 Gb/mm² vs. 0.309 Gb/mm² (Samsung 1b) and 0.192 Gb/mm² (Samsung 1z). GDDR7 has lower density than LPDDR5X due to higher periphery area for PAM3/QDR signaling.

**Samsung 4F² COP DRAM (Paper 15.10):** Cell-on-Peripheral (COP) architecture with vertical channel transistors (VCT) and hybrid bonding. Core circuitry area reduced from 17.0% to 2.7%. Key challenge: floating-body effect increasing leakage.

**SanDisk/Kioxia BiCS10 NAND (Paper 15.1):** 332 layers, 3 decks, highest reported NAND bit density at 37.6 Gb/mm² (QLC). 30% higher density than SK Hynix V9 (28.8 Gb/mm²). 6-plane configuration with 50% higher IO bandwidth. Die-gating reduces idle current by two orders of magnitude.

**MediaTek xBIT Logic-Based Bitcell (Paper 15.2):** Novel 10-transistor cell (xBIT) achieving 22-63% higher density than standard 8T bitcells. Average read/write power reduced by over 30%, leakage reduced 29% at 0.5V. Operates from 100 MHz at 0.35V to 4 GHz at 0.95V.

**TSMC N16 MRAM (Paper 15.4):** STT-MRAM on N16 node. Dual-port access, interleaved reads, 51.2 Gb/s at 200 MHz. 84 Mb macro achieves 7.5ns read access at 0.8V across -40°C to 150°C. Bitcell shrunk 25% to 0.0249 µm², macro density 16.0 Mb/mm². Meets automotive requirements (20-year retention at 150°C). Next-gen "Flash-Plus" variant planned with 25% smaller bitcell and 100× higher endurance.

## Optical Networking

**Nvidia DWDM (Paper 23.1):** Proposes 32 Gb/s per lambda with 8 wavelengths multiplexed using DWDM, plus 9th wavelength for clock forwarding. OCI MSA (Optical Compute Interconnect) standard focuses on 200 Gb/s bi-directional links using 4 lambdas of 50G NRZ. Three CPO integration levels: On-Board Optics, Substrate CPO (near-term), and Interposer CPO (long-term).

**Marvell Coherent-Lite Transceiver (Paper 23.2):** 800G transceiver for datacenter campuses (tens of km). Uses O-band wavelengths (near-zero dispersion) vs. C-band for traditional coherent. Only 3.72 pJ/b excluding silicon photonics, half of full coherent transceivers. Measured over 40km with <300ns latency.

**Broadcom 6.4T Optical Engine (Paper 23.4):** 64 lanes of ~100G PAM4 modulation. Tested in Tomahawk 5 51.2T CPO system. Uses Fan-Out Wafer-Level Packaging (will switch to COUPE in future).

## High-Speed Electrical Interconnects

**Intel UCIe-S (Paper 8.1):** Compatible D2D interface on Intel 22nm process, up to 48 Gb/s/lane (UCIe-S) or 56 Gb/s/lane (custom) over 16 lanes, up to 30mm on standard organic package. Likely prototype for Diamond Rapids Xeon CPUs.

**TSMC Active LSI (Paper 8.2):** Active Local Silicon Interconnect (aLSI) improves signal integrity, reduces PHY area. Bump pitch reduced from 45µm to 38.8µm, PHY depth from 1043µm to 850µm. Edge-Triggered Transceiver adds only 0.07 pJ/b. Total power 0.36 pJ/b at 0.75V. Can integrate embedded deep trench capacitors for power delivery.

**Microsoft D2D Interconnect (Paper 8.3):** Test vehicle on TSMC N3P. 20 Gb/s at 0.65V (0.25 pJ/b system power) and 24 Gb/s at 0.75V (0.33 pJ/b). Likely the interconnect used in Microsoft's Cobalt 200 CPU.

## Processors

**MediaTek Dimensity 9500 (Paper 10.2):** Focus on boosting and thermal management. Used larger 54nm CGP (vs. 48nm) on C1 Ultra cores for better power efficiency: 4.6% more performance at iso-leakage or 3% less power at iso-performance. Boost clocks increased from 4.21 GHz to 4.4 GHz.

**Intel 18A-on-Intel 3 Hybrid Bonding (Paper 10.6):** First hybrid bonded chip (M3DProc) using Foveros Direct at 9µm pitch. 14×4×2 3D mesh reduces latency and increases throughput by ~40%. Achieves 875 GB/s 3D bandwidth.

**AMD MI355X (Paper 2.1):** Moved from N5 to N3P, doubled matrix throughput per CU while keeping total area same. Two additional metal layers from N3P improved routing. Designed custom standard cells and used denser placement algorithms.
</summary>

This article discusses the end of SRAM memory scaling, a critical challenge for major chipmakers (NVIDIA, Intel, Apple, AMD, etc.). The author predicts SRAM will remain in use for L1/L2 cache for the next couple of decades, while new memory technologies may first appear in DRAM and L3 cache as they mature. - N2: 38 Mb/mm² (0.0175 µm²)

SRAM is noted as one of the hardest things to scale with modern process technologies due to design intricacies, stability/reliability requirements, and increased variability at smaller nodes. SUMMARY:
<summary>
Imec introduced the "outer wall forksheet" device architecture at VLSI 2025 as an improved evolution of their earlier "inner wall" forksheet design. The forksheet architecture was originally introduced in 2017 to extend the gate-all-around (GAA) nanosheet-based logic roadmap to the A10 technology node, bridging the gap before complementary FET (CFET) technology becomes viable for mass production starting at the A7 node.

The original inner wall forksheet placed a dielectric wall between nMOS and pMOS devices, enabling tighter n-to-p spacing and cell area scaling down to 90nm cell height. However, it faced manufacturability challenges: the wall needed to be extremely thin (8-10nm), was exposed to aggressive front-end-of-line (FEOL) etching steps, required precise p/n mask alignment, obstructed p-n connected gates, and used a tri-gate structure with limited channel control.

The new outer wall forksheet places the dielectric wall at the standard cell boundary (as a p-p or n-n wall), allowing it to be thicker (~15nm) and shared with neighboring cells. Key improvements include: (1) a wall-last integration approach using mainstream silicon dioxide, (2) relaxed wall width for process simplification, (3) easily connected n-p gates, (4) superior gate control via a Ω-gate structure (achieved by 5nm wall etch-back, boosting drive current by ~25%), and (5) the ability to achieve full channel strain through effective source/drain stressors, enabled by a Si spine that acts as a seed crystal template.

Benchmarking showed a 22% area reduction for outer wall forksheet-based SRAM cells compared to A14 nanosheet designs. Ring oscillator simulations indicated the outer wall forksheet maintains frequency performance at the A10 node, provided full channel stress can be enabled. Imec is now investigating compatibility of the outer wall design with CFET architecture.
</summary>

This webpage presents the paper "Low Voltage and Low Power in SRAM Read and Write Assist Techniques" by IJSTE - International Journal of Science Technology and Engineering. The paper discusses read and write assist techniques used to minimize the minimum operating voltage (Vmin) of SRAM cells. Read assist techniques help retain data at low voltage supply with reduced transistor size, while write assist techniques enable writing new data under similar constraints. Write and read failures (write-ability and read-ability) are key limitations to minimum supply voltage, and the 6T SRAM cell's properties are highly dependent on supply voltage. The paper compares several assist techniques:

**Read Assist Techniques:**
- Raised array global VDD
- Negative VSS at the cell
- VDD boost at the cell
- Word line (WL) droop

**Write Assist Techniques:**
- Negative Bit-Line (NBL) approach: Uses capacitive coupling to generate negative voltage on the bit line, strengthening access transistors to flip the bit cell more easily.
- Word Line Boosting: Boosts the word line voltage above supply voltage to increase access transistor strength; works on rows (unlike NBL which works on columns).
- VSS Raising: Raises the source voltage of the cell.
- VDD Lowering: Reduces the supply voltage by weakening the pull-up transistor relative to the pass gate transistor, though the gain is described as minuscule.

Key challenges include: the cell flipping during write assist at low voltage (more pronounced as transistor sizes shrink), process variations significantly impacting performance, and the need to balance reduced pull-up strength with retention voltage of unselected cells. The paper concludes that assist techniques improve SRAM write operation with better performance and stability, with supply voltage scaling reducing power dissipation quadratically but increasing sensitivity to process variations.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a US patent (US20140241089A1, granted as US9082507B2) assigned to Texas Instruments Inc, titled "Read assist circuit for an SRAM." The invention relates to memory circuits, specifically read assist circuits in Static Random Access Memories (SRAM). The primary problem addressed is that as transistor feature sizes shrink, increased variability in electrical characteristics raises the likelihood of read/write failures in SRAM cells. A particular failure mode occurs during read operations when the internal node holding a zero rises due to voltage division, potentially causing the bit to flip (data loss).

The key innovation is a **word line suppression circuit** coupled to the word line of an SRAM bit cell. The circuit includes a diode (NMOS transistor) and a switch (NMOS transistor) connected in series. The switch is responsive to the array supply voltage (VDDAR). The circuit limits the word line voltage to a value lower than VDDAR, thereby increasing the Static Noise Margin (SNM) of the bit cell for more robust read operations.

Several embodiments are described:
1. **FIG. 1**: A basic word line suppression circuit with a diode (NMOS transistor 120) and switch (NMOS transistor 125) in series. The switch provides self-regulation of the word line voltage over process, temperature, and voltage (PVT) variations via VGS and VBS control of the diode.
2. **FIG. 2**: Adds a control circuit (205) and a PMOS transistor (225). During read operations, the NMOS switch and diode are activated, suppressing the word line. During write operations, it uses a two-part approach: first write operation (suppression active to protect non-selected cells on the same word line), second write operation (suppression deactivated, PMOS activated to restore full word line voltage for the write).
3. **FIG. 3 & FIG. 4**: Alternative embodiments controlling the slew rate of the word line using a pre-word line driver and a final word line driver with two PMOS transistors of different strengths. A first phase provides a slower slew rate (word line suppression for SNM), and a second phase provides a faster slew rate (to benefit write operations).

The patent includes detailed descriptions of the 6T SRAM cell structure, timing diagrams (FIGS. 5, 6A, 6B), and the physical mechanism of read failures and how word line suppression mitigates them.

Benchmarking showed a 22% area reduction for outer wall forksheet-based SRAM cells compared to A14 nanosheet designs. **Key Concepts:**

- **6T SRAM Bit Cell:** Consists of two back-to-back inverters (pull-up PMOS P1/P2, pull-down NMOS D1/D2) plus two access transistors (A1/A2) controlled by wordline, connected to bitline (bit) and bitline bar (bit_b).

- **Read Operation:** Bitlines are precharged to VDD. Wordline goes high, enabling access transistors. If Q=0, A1 and D1 pull bit down. Critical design constraint: D1 must be stronger than A1 to prevent Q from rising and flipping the cell (read stability).

- **Write Operation:** Write driver forces bit=1, bit_b=0 (to write a 1). Access transistor A2 must overpower PMOS pull-up P2 to pull Q_b low, which then flips Q via positive feedback. Writeability requires P2 weaker than A2.

- **Transistor Sizing Hierarchy:** Pull-down (D) strongest > Access (A) intermediate > Pull-up (P) weakest. The β ratio (W/L of D divided by W/L of A) determines read margin; γ ratio affects write margin.

- **Read vs. Write Conflict:** Making D stronger helps read but hurts write; larger access transistors help write but hurt read. This is the fundamental tension of the 6T SRAM.

- **Static Noise Margin (SNM):** Measured using butterfly diagram (V2 vs. V1 transfer curves). The largest inscribed square defines the stability margin. Three modes: hold SNM, read SNM (reduced compared to hold), and write SNM.

- **Vmin:** The minimum reliable operating voltage. VT mismatch from random dopant fluctuations, work function variation, and gate length variation creates a distribution of margins. Any cell with negative SNM is inoperable. Vmin is driven by process quality, not design.

- **Periphery:** PMOS precharge to VDD with equalizer transistor; clocked differential sense amplifiers using regenerative feedback; NAND2+INV decoders; predecoders for large arrays; hierarchical wordlines (global in upper metal, local in lower metal).

- **Advanced Cells:** 8T SRAM adds dedicated read port to eliminate read-stability vs. cell-current conflict; 10T SRAM allows independent read/write paths for independent β/γ optimization.

- **Scaling Limits:** Area scaling has stalled due to limited dimensional scaling, Vmin stuck from process variation, and reliability degradation requiring larger ECC periphery.

- **Leakage:** All six transistors contribute leakage paths; differential VDD schemes shut off idle cells; worst-case leakage occurs during read.

--- SOURCE 25: 4.2 SRAM - Noise Margin Analysis - YouTube ---
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lZw_DUvMV6Q

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a lecture from the NPTEL-NOC course "Memory Device Technology for AIML Computing" presented by Dr. Shubhadeep, focused on SRAM cell noise margin analysis, including write timing, static noise margins in hold and read operations, and butterfly curve analysis.

**Key Topics Covered:**

1. **SRAM Write Operation Timing**: The write operation occurs in two phases. Phase 1: The storage node holding value 1 (N2) discharges from 1 to 0 when the pass gate transistor turns on, driven by the bit line bar pre-charged to 0. Phase 2: As N2 approaches 0, pull-up transistor PU1 turns on, charging storage node N1 from 0 to 1. The write process is initiated from the node that previously stored 1, and the crossover point of N1 and N2 occurs close to 0V.

2. **Noise Margin Definition**: The maximum allowable disturbance in internal storage nodes that does not cause the node to flip. The analysis uses static noise analysis (assuming DC/constant disturbance sources) as a simpler introductory approach.

3. **Butterfly Loops and Noise Margin**: The size of the smallest hysteresis loop in the butterfly curve determines the noise margin. Balanced inverters with high gain produce the largest loops and best noise margins.

4. **Ranking of SRAM Cell VTC Characteristics (highest to lowest noise margin)**: A (balanced, ideal/high gain) > B (balanced, poor gain) > C (unbalanced, ideal) > D (unbalanced, non-ideal).

5. **Hold Static Noise Margin (HSNM) Estimation**: Measured by the side of the largest square that can be nested inside the butterfly loop. Practically, this is done by rotating the coordinate axes by 45 degrees, finding the maximum difference between VTC1 and VTC2 (D1 and D2), and computing the side as min(D1/√2, D2/√2).

6. **Read Static Noise Margin (RSNM)**: Significantly smaller than HSNM because during read operations, pass gate transistors are active, disturbing internal storage nodes. The NMOS portion of the VTC gets distorted due to current flow, while the PMOS portion remains relatively unaffected. The internal node never reaches a true 0V (it is 0 + ΔV'), further shrinking the butterfly loop.

7. **Impact of Voltage Scaling**: As supply voltage (VDD) scales down, the butterfly loop shrinks, reducing RSNM. For example, at 400mV VDD, the nested square was 105mV; at 250mV VDD, it shrinks to 45mV. Improving the cell ratio (beta factor) from 2 to 3 can help boost noise margins, but this creates trade-offs with the pull ratio required for write operations, leading to read-write conflicting requirements.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Noise margins were the maximum allowable disturbance in the internal storage nodes of the SRAM cell which does not allow the node to flip."
</key_excerpts>
