## Fully Comprehensive Findings

### (1) Process-Level Parameters Affecting SRAM Static Noise Margin (SNM)

**General Background on SNM and Scaling**

A key figure of merit for an SRAM cell is its static noise margin (SNM). It can be extracted by nesting the largest possible square in the two voltage transfer curves (VTC) of the involved CMOS inverters. If external DC noise exceeds the SNM, the cell state can flip and data is lost [13, 16]. The underlying assumption of the traditional SNM metric is that in a worst-case scenario, two voltage sources of magnitude Vn with opposite polarities are connected to the internal data nodes [2]. A negative SNM implies that the circuit is mono-stable by design, and therefore a hold failure is guaranteed to occur, even under noise-free conditions [2]. SRAM stability is projected to decrease by 4×, as CMOS technology scales from 250 nm to 45 nm [1]. The stability of the memory cell can be affected during read or standby mode. The disturbances produced during the read operation, read access disturbance, affects the cell stability during read mode. During the standby mode, the stability of SRAM is mainly affected by radiation induced errors [1]. Aggressive technology scaling in semiconductor devices has resulted in stability reduction for classic SRAM designs [1].

The read static noise margin (RSNM) is significantly smaller than the hold static noise margin (HSNM) because during read operation, pass gate transistors are active, causing disturbance to internal storage nodes. The PMOS part of VTC remains unaltered, but the NMOS part gets distorted. The butterfly loop shrinks, reducing the maximum nested square size [5]. Reducing supply voltage (e.g., from 400mV to 250mV) significantly reduces RSNM (from 105mV to 45mV) [5].

**Channel Doping Profiles and Halo Implants**

The paper "Sensitivity of static noise margins to random dopant variations in 6-T SRAM cells" (Oniciuc and Andrei, 2008, Solid-State Electronics) investigates the sensitivity of SNM to random dopant variations. Using simulation results for a well-scaled SRAM cell with 30 nm channel length transistors, the study finds that the most sensitive regions to doping fluctuations extend approximately 10 nm below the oxide/semiconductor interface and are located in the middle of the conduction channels for both p-channel and n-channel transistors [3].

The paper "Investigation of Proximity Effects in a 6T SRAM Cell Using Three-Dimensional TCAD Simulations" (Kucherov and Tian, IEEE Transactions on Electron Devices, 2000) finds that proximity effects significantly influence doping and stress profiles in 6T SRAM cells, impacting performance by over 10%. Simulating a 6T SRAM cell as a single continuous 3-D structure yields different electrical characteristics than discrete simulations. The static noise margin (SNM) exhibits a 6-8% difference between continuous and discrete 6T SRAM cell simulations. Doping shadowing and stress reduction have counteractive effects on SRAM cell characteristics, complicating performance prediction. Accurate predictions of 6T SRAM behavior in 32-nm technology necessitate full 3-D TCAD simulations. The simulated SRAM cell area is 0.17 μm² with a gate length of 30 nm and gate pitch of 112.5 nm [4].

The paper "Scalability of 28-nm Ternary CMOS Technology Using Halo Implantation" (JSTS) proposes a highly scalable ternary CMOS (T-CMOS) technology using halo implantation in a commercial 28-nm process. The key innovation is forming a locally confined halo profile that enables V_DD-scalable subthreshold ternary operation with constant band-to-band tunneling (BTBT) current. The paper demonstrates that halo energy and tilt angle serve as additional design knobs to reduce tunneling current, expanding the T-CMOS design window. Compared to retrograde doping profiles, halo T-CMOS exhibits improved short-channel behavior and enables leakage suppression with reduced ion dose while maintaining equivalent V_T [10]. The T-SRAM achieves 0.62 pW/bit leakage power and nearly a 10× improvement in the figure-of-merit (cell density / leakage power) over prior reported low-leakage SRAMs. Owing to the exponential dependence of I_BTBT and V_DS, 93% lower standby leakage is achieved in ternary data storage [10].

The IBM ultralow-power SRAM technology paper (Mann et al., 2003, IBM Journal of R&D) reviews five dominant parametric leakage mechanisms in 6T SRAM cells: 1) threshold voltage optimization, 2) gate tunneling leakage, 3) subthreshold leakage, 4) reverse-bias diffusion leakage, and 5) gate-induced drain leakage (GIDL). A significant portion of the development effort focused on GIDL reduction through halo and extension implant engineering. The paper also notes that statistical Vt variation becomes significant when σ(Vt) exceeds 30 mV [7].

**Gate Oxide Thickness Scaling**

The transition to high-k gate stacks (e.g., HfO₂) was driven by the limitations of traditional SiO₂ scaling at the 45nm node. At the 45nm node, geometric scaling of SiO₂ gate oxide is strongly impeded due to tunneling leakage at ~7.5Å thickness. The switch to high-k + metal gate states one of the major cuts since the advent of CMOS technology. The first high-k + metal gate transistors in a high volume manufacturing process were reported in Mistry et al. 2007. Mistry et al. employed a high-k first and metal gate last process, using hafnium-oxide gate dielectric, dual workfunction metal gates, achieving 25× (NMOS) and 1000× (PMOS) gate leakage reduction, and 32% drive current improvement at the 45nm node. Further scaling demands an even smaller EOT (32nm → 8Å and 22nm → 6Å) [9].

HKMG is not merely a materials swap — it represents a fundamental rethinking of gate stack physics, process integration strategy, and device design methodology. The elegant physical insight behind high-k dielectrics is that gate capacitance depends on the ratio of dielectric constant to physical thickness, not on physical thickness alone. Equivalent Oxide Thickness (EOT) is the metric comparing different dielectrics. A subtle but important finding in scaled HKMG devices is that effective work function (EWF) is not purely an intrinsic material property: it is also influenced by the physical geometry of the gate trench, becoming increasingly significant at sub-28nm dimensions [10].

Gate-oxide tunneling establishes minimum gate-oxide thickness (~2.75 nm) for ULP technologies [7].

**Threshold Voltage (Vt) Engineering**

For 6T-SRAM, cell stability (SNM) can be improved by selecting device threshold voltages (low pFET VT for pull-up, high nFET VT for pass-gate) [17]. The paper "Stable SRAM cell design for the 32 nm node and beyond" (Chang et al., 2005 VLSI Symposium) demonstrates that 6T-SRAM can be optimized for stability by choosing the cell layout, device threshold voltages, and the ß ratio [17].

Work function setting in high-k metal gate devices (IntechOpen, 2018) explains that as transistor size continues to shrink, SiO2/polysilicon gate stack has been replaced by high-k/metal gate to enable further scaling. The work function difference between channel material and gate electrode should be small to ensure a low threshold voltage. Two main integration approaches are used: gate first and gate last (replacement gate). Both require precise work function (WF) tuning for NMOS (~4.1 eV) and PMOS (~5 eV) to achieve correct threshold voltages. In Gate First Technology, WF is set via dipole formation at the interface between the SiON interfacial layer and high-k dielectric, using La for NMOS and Al for PMOS, driven in by high-temperature anneal. SiGe channels can further tune PMOS Vt (10mV shift per 1% Ge). In Gate Last Technology, NMOS uses Al (WF 4.1 eV) with TiN/TaN protection layers to prevent Al spiking; PMOS uses TiN (WF tunable ~5 eV). WF is defined by metal-metal interdiffusion in a multilayer stack rather than a single metal [7].

**Strain Engineering (Stress Liners, SiGe Channels)**

The paper "New structure transistors for advanced technology node CMOS ICs" (National Science Review, 2024) notes that key innovations in the FinFET era included SiGe strain engineering, high-κ/metal gates (HKMG), and contact-on-gate structures [1, 6].

The paper "What Silicon Really Says: Diffusion Breaks, Gate Cuts, and the Anatomy of Stress-Related LLEs" (PDF Solutions) examines stress-related Local Layout Effects (LLEs) in advanced 7nm FinFET CMOS devices. Key findings include:
- P-type FinFETs are consistently more sensitive to local layout perturbations than n-type devices. PMOS current variations can exceed 10% (approaching ±12% in calibrated models), while NMOS shifts typically stay below 5%. This is because PMOS is strongly driven by longitudinal stress variations, whereas NMOS responds to a mixed combination of stress components that can partially compensate.
- The strongest layout-dependent effects appear around structures that modify the local mechanical boundary conditions of the channel, especially Diffusion Breaks and Gate Cuts.
- In the measured 7nm structures, p-type variations can exceed 10% and, in some modeled cases, approach ±12%, whereas n-type shifts are typically below 5%.
- The layout is part of the physics. The local neighborhood around the device is not a passive backdrop. It contributes directly to the channel stress state and therefore to the electrical response [9].

The paper "Investigation of Proximity Effects in a 6T SRAM Cell Using Three-Dimensional TCAD Simulations" finds that proximity effects significantly influence doping and stress profiles in 6T SRAM cells, impacting performance by over 10% [4].

**FinFET and Alternative Device Benefits**

FinFET-based SRAM cells with built-in feedback (back-gate biasing) achieve significant improvements in static noise margin (SNM) without area penalty [6]. Conventional 6-T FinFET DG cells with high Vt achieve 175mV read SNM (30% improvement over bulk-Si with β-ratio=1.5). Upsizing the pull-down transistor by 1 fin yields 240mV SNM (16.6% area penalty); rotating NPD to (100) plane yields 200mV SNM (13.3% area penalty). 6-T FinFET with built-in feedback achieves 300mV SNM — a 71% improvement over conventional DG design — with no area penalty (2% area reduction). Standby leakage <0.2nA/cell. The elimination of heavy doping in the channel minimizes Vt variations due to statistical dopant fluctuation effects. 6-T FinFET-based SRAM cells can achieve less than 0.2nA/cell of standby current just by using high Vt devices [6].

**Beta Ratio (β-ratio) and Transistor Sizing**

The stability of the SRAM cell can be improved by modulating the transistor sizing ratio (β-ratio, i.e., pull-down to access transistor ratio). Increasing β from 1 to 3 improves Static Noise Margin (SNM) and critical charge (Qcrit) at the expense of write time and power consumption. For a 6T-SRAM cell in 32 nm technology:
- β=1: SNM=27.4 mV, Qcrit=1.64 fC, Write time=35.38 ps, Power=6.54 µW
- β=2: SNM=79.7 mV, Qcrit=1.86 fC, Write time=47.48 ps, Power=9.38 µW
- β=3: SNM=102.8 mV, Qcrit=2.04 fC, Write time=57.17 ps, Power=12.03 µW

SNM improves more than 2x as the β-ratio of SRAM changes from 1 to 3 [1]. Optimizing the beta (ß) ratio enhances stability while minimizing cell area, ideally set at ß~2-3 [16, 17].

The read margin and write margin are in direct conflict. Making the pull-down (D) stronger helps read but hurts write. The sizing hierarchy is: NMOS pull-down (D) strongest, access transistors (A) intermediate, PMOS pull-up (P) weakest. This is captured by the β ratio (W/L of pull-down divided by W/L of access transistor) [18]. The 6T SRAM cell has one fundamental tension: the same feedback strength that makes it stable during hold makes it hard to read without disturbing the state, and hard to write against its own resistance [18].

### (2) Cell Layout Optimizations and Patterning Techniques

**EUV Lithography for Tighter Cell Pitches**

EUV lithography (13.5nm wavelength) is replacing 193i lithography for critical chip layers due to its shorter wavelength, enabling single exposure lithography beyond 193i's resolution limits [7]. The tipping point for EUV adoption occurs at the 5nm node for logic and the 1a node for DRAM devices. At 7nm, manufacturers use EUV on select layers to reduce multi-patterning requirements. At 5nm, 193i becomes too costly, requiring unsustainable numbers of process steps. Single patterning with EUV requires only 10 process steps per mask compared to 120 for SAQP [7].

EUVL single-patterning reaches limits at 32-30nm pitches with current 0.33 NA technology, primarily due to stochastic failures. For imec N5 (foundry N3) with 21nm pitches, EUVL multi-patterning techniques are needed: SADP (self-aligned double patterning), LELE (litho-etch litho-etch), or 193nm immersion-based SAQP/SAOP. For 16nm pitch lines, four options were explored: 193nm immersion-based SAOP, EUV-based SADP, EUV-based SAQP, and eSALELE (self-aligned litho-etch litho-etch). Trade-offs exist in process complexity, cost-of-ownership, scalability, design freedom, and line-edge roughness (LER). Next-generation high-NA EUVL systems (NA=0.55) are being developed to push single-exposure resolution further [8].

Imec calculated a 20% reduction in wafer cost when transitioning from an all 193nm immersion-based solution to a solution where blocks and vias are patterned with EUV single exposure [9]. Stochastic failures depend heavily on exposure dose, target CD, and pitch. Higher exposure doses (45mJ/cm2 for logic, 33mJ/cm2 for memory) help mitigate failures despite cost trade-offs. Post-processing resist smoothening techniques (e.g., quasi-atomic layer etching) show 20-30% LER improvement. Computational lithography techniques like SRAFs and retargeting improve exposure latitude, depth-of-focus, and defect-free CD process windows [9].

**Self-Aligned Contacts (SAC)**

TSMC introduced Self-Aligned Contacts (SAC) for the first time at N3B (Intel has used since 22nm). SAC reduced contact resistance by 45% and variation by 50%. TSMC's scheme on N3B allows for the leakage at the gate-contact junction to remain constant even at wider gate lengths and process variations. However, SAC was removed in N3E. TSMC noted FinFET architecture has reached its limit and nanosheet transistors are essential [3].

The 1997 ISSCC conference noted that the self-aligned contact (SAC) process improved cell size reduction [4].

**Diffusion Breaks (Single/Double Diffusion Breaks)**

The paper "What Silicon Really Says: Diffusion Breaks, Gate Cuts, and the Anatomy of Stress-Related LLEs" (PDF Solutions) provides detailed analysis:
- Single Diffusion Breaks (SDB)—etched late in the process after epitaxial growth—act as a sudden release of mechanical energy, causing PMOS to lose up to 15% of linear drain current.
- Double Diffusion Breaks (DDB), defined early in the process, limit degradation to approximately 8%. NMOS shows a more complex response (-2% to +5%) due to competing effects from trench etch relaxation and dielectric fill recompression.
- A PMOS device near an SDB can lose up to 15% of its linear drain current, whereas a DDB, being pre-formed, limits this degradation to approximately 8% [9].

Cell heights depend on contacted poly pitch (CPP) and whether a cell uses DDB or SDB. Cell widths are calculated for two-input NAND cells (4×CPP for DDB, 3×CPP for SDB) and scanned flip-flop cells (20×CPP for DDB, 19×CPP for SDB). A DDB adds an additional one half CPP to each side of a cell. CPP is limited to about 40nm due to device issues [7].

TSMC's N5 uses Continuous Diffusion (CNOD) for horizontal cell separation, which sacrifices some vertical scaling (cell height) to achieve horizontal savings, unlike the more common Single Diffusion Break (SDB) approach [8].

**Buried Power Rails**

Buried Power Rail (BPR) is a power rail found inside the semiconductor substrate (below the active layer where transistors/diodes reside) rather than on a metal layer like traditional M1 routing [1, 3]. IMEC first announced BPR in 2019. In 2021, they demonstrated backside connectivity through nano TSVs. In 2022, they presented the first experimental demonstration of routing for logic ICs with backside power delivery using nano-through-silicon-vias landing on BPRs [1].

A 2019 paper by ARM and IMEC researchers showed BPRs with front-side power delivery improved worst-case IR drop from 70mV to 42mV (1.7× reduction). BPRs with backside power delivery reduced IR drop to 10mV (7× reduction) [1, 3, 4]. The addition of BPR reduces the dynamic IR drop by 26% and the addition of BSPD improves the IR drop by an additional 75%. Static IR drop is reduced by 23% by BPR and an additional 95% by adding BSPD [4].

For SRAM specifically, the imec team etched deep, narrow trenches between transistor fins and filled them with ruthenium to create the buried power lines. The read-from speed of the resulting memory cells was about 31 percent faster than conventional SRAM, and writing to them required 340 millivolts less than what it takes to power memories whose interconnects aren't buried. Wider bit lines were nearly 75 percent less resistant and the new word lines cut resistance by more than 50 percent, leading to the improved read speed and lower write voltage. Grid power distribution can improve SRAM by 28.2% [3, 5].

The BPRs developed by IMEC are made from tungsten (4× higher resistance than copper), with via interconnects using ruthenium. The BPRs showed no electromigration failures after 900 hours of continuous use at 330°C at 4 mA/cm² [1, 3]. IMEC's demonstration showed fully functional devices down to 3nm scale. BPR replaces wide-thin power rails in metal 2 with tall-narrow rails buried in the substrate, enabling 5-track or smaller cells for nanosheets [4].

Intel has announced BSPD (called PowerVia) for 20A/18A without BPR, and TSMC has announced BSPD for 2nm. BPR likely won't be used in first-generation BSPD but should be considered for further scaling. BSPD also offers potential for adding backside functionality like ESD devices and MIM capacitors [4].

The Advanced Process and Electron Device Technology paper (2021) concludes that for favorable integration of more complex devices such as CFETs with BPR, BS PDN or monolithic 3D ICs and heterogeneous integration systems, a system technology co-optimization (STCO) method must be established for sustained development of advanced ICs [6].

**Alternative Cell Architectures for Stability**

8T-SRAM provides a much greater enhancement in stability by eliminating cell disturbs during a read access, thus facilitating continued technology scaling. The addition of two FETs in 8T-SRAM eliminates read disturb issues, improving static noise margin (SNM). A ~30% area penalty is incurred with the addition of two extra FETs, but 8T-SRAM can allow for continued scaling beyond that which is possible with traditional 6T-SRAM [16, 17]. The smallest demonstrated 6T half-cell was 0.124 μm² and the smallest full 8T cell was 0.1998 μm² [17].

A straight line layout minimizes variability by reducing overlay errors and improving mismatch control, increasing static noise margin [16, 17].

The 9T SRAM was found to have a higher stability in the read margin due to the use of pass-gate transistors and also isolating the read current path by using transistors of minimum feature size; less leakage current and power than the 6T SRAM. The N-curve metric is used for inline testers; it gives both information for voltage and current and in addition it has no voltage scaling delimiter as found in VTC approach [11]. At 45nm/1V, 27°C: 6T shows SVNM=320.9mV, SINM=181.2μA, WTV=547.5mV, WTI=78.96μA, Leakage=13.84pA; 9T shows SVNM=321.67mV, SINM=382.6μA, WTV=594.5mV, WTI=122.4μA, Leakage=11.1pA [11].

The 7T SRAM cell (Akashe, 45nm) consists of two cross-coupled CMOS inverters with an additional NMOS transistor for read line and two pass NMOS transistors for bit lines. Cell stability can be improved by: (1) reducing word-line voltage (lower word-line voltage increases SNM), (2) transistor width modulation, and (3) power-supply voltage modulation (reducing bit-line voltage below Vdd increases SNM during read). Cell ratio (CR) and pull-up ratio (PR) ranges are 1.0-2.5 and 3-4 respectively; increasing driver transistor width increases CR, SNM, and speed [3].

The RHHS16T cell (2024) demonstrates highest read stability (RSNM) among all compared cells due to isolating the storage node from the bit line during read operations and having the highest cell ratio (CR=3.3). The proposed cell can fully recover to its initial state even if soft errors affect nodes Q, QB, S1, or the storage node pair Q-QB [19].

The 1.5nm SGT SRAM cell (Unisantis) achieves an area of 0.0071µm² with a scaling factor of 1.40 per node, achieved through: (1) a staggered pillar arrangement that provides a 20nm bottom contact width (vs. 4nm in mirror-symmetric layouts), (2) self-aligned patterning with sidewall spacers for gate formation, and (3) bottom contacts for cross-coupling embedded below the gate. The staggered layout uses orthogonal self-aligned double patterning (SADP) with EUV lithography. Read static noise margins (RSNM) >100mV are secured down to 0.5V VDD [2].

### (3) Manufacturing Process Variations That Degrade SNM and Mitigation Strategies

**Random Dopant Fluctuations (RDF)**

The paper "Sensitivity of static noise margins to random dopant variations in 6-T SRAM cells" (Oniciuc and Andrei, 2008, Solid-State Electronics) finds that the most sensitive regions to doping fluctuations extend approximately 10 nm below the oxide/semiconductor interface and are located in the middle of the conduction channels for both p-channel and n-channel transistors [3].

The IEDM 2009 paper on metal grain work function variability predicts that at the 22nm technology node, among the three device variability sources: random dopant fluctuation (RDF), line edge roughness (LER) and WFV, WFV will cross over RDF and becomes the dominating factor [11].

The FinFET SRAM paper (Guo et al., ISLPED'05) notes that the elimination of heavy doping in the channel minimizes Vt variations due to statistical dopant fluctuation effects. 6-T FinFET-based SRAM cells have tighter SNM distributions (sigma=5-6.6mV) vs. bulk-Si (sigma=16mV) [6].

The paper "Interactions Between Line Edge Roughness and Random Dopant Fluctuation in Nonplanar Field-Effect Transistor Variability" (2013, IEEE TED) finds that LER and RDF must be modeled together for accurate IM-FinFET and TFET variability predictions. JL-FinFETs exhibit independent behavior between LER and RDF, with less than 10% error in estimations. Significant variations in σI_OFF for IM-FinFETs can reach 97% when assuming LER and RDF independence. Different transistor structures yield varying dependencies between LER and RDF due to localized versus distributed variability [12].

The GAA Si NS CFET study (2025, Nanomaterials) finds that the statistical sum (RSD) of the fluctuation for each factor is overestimated by less than 50% compared with the simultaneous fluctuations of PVE, WKF, and RDF factors. The sensitivity to process-induced variability is found to be particularly pronounced in the P-FETs, primarily due to the enhanced parasitic conduction associated with the bottom nanosheet channel. The static power dissipation remains relatively small compared to dynamic and short-circuit power components, it exhibits the largest relative fluctuation (approximately 82.1%), posing critical challenges for low-power circuit applications [13].

**Line-Edge Roughness (LER)**

The computational study on LER from EUV to FinFET (Kim, 2021, Micromachines) finds that LER and line-width roughness (LWR) are caused by EUV stochastic events such as shot noise of incident photons, chemical concentration shot noise, and molecule reaction-diffusion in resists. Since numbers of photons in EUVL are 14 times smaller than those of ArF lithography, stochastic EUV photons can result in photon shot noise, which makes poor performance in EUV resist. LER decreases with increasing exposure dose before saturating. There exists an optimum acid diffusion length that minimizes LER. According to a neural method, PEB temperature (T_PEB) and PEB time (t_PEB) are dominant factors. This means that PEB process is the most dominant process for LER in EUVL processes. For 5-nm gate length FinFETs, absolute drain currents with fat-fin, thin-fin, and big-drain FWRs shifted rightward with increasing gate voltage [14].

The primary causes of process-induced random variation can be classified as (i) line edge roughness (LER), (ii) random dopant fluctuation (RDF) [15].

**Metal-Gate Workfunction Variation (WFV)**

The IEDM 2009 paper (IBM Research) presents a new physical model of work function variability (WFV) in dual metal gate MOSFETs, based on grain orientation differences in polycrystalline metal gates. The model predicts that at the 22nm technology node, among the three device variability sources: random dopant fluctuation (RDF), line edge roughness (LER) and WFV, WFV will cross over RDF and becomes the dominating factor. The SRAM circuit analysis shows that write/read failures are underestimated by 9 orders of magnitude by the area weighted averaged work function model [11].

The PatSnap article on metal gate granularity at 5nm finds that as gate dimensions contract below 5nm, the number of grains under the gate shrinks to single-digit figures, transforming MGG from a statistical nuisance into a device-limiting, quasi-deterministic mismatch source. Research from IIT Bombay (2018) established that MGG is "of paramount importance due to its large impact on VT variability" compared with other process-induced variabilities such as random dopant fluctuations (RDF) or line edge roughness (LER). Below 5nm, the gate volume accommodates only a handful of metal grains, invalidating central-limit-theorem averaging and making σVt non-Gaussian [6].

The POSTECH (2022) study in silicon nanowire FETs with gate lengths of 15–22nm and channel diameters of 7, 9, and 12nm found that WFV from metal grain orientation was the dominant variability contributor across all geometries. Gate-all-around nanosheet architectures at 2nm-class nodes intensify MGG because metal must fill nanoscale slits between stacked sheets, constraining grain growth [6].

The Seoul National University paper on WFV for vertical nanoplate FET in 6-T SRAMs (2017, SNW) investigates WFV on 5 nm node gate-all-around (GAA) Vertical Nanoplate FET (NP VFET) in 6-T SRAM. As WFV effects become intensified, the authors investigate the WFV effects for an accurate guideline with regard to grain size (GS) and channel area of NP VFET in SRAM bit cells [8].

The GAA Si NS CFET study (2025, Nanomaterials) finds that WKF emerges as the dominant source impacting Vth, subsequently influencing the SS and gm characteristics for both N-FETs and P-FETs [13].

**Oxide Thickness Variation**

The IBM ultralow-power SRAM paper (Mann et al., 2003) notes that gate-oxide tunneling establishes minimum gate-oxide thickness (~2.75 nm) for ULP technologies. Narrow-channel effect (NCE) causes Vt roll-off below active widths of 0.20 μm (n-FET) and 0.4 μm (p-FET). Three unique challenges for future scaled ULP technologies include channel-size-dependent threshold voltage variations and channel width dependence on both device threshold (NCE) and GIDL [7].

**Mitigation Strategies**

*Advanced Annealing (Laser Spike Anneal - LSA)*

Laser Spike Anneal (LSA) is an advanced semiconductor thermal processing technology that uses short, intense laser pulses to rapidly heat only the near-surface region of a silicon wafer to ultra-high temperatures for sub-millisecond to nanosecond durations. This non-equilibrium thermal process allows the crystal to recrystallize and the dopants to activate before Fickian diffusion can smear the precisely implanted spatial profiles [11]. LSA creates highly activated, ultra-shallow junctions with near diffusion-less boundaries in silicon. This produces more uniform temperature and stress distributions in product wafers than lamp-based short-time annealing processes [14].

LSA became essential at 65nm CMOS, standard at 28nm planar for source/drain extensions, and evolved for 14nm FinFETs to provide conformal activation across high-aspect-ratio fins. At 7nm and beyond, sub-millisecond to nanosecond regimes are required to preserve delicate strain engineering [11]. LSA has long been the process of record for most of the industry's foundries and IDMs for high-performance logic devices due to its unique hardware configuration and real-time process control capability [14].

Dual-beam LSA configurations provide: Long Dwell Applications (~10 msec) using a second preheat laser to enable defect annealing, solid phase regrowth, and stress reduction; Low Temperature Applications (500-1000°C) enabling nickel silicide formation and post-silicide dopant re-activation with minimal pattern effects. Fast cool-down allows active carrier concentration to increase with dwell time (unlike lamp-based annealing where deactivation occurs). Stress reduction achieved by reducing thermal gradients during ramp-up; dual beam LSA can achieve higher maximum temperature without slip. Short dwell times reduce wafer warpage and overlay errors. LSA configuration (CO2 laser, Brewster angle, p-polarization) almost eliminates sensitivity to thin-film interference variations, providing superior pattern effect control [13].

Veeco's LSA system is widely acknowledged as the optimum annealing solution for low thermal-budget applications, and as device geometries and performance requirements at advanced nodes continue to evolve, precise annealing by the LSA platform has become increasingly critical. Two leading-edge logic customers have selected Veeco's LSA Platform as their Production Tool of Record for new applications at their gate-all-around (GAA) nodes [15].

*High-k/Metal Gate Optimization and Workfunction Engineering*

Process engineering strategies for mitigating metal gate granularity (MGG) include:
1. Equiaxed grain deposition by RF-PVD (STMicroelectronics, 2019) — produces geometrically uniform grains
2. Amorphous interlayer insertion (Shanghai Huali) — 5–50Å silicon layer between TiN and TaN, annealed to form amorphous TiSiN/TaSiN
3. Oxygen vacancy passivation in HfO₂ via compressive strain (Vellore Institute of Technology, 2024)
4. Amorphous top-cap barrier layers to block oxygen diffusion (Shanghai Huali, 2022) — addressing TiAl oxidation that shifts work function by 66–157%

Oxidation of TiAl (used for NMOS work function) during wafer queue time converts Al to Al2O3, shifting the local work function by 66–157% [6].

The HKMG process integration article (SemiFlows) notes that key process parameters affecting outcomes include: thermal budget, high-k composition/stoichiometry, metal gate work function layer deposition (via ALD), interface passivation quality, and gate trench fill quality. Challenges include threshold voltage instability (Bias Temperature Instability), Fermi-level pinning, EOT creep from interfacial SiO₂ growth, channel mobility degradation from enhanced phonon scattering, work function metal fill issues in narrow gates, and trap-assisted tunneling through oxygen vacancies in HfO₂ [10].

The high-k gate stacks paper (IuE) notes that threshold voltage (V_t) tuning is achieved through channel engineering, metal selection, and capping layers. Tseng et al. showed V_t control via dipole-induced shifts at the high-k/SiO₂ interface [9].

*Process Control Techniques*

The SRAM design tradeoffs approach (Rajendran, 2011) enables constraint-driven optimization where designers can select β-ratios that satisfy constraints on Qcrit, write time, and power while maximizing SNM. The solution is expressed as: βq ≤ βi ≤ min{βt, βp}, where βq, βt, βp are the minimum β satisfying Qcrit, write time, and power constraints respectively [1].

Vmin is a measure of the process quality and it is driven by basically the control of defect — so it's not a design parameter but rather it is controlled by the foundry [18].

The 9T SRAM configuration is a design paradigm for ultra-low power and robust logic circuit under process variation that reduces to the barest minimum dynamic and static current (power) consumption in 9T SRAM bit cell [11].

The paper "Systematic and random variability analysis of two different..." (Amat et al., 2013) studies the device variability influence on 6T-SRAM cells. SNM has been seen as the parameter that suffers the highest impact with respect to cell variability [12].

The paper "Direct Measurement of Correlation Between SRAM Noise Margin and Individual Cell Transistor Variability by Using Device Matrix Array" establishes a direct correlation between SRAM noise margin and transistor variability using a 16-kb device matrix array [15].

The review paper "Review of 6T SRAM for Embedded Memory Applications" (2023, IJVLSID) discusses many SRAM factors, including Static Noise Margin (SNM), Read Access Time (RAT), Write Access Time (WAT), Read Stability and Write Ability, Power, Data Retention Voltage (DRV), and Process Control [19].

The leakage power reduction techniques paper (Singh et al., 2011) investigates five circuit-level leakage reduction techniques: Body Biasing (reverse body biasing raises Vt to reduce sub-threshold leakage, but effectiveness decreases with scaling; maximum leakage savings of 1.18x for raising VNWELL to 1.4V and 1.46x for VPWELL at -0.4V), Source Biasing (raising source voltage to 0.4V achieved 8.16x leakage reduction, but at the cost of decreased SNM and increased delay), Dynamic VDD (0.5V standby VDD obtains maximum 15.8 times leakage energy saving, but reduces hold-SNM to only 169.2 mV, which may cause retention data flipping failures), Negative Word Line (maximum 1.22x leakage reduction at -1.2V, but gate leakage increases), and Bit Line Floating (maximum 1.25x leakage reduction; saves 24% leakage power in I-cache memories) [8].

The dynamic stability and noise margins paper (Teman, EPFL, 2014) argues that traditional SNM metrics are no longer sufficient under scaled supply voltages and increased process variations. The paper introduces dynamic stability and Dynamic Noise Margin (DNM) concepts, which analyze SRAM behavior using state-space analysis, phase portraits, and the separatrix (the stability boundary separating regions of attraction). Key DNM definitions include: DNM_read = Tacross - Tread (time to cross separatrix minus read access time) and DNM_write = Twrite - Tacross [2].

## 1. BETA RATIO OPTIMIZATION (TRANSISTOR UPSIZING) AND THE FUNDAMENTAL 6T TRADE-OFFS

The 6T SRAM cell consists of two back-to-back inverters (pull-up PMOS P1/P2, pull-down NMOS D1/D2) plus two access transistors (A1/A2) controlled by the wordline, connected to bitline and bitline bar. The 6T SRAM cell has one fundamental tension: the same feedback strength that makes it stable during hold makes it hard to read without disturbing the state, and hard to write against its own resistance. Every circuit in the SRAM periphery — the access transistors, write drivers, sense amps, and cell sizing ratios — exists to manage this single trade-off. [45]

**Transistor sizing hierarchy:** Pull-down (D) must be strongest > Access (A) intermediate > Pull-up (P) weakest. The β ratio (W/L of pull-down divided by W/L of access transistor) determines read margin; the γ ratio (W/L of access divided by W/L of pull-up) affects write margin. The 6T-SRAM cell has inherent trade-offs between read stability (requiring cell ratio CR > 1) and writability (requiring pull-up ratio PR < 1), with conflicting device sizing requirements. [36][45]

**Read operation constraint:** During read, bitlines are precharged to VDD. Wordline goes high, enabling access transistors. The critical design constraint is that D1 must be stronger than A1 to prevent the internal node Q from rising and flipping the cell (read stability). [45]

**Write operation constraint:** The access transistor must overpower the PMOS pull-up to flip the cell. Writeability requires P2 weaker than A2. [45]

**Quantitative beta ratio results (32nm technology):** Rajendran et al. (2011) presented a design trade-offs approach that improves SRAM characteristics by modulating the transistor sizing ratio β (pull-down to access transistor ratio). Testing four SRAM cell designs (6T-SRAM, SRAM-C capacitor-based, SRAM-T tristate, and SRAM-NSP tristate with separate read port) in 32nm technology, they varied β from 1 to 3. For the standard 6T-SRAM at 32nm:
- At β=1: SNM = 27.4 mV, Qcrit = 1.64 fC, Write time = 35.38 ps, Power = 6.54 µW
- At β=2: SNM = 79.7 mV, Qcrit = 1.86 fC, Write time = 47.48 ps, Power = 9.38 µW
- At β=3: SNM = 102.8 mV, Qcrit = 2.04 fC, Write time = 57.17 ps, Power = 12.04 µW

SNM improves more than 2x as the β-ratio changes from 1 to 3, while Qcrit, write time, and power consumption also increase. A constraint-driven approach was formalized to select β-ratios that satisfy designer constraints on Qcrit (minimum), write time (maximum), and power (maximum) while optimizing SNM. The solution involves finding β subsets where βq ≤ βi ≤ min{βt, βp}. [1][24]

**Impact of voltage scaling on noise margin:** As supply voltage (VDD) scales down, the butterfly loop shrinks, reducing RSNM. For example, at 400 mV VDD, the nested square was 105 mV; at 250 mV VDD, it shrinks to 45 mV. Improving the cell ratio (beta factor) from 2 to 3 can help boost noise margins, but this creates trade-offs with the pull ratio required for write operations, leading to read-write conflicting requirements. [47]

**Aspect ratio optimization (90nm):** Sachdeva and Tomar (2021) presented aspect ratio optimization of conventional 6T SRAM cell transistors to improve cell stability using gpdk 90nm technology with Cadence Virtuoso tool, showing significant improvement in stability parameters. [46]

## 2. CELL TOPOLOGY COMPARISONS (6T, 7T, 8T, 9T, 10T, 11T, 12T, 14T)

### 6T versus 8T
Birla et al. analyzed the stability and leakage performance of different SRAM cell designs (6T, 7T, 8T, 10T, 11T) at 65nm process technology. The proposed 8T SRAM cell improves read SNM to 1.22, significantly enhancing data stability compared to 6T (which can be as low as 0.20). At 65nm technology, the conventional 6T SRAM has a write margin of only 0.6V, indicating limited write capability. The 8T SRAM involves approximately 30% area overhead compared to conventional 6T design. [2]

A separate optimized 8T cell design shows a 2.1x improvement in read margin over the 6T cell in 90nm technology with a 24% area penalty, and a 9.78x improvement in 32nm technology with a 29% area overhead. The 8T cell also enables simultaneous read and write operations while maintaining the layout advantages of the 6T cell. Therefore, the 8T cell is best suited to replace the 6T cell in advanced processes. [4]

Choudhary and Yadav (2021) compared 6T and 8T SRAM cells on 180nm technology using Cadence Virtuoso. Results illustrate that read delay and write delay will decrease for the 8T cell compared to the 6T. Although the six-transistor cell consumed lower dynamic power than the eight-transistor cell design and was more area efficient, these findings demonstrate the natural trade-offs between stability, speed, and area for low-voltage and energy-restricted applications. [42]

### 7T
The 7T SRAM design enables a 49% reduction in write power while maintaining static noise margins. [2]

### 9T
A novel PP-based 9T SRAM at 45nm technology has 33% increased SVNM (Static Voltage Noise Margin) from 6T and also reduced leakage power. [4]

### 10T
The 10T architecture was selected as optimal over 6T, 8T, and 12T designs due to its superior balance of stability, power efficiency, and performance. [3][16]

**MTCMOS 10T at 90nm:** The MTCMOS-based 10T SRAM cell achieved the highest stability with an SNM of 379.456 mV, compared to stacked and conventional designs. The MTCMOS design had the lowest power consumption at 13.8 µW, significantly outperforming the conventional 10T (2.09 mW) and stacked 10T (78.7 µW). For leakage, the MTCMOS 10T had the lowest value, around 720 µW across all process corners. All cells performed best at the FF (Fast-Fast) corner; the worst-case scenario occurred at the SS (Slow-Slow) corner. The stacked 10T showed better read/write performance and output quality, but the MTCMOS scheme excelled in static power reduction. The post-layout MTCMOS 10T layout was verified with clean DRC/LVS checks and parasitic extraction. [3][16]

**OHP10T at 22nm:** An Optimized High Performance 10T (OHP10T) SRAM cell was proposed for low power and high speed cache memory applications at 22nm technology node using HSPICE, featuring two independent read access mechanisms (direct and indirect read drivers) controlled by an XOR gate driven by read and write word lines, along with a tail transistor for leakage reduction. Key results: 40% smaller read delay compared to LP10T, 12% smaller than 6T; 15% higher Write Static Noise Margin (WSNM) compared to LP10T (286 mV vs 312 mV); 48% higher Read SNM (RSNM) compared to 6T (214 mV vs 81 mV at VDD=0.8V); 40% smaller standby leakage power compared to 6T and 9T (similar to LP10T); 38% area overhead compared to 6T (54λ × 32λ vs 53λ × 24λ), but similar to LP10T. [43]

**MediaTek xBIT (logic-based bitcell, ISSCC 2026):** MediaTek presented a novel 10-transistor cell (xBIT) achieving 22-63% higher density than standard 8T bitcells. Average read/write power reduced by over 30%, leakage reduced 29% at 0.5V. Operates from 100 MHz at 0.35V to 4 GHz at 0.95V. [6]

### 11T
An 11T SRAM design achieves SNM improvement of more than 6x in some cases compared to 6T, with speed four times higher. [2]

### 8T CNTFET
A novel 8T SRAM cell using Carbon Nanotube Field-Effect Transistors (CNTFET) with Positive Feedback Control (PFC) and Positive Power Supply Control (PPC) techniques at 32nm technology achieves 99.99% improvement in Power-Delay Product (PDP) compared to conventional 6T SRAM cells. Static noise margin of 300 mV ensures robust noise immunity. Mean power consumption: 43.19 nW (standard deviation σ=305.2 nW). Mean delay: 14.71 ps (standard deviation σ=10.05 ps). Leakage power: 0.322 pW (99.9% reduction compared to prior designs). Minimum PDP: 9.825 × 10⁻²¹ J. Total delay: 29.384 ps. The PFC transistor introduces voltage equalization during read and write operations, minimizing the voltage swing required for switching, while the PPC transistor employs power gating to suppress leakage currents during standby modes. [41]

### 5nm GAA CNTFET SRAM
Low-power circuit-level techniques applied to a 5nm node GAA CNTFET 6T SRAM cell show: The Sleepy approach demonstrated the lowest leakage power (8.56E-8 pW), significantly outperforming the basic 6T cell (378.6 pW). Sleepy and Zigzag approaches showed the best write delay reductions (3.89% and 5.03% respectively vs. baseline). Footer and Header approaches showed significant WSNM increases (~21.58% and 20.95% respectively). For RSNM, the footer, sleepy, and header approaches showcased notable increases of 53.57%, 70.29%, and 18.11% respectively, in comparison to the corresponding values from 32nm CNTFET SRAM cell. [44]

## 3. READ AND WRITE ASSIST TECHNIQUES AND TRADE-OFFS WITH SNM

### Write Assist Techniques
Four main write assist techniques have been identified, all of which improve write margin but degrade read noise margin (RNM) and static noise margin (SNM): [25][26]

**1. Reducing VDD of the SRAM cell:** Lower cell voltage reduces the charge to be discharged, speeding up flipping and reducing the critical word line pulse width (WL critical). [25]

**2. Increasing VSS (cell ground):** Raising the cell's ground voltage moves the metastability point (separatrix) higher, making discharge easier and writing faster. [25]

**3. Word Line Boosting:** Boosts the word line voltage above supply voltage to increase access transistor strength; works on rows (unlike NBL which works on columns). However, half-selected cells in the same row may be disturbed during read. [25][26]

**4. Negative Bit Line (NBL):** Uses capacitive coupling to drive bit lines below ground, increasing Vgs of access transistors. However, unselected cells in the same column can experience leakage-induced flips. [25][26]

The major problem is faced during write assist at low voltage as the cell gets flipped and the data cannot be written. Process variations significantly impact SRAM performance and increase memory failure risks. Supply voltage scaling reduces power dissipation but complicates performance due to increased sensitivity. [26]

### Read Assist Techniques
Read assist techniques are the opposite of write assist techniques: under-driven word line, reduced bit line VDD, and suppressed word line — these improve read static noise margin by reducing read disturb. [25]

**Word Line Suppression Circuit (Texas Instruments patent):** A word line suppression circuit includes a diode (NMOS transistor) and a switch (NMOS transistor) coupled in series. The switch is responsive to the array supply voltage (VDDAR). The word line suppression circuit limits a word line voltage to a value lower than the array supply voltage such that the static noise margin (SNM) of the bit cell is increased. The need for a two-part write operation arises from the fact that the bit cell coupled to the word line, but not intended/selected for a write operation, undergoes a default read operation and hence is subject to the same SNM issue. [29]

**Read-assist sense amplifier:** A proposed read-assist sense amplifier in 65nm CMOS technology expedites differential voltage development on bitlines while reducing voltage swing, increasing sensing speed, lowering power, and shortening WL activation time. It enables reduced cell VDD for the same sensing speed, reducing leakage power. Compared to conventional SA: 56.1% speed improvement, 25.9% power reduction with negligible area overhead. [27]

**Variation-tolerant assist circuits:** Abu-Rahma and Anis (2013) presented variation-tolerant assist circuits that result in 83% improvement of the cell current compared with conventional assist circuits. The 6T SRAM cell will be allowed long reign, even in the 15-nm process node, if ΔVT can be suppressed to < 70 mV. [28]

### TSMC's Write Assist at 5nm (ISSCC 2020)
Two major write assist methods were described to enable lower minimum operating voltage (Vmin) for power reduction: [9]

**1. Negative Bit Line (NBL):** Uses a metal capacitor-coupled scheme (instead of MOS capacitor) to generate a negative bias on the bit line, avoiding overboost and area overhead. The metal capacitor length can be modulated with SRAM array bit line length. Measured: NBL improves Vmin by 300 mV.

**2. Lower Cell VDD (LCV):** Uses Charge Sharing (CS) with metal wire charge sharing capacitors on top of the array. Three LCV-VDD ratios are implemented: 6%, 12%, and 24%. Measured: 24% LCV improves Vmin independently by over 300 mV.

### Samsung's Adaptive Dual-Bitline (ADBL) and Adaptive Cell-Power (ACP) (ISSCC 2021)
Samsung's 3nm GAA SRAM test chip featured an Adaptive Dual-Bitline (ADBL) and Adaptive Cell-Power (ACP) assist circuit. Samsung exploited the ability to adjust nanosheet width to tune SRAM bitcell transistors (improving the PU:PG:PD ratio beyond the 1:1:1 limitation of finFETs). ADBL adds a switchable second bitline to reduce write resistance by 70%, while ACP uses two power switches at the array top and bottom to selectively increase write margin. The cumulative VMIN reduction was up to 230 mV. The test chip was a 6T-cell, 56 mm², 256-Mb design with at least ten copper metallization layers and a stack of three nanosheets. [34]

## 4. TSMC SRAM RESULTS (N5, N3, N2, A16)

### TSMC N5 (5nm) — ISSCC 2020
TSMC's 5nm process featured the world's smallest SRAM cell at 0.021 µm². The 5nm process uses more than 10 Extreme Ultra-Violet (EUV) mask patterning steps and High Mobility Channel (HMC) technology for higher performance. The 5nm process was quoted to have 1.84x logic density improvement compared to 1.35x SRAM density improvement. A Flying Bit Line (FBL) architecture was implemented for 5% area savings. High Mobility Channel (HMC) provides ~18% drive current gain. A high-speed SRAM array for L1 cache application achieved 4.1 GHz cycle time at 0.85V, demonstrated on a 135 Mb test chip. The technology was in risk production since April 2019 and was scheduled for full production in 1H2020. [9]

### TSMC N3 (3nm) — IEDM 2022 / ISSCC 2023
N3 is TSMC's last FinFET node. N3E (second-generation) is a more relaxed process than N3, presumably to improve yields and reduce costs by requiring fewer EUV layers. N3E has the same SRAM bit-cell size as the N5 family of nodes (0.021 µm²). The N3 processes use FINFLEX technology, which allows for variable numbers of fins to have different power/performance/area points in the same process. [33]

According to TechPowerUp (2023), N3's SRAM bit cells are nearly identical to those of N5. While TSMC initially claimed N3B offered 1.2x SRAM density improvement over N5, recent data indicates only about a 5% difference. SRAM scaling has completely decoupled from logic scaling, which continues to improve. [7][8]

The N3 node delivered 1.7x transistor scaling but only 1.0x SRAM scaling — the same 0.021 µm² bit cell size as N5. [6][7]

### TSMC N2 (2nm) — IEDM 2024 / ISSCC 2025
TSMC's N2 process with Gate-All-Around (GAA) nanosheet transistors achieves a high-density SRAM bit cell size of approximately 0.0175 µm², enabling SRAM density of approximately 38 Mb/mm². This is down from 0.021 µm² on N3 and N5 nodes. [7][15]

**Performance/Power:** N2 delivers 24-35% less power consumption or 15% more performance at the same voltage, and 1.15x higher transistor density compared to N3. [30] N2 includes N2 NanoFlex DTCO, enabling designers to develop short cells with minimum area and enhanced power efficiency, or tall cells optimized for maximum performance. [30] Geoffrey Yeap of TSMC stated: "N2 delivers a full node benefit from the previous 3nm node in offering a 15% speed gain or a 30% power reduction with a >1.15x chip density increase." [19]

**Transistor and interconnect improvements:** I/CV speed gains of ~70% (N-type) and ~110% (P-type) nanosheet transistors; ~20% clock boost and ~75% standby power reduction at 0.5V-0.6V low voltage ranges; 20-35 mV reduction in minimum operational voltage (Vmin) for SRAM; barrier-free tungsten wiring cutting vertical gate contact resistance by 55% (increasing ring oscillator frequency by about 6.2%); new EUV 1P1E process for M1 reducing standard cell capacitance by nearly 10%; super high-performance MiM capacitors providing ~200 fF/mm² for HPC applications. Six voltage threshold levels (6-Vt) spanning a 200 mV range. [30]

**ISSCC 2025 SRAM details:** TSMC described an SRAM design for N2 using nanosheet FET transistors. The 2nm-based SRAM has a capacity of 580 kb with 0.021 µm² cells (possibly referring to a different cell variant), achieving 38.1 Mb/mm² density — a 10% improvement over the previous node. TSMC's design doubles the maximum bitline loading from 256 to 512 cells per bitline due to improved on-to-off current ratios in nanosheet technology. [19]

**Yield:** TSMC reports >80% average yield and >90% peak yield on a 256 Mb SRAM array. Yields for 256 Mb SRAM devices had reached approximately 70% average (March 2024), up from 35% in April 2023, with some batches surpassing 80%. [7][32]

**3D stacking:** N2 supports 3D stacking with SoIC bond pitch of 4.5 µm. [30]

**Production:** N2 is scheduled for high-volume manufacturing (HVM) in the latter half of 2025. [7][30]

**TSMC at IEDM 2024:** TSMC presented 19 papers including the first demonstration of monolithic CFET inverter at 48nm gate pitch, next-generation TSMC-SoIC platform for HPC, and advancements in 2D materials, MRAM, and ferroelectric FET memory. [31]

### TSMC A16 (expected 2026-2027)
TSMC's A16 node will use direct backside connection. HPC customers want backside power delivery while mobile customers do not due to cost. [32]

## 5. SAMSUNG SRAM RESULTS (3nm GAA MBCFET, SF2, SF3)

### Samsung 3nm GAA MBCFET — Overview
Samsung's 3nm Gate-All-Around (GAA) process, branded as MBCFET (Multi-Bridge-Channel FET), uses horizontal nanosheets which are the most suitable post-FinFET architecture due to superior electrostatic performance, process integration, patterning, contact/routing, and designability. Samsung evaluated four GAA architectures — vertical nanowires, vertical nanosheets, horizontal nanowires, and horizontal nanosheets — and concluded that horizontal nanosheets (MBCFET) are the most suitable. Samsung began working on GAA technology with patents dating back to 2002, and demonstrated a fully working MBCFET SRAM at IEDM in 2018. [10][11]

Production began on June 30, 2022 — the industry's first implementation of MBCFET technology. [11][13]

**Performance claims vs 5nm:**
- First-generation 3nm: 45% reduced power consumption, 23% improved performance, 16% smaller surface area
- Second-generation 3nm: 50% reduced power consumption, 30% improved performance, 35% smaller area

Samsung's proprietary technology utilizes nanosheets with wider channels, which allow higher performance and greater energy efficiency compared to GAA technologies using nanowires with narrower channels. [13]

### Samsung 3nm GAA SRAM at ISSCC 2021
Samsung demonstrated a 256 Gb SRAM memory chip at ISSCC 2021, the first time the company manufactured a chip using MBCFET on the 3nm semiconductor node. The chip has an area of 56 mm² and uses 230 mV less power for writes compared to standard approaches due to power-saving techniques enabled by MBCFET transistors. The 3nm GAA process has 216.37 MTr/mm². [14]

### Samsung 3nm GAA SRAM Design Flexibility
Samsung's 3nm GAA MBCFET technology offers "Unrivaled SRAM Design Flexibility." The MBCFET allows adjustment of nanosheet width to tune SRAM bitcell transistors, improving the PU:PG:PD ratio beyond the 1:1:1 limitation of finFETs. [10][34]

### Samsung Process Technology Timeline
- **SF3** (3nm GAA): Started mass production in 2022. Uses gate-all-around architecture with advanced nanosheet channels for improved PPA. [35]
- **SF2** (2nm-class GAA): Started mass production in 2025. Second-generation MBCFET(GAA)-based node for mobile, HPC, AI, and automotive applications. [35]
- **SF4** (4nm FinFET): Started mass production in 2021. [35]
- **SF5** (5nm FinFET): Started mass production in 2021. [35]

### Samsung eMRAM Roadmap
Samsung's next-generation MRAM technology at IEDM 2022 achieved: enhanced MTJ stack process lowering Write Error Rate to single-digit ppb; 33% area scaling from 28nm to 14nm; 2.6x faster read cycle time; packaging size reduced to 30 mm² at 16 Mb; near unlimited endurance of >1E14 cycles at -25°C; best-in-class energy efficiency with active read and write power consumption of 14 mW and 27 mW respectively at 54 MB/s bandwidth. Samsung's eMRAM roadmap: 8nm by 2026, 5nm by 2027 (industry's first 5nm eMRAM). Compared to 14nm, 8nm eMRAM is expected to deliver 30% increase in density and 33% increase in speed. [38]

## 7. IMEC ROADMAP FOR SUB-2nm SRAM (FORKSHEET, CFET, DOUBLE-ROW CFET)

### IMEC Overall Roadmap
IMEC's chip scaling roadmap projects an introductory pace of 2 to 2.5 years per node, reaching from 7nm to 0.2nm (2 ångström) by 2036. The roadmap outlines: standard FinFET transistors lasting until 3nm, then transitioning to GAA nanosheet designs entering high-volume production in 2024, followed by forksheet designs at 2nm and A7 (0.7nm), Complementary FET (CFET) at A10 (1nm, 2028), and 2D monolayer materials (WS2, molybdenum) for the ångström age (0.2nm/2Å by 2036). [20][24]

### Forksheet Architecture
The forksheet device architecture was introduced by IMEC in 2017 to extend the GAA nanosheet-based logic roadmap to the A10 technology node, bridging the gap before CFET technology becomes viable. [21][22]

**Original inner wall forksheet (IEDM 2019):** Placed a dielectric wall between nMOS and pMOS devices, enabling tighter n-to-p spacing and cell area scaling down to 90nm cell height. TCAD simulations showed: 10% performance increase compared to nanosheet devices, 24% power reduction at constant speed, more than 20% cell area reduction, and the ability to reduce logic standard cell height to 4.3 tracks. For SRAM designs, simulations showed 30% combined area scaling and performance increase at 8nm p-n spacing. The process flow is similar to nanosheet devices with only limited additional steps. [22][23]

**First electrical demonstration (VLSI 2021):** IMEC demonstrated the first fully functional integrated forksheet FETs with short-channel control (SSSAT=66-68 mV/dec) comparable to GAA nanosheet devices down to 22nm gate length. Dual work function metal gates were integrated at 17nm spacing between n- and pFETs, highlighting the key benefit for advanced CMOS area scaling. The forksheet allows track height scaling from 5T to 4.3T while still offering a performance gain. The architecture is "the most promising device architecture to extend the logic and SRAM scaling roadmaps beyond 2nm leveraging the nanosheet integration in a non-disruptive way." [23]

**Outer wall forksheet (VLSI 2025):** IMEC introduced the "outer wall forksheet" as an improved evolution. The new design places the dielectric wall at the standard cell boundary (as a p-p or n-n wall), allowing it to be thicker (~15 nm) and shared with neighboring cells. Key improvements: (1) a wall-last integration approach using mainstream silicon dioxide, (2) relaxed wall width for process simplification, (3) easily connected n-p gates, (4) superior gate control via a Ω-gate structure (achieved by 5nm wall etch-back, boosting drive current by ~25%), and (5) the ability to achieve full channel strain through effective source/drain stressors, enabled by a Si spine that acts as a seed crystal template. Benchmarking showed a 22% area reduction for outer wall forksheet-based SRAM cells compared to A14 nanosheet designs. Ring oscillator simulations indicated the outer wall forksheet maintains frequency performance at the A10 node, provided full channel stress can be enabled. IMEC is now investigating compatibility of the outer wall design with CFET architecture. [21]

### CFET (Complementary FET)
**IMEC double-row CFET (IEDM 2024):** IMEC proposed a new CFET-based standard cell architecture featuring two rows of CFETs with a shared signal routing wall in between, called the "double-row CFET" architecture, designed for the A7 technology node. It allows standard cell heights to be reduced from 4 to 3.5T compared to conventional single-row CFETs. This translates to a 15% area reduction for SRAM cells, and more than 40% area shrinkage compared to A14 NSH (nanosheet) technology. The architecture simplifies middle-of-line (MOL) processing by eliminating the need for an extra high-aspect-ratio via to connect top and bottom devices. The design uses a base cell with one side optimized for power connections (VSS from backside) and the other side optimized for signal connections via a middle routing wall (MRW). Two base cells are mirrored to share the same MRW, with one shared MRW for every 3.7 FET being sufficient. IMEC validated the concept with a functional monolithic CFET demonstrator featuring direct backside contact using EUV patterning with <3nm overlay accuracy, fabricated in IMEC's 300mm cleanroom. [39]

**Scaling monolithic CFET (IMEC, February 2026):** A DTCO study on scaling mCFET across A7, A5, and A3 nodes identified required performance boosters:
- **A7 node**: Minimizing gate parasitic capacitance is essential; optionally implementing an M0 power rail gives additional benefit.
- **A5 node**: Requires introduction of an outer wall forksheet architecture with omega-shaped gate to enhance drive current and reduce parasitic capacitance.
- **A3 node**: Requires hybrid channel orientations (different orientations for n- and pMOS) in addition to the above boosters, enhancing drive current by up to 20%.

IMEC experimentally demonstrated the key enabling module — the embedded Middle Dielectric Isolation (eMDI) — which allows integrating channels with different orientations for top nMOS and bottom pMOS devices in a monolithic CFET process flow. The eMDI uses wafer fusion bonding to combine separately grown epitaxial stacks with different crystal orientations. Functional mCFET devices with (100) Si top nFETs and (110) Si bottom pFETs with direct backside contacts were demonstrated. Future work will extend to different channel materials (e.g., Ge for pMOS, Si for nMOS) and an embedded Bottom Dielectric Isolation (eBDI) module for improved backside connections and thermal management. [40]

### IBM NanoStack (0.7nm)
IBM announced a 0.7nm process node technology called "NanoStack" featuring a staggered sequential Complementary FET (CFET) design. Key specifications compared to IBM's own 2nm process: 50% logic area scaling, 50% performance at iso-power, 70% efficiency at iso-performance, 40% SRAM scaling, 666 million transistors per mm². IBM's staggered design differs from conventional CFET by offsetting NMOS and PMOS transistors from each other, enabling direct connectivity from either direction, allowing wider sheets and higher performance — up to 65% increase in effective gate width per 4-track cell compared to aligned sCFET designs. Dual crystal orientation is used: NMOS transistors use (001) silicon orientation while PMOS use (110), enabling independent optimization. The bonding process (called "gate merge") uses a sub-30nm bonding layer verified to within 1.5nm across a full 300mm wafer. IBM expects the technology to take approximately five years to reach market. [48]

## 8. SRAM SCALING CHALLENGES AND MARKET CONTEXT

### SRAM Scaling Has Stalled
SRAM scaling is a critical challenge for major chipmakers. Despite logic area decreasing by 40% from N5 to N2, 8-transistor high-current SRAM bitcells have only decreased in area by 18%. [6] TSMC's N3 node delivered 1.7x transistor scaling but only 1.0x SRAM scaling (same 0.021 µm² bit cell size as N5). [6][7][8]

Backside power delivery (PowerVia for Intel, BPDN for TSMC N2P in 2026) and nanosheet transistors are expected to help with SRAM scaling. Die-stacked SRAM (like AMD's 3D V-Cache) and emerging memory technologies (MRAM, FeRAM, RRAM, PCM) are also being explored. [7][8]

### Market Context
Modern SoCs contain about 90% memory transistors, with only 10-15% for logic. The semiconductor memory market was expected to surpass USD 730 billion by 2024. Microprocessors use SRAM cells in the cache memory design, and their performance is critical. [36]

### Emerging Memory Alternative
Stanford researchers published a paper in Nature on a new PCM material called GST467 (chalcogenide alloy superlattice) achieving nanosecond access times, low voltage operation, and a density of 0.016 µm² — about 23% more area-efficient than TSMC's N3 SRAM. However, SRAM memory as currently known, based on latches, is expected to remain in use for L1 and L2 cache for at least the next couple of decades. [6]
